criteria.text: A runtime split point can produce two non-overlapping ViewMut values without user-written unsafe code.
A checked multi-index or multi-key API returns distinct mutable views or a clear overlap error.
Mutable iteration lends one exclusive element view at a time and cannot store an invalid alias.
JIT, dev, and AOT share bounds, duplicate, overlap, and invalidation behavior.
Differential tests cover Rust split_at_mut and get_disjoint_mut class programs.

cards.title: Structured concurrency: scoped borrowed task captures
cards.body: Rust scoped threads can borrow stack data because the scope joins every child. Jet taskgroup also joins children, but it applies detached-task capture rules. It rejects read views and every mutable capture with E1102 or E1101.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Close field-audit G3 under D-TASKBORROW1=A: taskgroup children may borrow reads freely and borrow writes only when sema proves disjoint places. Keep `tasks.spawn` / detach ownership-only.

## Law (ratified)
- Keep `g.task` spelling; no second borrowed-task form.
- Loans start before launch and end after join or group cleanup.
- Cancellation, panic, return, and error paths join before owner invalidation.
- Detached tasks, channels, and `tasks.spawn` still reject borrowed captures (E1101/E1102).

## Scope
In: taskgroup capture checking; scheduler/loan lifetime across group edges; nested groups; stress tests.
Out: provenance unions except as needed for borrowed views (#1197); disjoint APIs (#1198) as the proof source for write splits; pin/Cell/Shared.

## Owned paths
- `crates/jet-sema` task/lambda capture paths (`E1101`/`E1102` context flags)
- taskgroup lowering / runtime join and cancellation
- `tests/concurrency_boundaries.rs` + ownership interaction tests
- examples showing banded parallel filters over one image
- docs/spec concurrency + syntax-decisions notes

## Steps
1. Distinguish taskgroup child capture from `tasks.spawn` capture in sema.
2. Admit shared read borrows of stack/owner data tied to group scope.
3. Admit mutable borrows only with compile-time disjoint places (reuse #1198 proof where ranges are dynamic only if already available; otherwise constant/field disjoint first).
4. Prove every exceptional exit joins before owner move/drop.
5. Keep detach/channel/`tasks.spawn` rejection identical to today.
6. Nested group + cancellation stress; independent review.

## Acceptance / proof
Criteria 1–5. Proof: concurrency_boundaries + new scoped-borrow cases; no regression on detached-task rejects.

## Blockers
blockedBy: none. D-TASKBORROW1 ratified (=A). Coordinate with #1198 for dynamic disjoint write bands.

log.text: prep: thorough plan under ratified ballot; advancing planning → ready

criteria.text: A taskgroup child can read borrowed stack data that outlives the group.
Several children can borrow disjoint mutable places with no data race.
Group exit, cancellation, panic, return, and error paths join children before any borrowed owner can move or drop.
Detached tasks, channels, and tasks.spawn still reject borrowed captures.
Native scheduler stress and sema tests cover nested groups, cancellation, and overlapping writes.

cards.title: Expert memory parity: address-stable values and safe pin contracts
cards.body: Rust Pin lets libraries expose safe interfaces for self-referential and intrusive values. Jet has raw pointers, arenas, and Fixed storage, but no reusable safe contract that prevents a live address-sensitive value from moving. Representation workarounds do not give the same compositional guarantee.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Close field-audit G4 under D-PIN1=A: `mem.pin(&place) -> Pin<T>` as a tracked write view that blocks move/replace while live.

## Law (ratified)
- Pin reuses the owner/provenance graph; no second memory model.
- Structural field projection is declared by the type implementation.
- Dropping the final pin ends the no-move loan.
- Unsafe construction stays local; safe callers use `Pin<T>` APIs.
- Support stack, Fixed, arena, and owned heap places.

## Scope
In: `Pin<T>` type, `mem.pin`, move/replace rejection, projection rules, cleanup/cancel/panic paths, self-referential + intrusive examples.
Out: Pool/Shared as substitutes; Cell (#1201); Shared guards (#1202).

## Owned paths
- foundation/core `mem` surface + Syntax.rs if `Pin` is user-typeable
- sema move/replace/projection checks for pinned places
- tests (`tests/arena.rs`, `tests/resource_close.rs`, new pin tests)
- examples: zero-allocation queue node / intrusive list
- docs/spec memory + syntax-decisions

## Steps
1. Add `Pin<T>` as expert tracked view; `mem.pin(&place)` entry point.
2. While any pin is live: reject move, replace, and resize of the pinned storage.
3. Declare structural pin projection on implementing types; reject undeclared projections.
4. Ensure drop/cancel/panic/owner destruction preserve the contract.
5. Example: audited unsafe constructor + safe `Pin` use at call sites.
6. No-allocation / caller-storage parity cases where Rust Pin can; independent review.

## Acceptance / proof
Criteria 1–5. Proof: focused pin tests + examples; verify skill syntax chores if new names land.

## Owner gates
`Pin` / `mem.pin` names were chosen by D-PIN1=A. If additional user-typeable keywords beyond that ruling appear, raise a syntax ballot before shipping. Otherwise blockedBy: none.

log.text: All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.
prep correction: raised D-PIN2 for pin field-projection declaration left open by D-PIN1
prep: thorough plan under ratified ballot; advancing planning → ready

criteria.text: Safe code cannot move or replace a value after its address-sensitive state starts.
A library can use a local #Unsafe block and expose a safe pinned API without unsafe call sites.
Pinned field projection preserves declared structural pin rules.
Cleanup, cancellation, panic, and owner destruction preserve the address-stability contract.
Self-referential state and an intrusive collection have no-allocation or caller-storage examples where Rust can do the same.

cards.title: Memory polish: local interior mutability and guard APIs
cards.body: Jet can place mutable state in Shared<T>, but Shared always uses a copyable synchronized handle. Rust Cell and RefCell cover local mutation, runtime borrow guards, and mapped guards without cross-thread overhead.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Ship D-LOCALCELL1=A: one non-sendable `Cell<T>` family for local interior mutability, with value ops and runtime-checked guards.

## Law (ratified)
- Keep `Shared<T>` as the cross-task synchronized default.
- One local `Cell<T>`: get/set/replace/init plus read/edit/guard methods.
- Runtime borrow state: many readers or one writer; guards carry view provenance.
- Sema rejects task, channel, Shared, and parallel crossings of `Cell`.

## Scope
In: `Cell<T>` type and methods; guard map/split; diagnostics; local cache examples.
Out: Shared guards/Condition (#1202); pin (#1200); second BorrowCell type.

## Owned paths
- corelib `Cell` implementation + sema sendability / crossing checks
- `tests/ownership.rs`, `tests/concurrency_boundaries.rs`
- example: lazy line-index cache on a local syntax tree
- docs/reference/core-library.md + spec notes

## Steps
1. Add `Cell<T>.new` and value methods (`get`/`set`/`replace`/`get_or_set` as needed).
2. Add `read`/`edit` closures and `guard_read`/`guard_edit` with runtime conflict checks.
3. Guard mapping/splitting preserves the dynamic loan; release on all exits.
4. Sema: reject Cell across tasks/channels/Shared/parallel.
5. Teach value access vs guard access clearly in docs.
6. Independent review.

## Acceptance / proof
Criteria 1–4. Proof: ownership + concurrency reject tests; local-cache example golden.

## Blockers
blockedBy: none. D-LOCALCELL1 ratified (=A). Syntax chores if `Cell` needs Syntax.rs entry.

log.text: prep: thorough plan under ratified ballot; advancing planning → ready

criteria.text: A read receiver can update private local state without Arc or operating-system lock overhead.
Runtime read and write guards enforce many readers or one writer and release on every exit path.
Guard mapping and splitting preserve the original dynamic loan.
Cross-task use is rejected unless the value uses Shared<T> or another synchronized type.

cards.title: Memory polish: Shared guards and wait protocols
cards.body: Shared<T> limits each lock to one read or edit closure. Rust guards can span several calls, map to a field, split into disjoint parts, and wait on a condition while atomically releasing the lock. Jet can rewrite many cases, but the result is less direct.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Ship D-SHAREDGUARD1=A: expert `guard_read` / `guard_edit` and `Condition` on `Shared<T>`, keeping beginner `read`/`edit` closures unchanged.

## Law (ratified)
- Short closures remain the default.
- Guards are owned lock tokens with safe cleanup on return/error/panic/cancel.
- Wait atomically registers, releases, parks, reacquires, and rechecks the predicate.
- Cancellation unregisters before guard release.
- Lock-order receipts cover nested guards; dossier/audit integration where grant graph already exists.

## Scope
In: Shared guard APIs, Condition, map/split, wait protocols, diagnostics for long lock scopes.
Out: Mutex/RwLock/Condvar family; changing beginner Shared surface; Cell (#1201) except parallel teaching.

## Owned paths
- `Shared` corelib + runtime wait/park
- sema cleanup tracking for guards
- `tests/ownership.rs`, `tests/concurrency_boundaries.rs`
- example: bounded work queue with full/empty wait
- docs + lock-order audit output

## Steps
1. Add `guard_read` / `guard_edit` without changing `read`/`edit`.
2. Map/split guards preserve lock + provenance.
3. Add `Condition` with `wait` / `notify_one` / `notify_all` semantics as ratified.
4. Prove no lost wakeups; cancel/panic/return always release and unregister.
5. Lock-order / nested-guard audit facts; diagnostics for long scopes.
6. Independent review.

## Acceptance / proof
Criteria 1–5. Proof: concurrency stress for wait; cancellation races; beginner API unchanged snapshot/tests.

## Blockers
blockedBy: none. D-SHAREDGUARD1 ratified (=A).

log.text: All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.
prep correction: raised D-SHAREDGUARD2 for SharedGuard/Condition names left open by D-SHAREDGUARD1
prep: thorough plan under ratified ballot; advancing planning → ready

criteria.text: Experts can hold a Shared read or write guard across several helper calls when required.
Mapped and split guards preserve the original lock and view provenance.
A wait operation atomically releases and reacquires the write guard without lost wakeups.
Cancellation, panic, return, and error propagation always release guards and unregister waiters.
The beginner Shared.read and Shared.edit closure surface stays unchanged.

Implementer: const retired (E0146), Persist bare bind landed. Scoped proof green. Awaiting independent criteria verify.
Owner correction: Persist host is bare binding (`#Persist name := …`), not `#Persist comptime`. Redirected implementer.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-1231-2): #Persist is a marker on a bare module binding (name :: / name :=), not on comptime. Example: `#Persist counter := 0`. Keyword const remains retired in favor of comptime for former const cases; Persist does not use the comptime keyword form.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-1231-1): User-facing `const` is retired. The only module immutable binding keyword is `comptime` (S57). `#Persist` is a marker on a binding that preserves that binding across jet-dev reloads; it is not tied to a `const` keyword. `#Static`/`#Inline` attach to `comptime` bindings. Writing `const` gets a teaching diagnostic pointing at `comptime`.

cards.title: Cut pasted lines: fenced-name expansion
cards.body:
Sixteen of the twenty-nine body lines in `examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet` are the same spawn and the same wait, eight times each, differing only by handle name. Owner wants one written line to stand for several: `<: t1, … t8 :> :: tasks.spawn(…)` expands to eight bindings, `<: t1, … t8 :>.wait()` to eight waits.

This is statement expansion, not mapping — nothing is collected and no list type appears. S75 `f.[a, b, c]` and `taskgroup` are untouched.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Implement both ratified rulings on this card:
- D-FANOUT3=C: ship `tasks.join_all(handles)` on `core.tasks`.
- D-EACH1=C: fenced-name expansion plus numbered names from a range (`<: t1..t8 :>`).

Then rewrite `examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet` to stop pasting eight spawn/wait lines.

## Law (ratified)
### join_all
- `tasks.join_all([Task<T>]) => [T]`: wait in list order; consume each handle.
- Docs state when to use it vs `g.all` inside a taskgroup.
- Does not replace taskgroups for structured ownership.

### fenced names (D-EACH1=C)
- `<: … :>` expands a statement once per entry; lock-step when multiple fences appear.
- Range form `<: t1..t8 :>` in a binding target generates `t1`…`t8`.
- Not a list value; not S75 fan-out; not destructuring.
- Lexer: `<:` / `:>` longest-match digraphs; `:>` in `suppresses_terminator`; neither in `ends_statement`.
- Allowed in binding targets and expression statements; not in if/loop/switch headers or item decls in this pass.
- Diagnostics (I4): empty fence; duplicate name; disagreeing fence counts; rejected position; double-bind; each with UI snapshot.
- Spans: every expanded copy points at original line + entry.
- Formatter emission + fmt stability; wrapping rule for wide fences.
- Tooling: jump-to-definition / search must understand generated range names.

## Scope
In: lexer/parser expansion, sema, fmt, diagnostics+snapshots, `join_all`, example rewrite, Syntax.rs + syntax-decisions + grammar regen.
Out: changing S75; adding `g.borrow`; reopening D-FANOUT3 to drop join_all.

## Owned paths
- `crates/jet-foundation` Syntax + lexer/terminator tables
- parser expansion + span mapping
- `core.tasks` `join_all`
- formatter + grammar packages
- `examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet`
- dedicated fence + join_all examples (I5)
- diagnostic registry + UI snapshots
- `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md`

## Steps
1. Syntax.rs entries + syntax-decisions log for fence digraphs, range form, and `join_all` library surface as required by verify skill.
2. Lexer digraphs + terminator behavior; parser expansion with lock-step and range binding; per-copy spans.
3. Implement `tasks.join_all`; tests for order, consumption, L1101 interaction.
4. Diagnostics + UI snapshots for every fence error class.
5. Formatter + grammar regen + snapshot bless.
6. Rewrite shared_transact: prefer either range fences + expanded waits, or list + `join_all` (both legal; pick the form that best teaches the demo’s `#Transact` point without eight pasted lines). Add a second small example if one form would otherwise go unshown.
7. Verify skill closeout; independent review.

## Acceptance / proof
Existing syntax criteria plus behavioral proof: shared_transact golden unchanged in output; fence and join_all tests green; grammars regenerated.

## Blockers
blockedBy: none. D-EACH1 and D-FANOUT3 both ratified (=C).

cards.title: I2 violation: Debug interpolation on core IOError breaks generated Rust
cards.body:
Writing `"{e#Debug}"` where `e` is a core `IOError` passes sema, then emits Rust that calls `jet_debug` on a type that does not implement it. rustc rejects the generated code.

This breaks invariant I2: rustc rejection of generated code is an internal compiler error, never something a user can reach from ordinary Jet source. Sema must own this check.

Found while building card #771 slice 1; not caused by it.
cards.plan: Implement S55/D-DISPLAYDBG1 capability parity: add the missing IOError JetDebug bridge, add a separate same-source AOT/default-dev exact-output regression, and canonicalize the TIR evaluator's IOError/IOContext Debug rendering without changing generic user Debug. Preserve the broad IOError fixture, migrating only its retired value-if spellings. blockedBy: none.

Authority check resolved the card choice without a ballot: S55 auto-derives Debug for qualifying core values. IOError derives Rust Debug and sema correctly admits it; codegen/runtime omitted its JetDebug bridge. Fix capability parity, not rejection.

Scope is wider than first recorded. Confirmed independently while building #1253: '{e#Debug}' on an IOError does not only break the dev lens. It ICEs under AOT as well, with 'no method jet_debug found for enum IOError'. So both lenses reject generated code from ordinary Jet source, which is an I2 violation on the shipped path, not a JIT-only defect.

cards.title: JIT: zero-arg ProcessSpec builders missing from the host table
cards.body:
Default `jet run` deopts to the interpreter for any zero-argument ProcessSpec builder, because the JIT host table has no entry for `env_clear`, `detached`, or `terminal`. The interpreter then raises E0956 on `process.cmd`, so the program fails under `jet run` while it works under `jet build`.

Repro on untouched code: `process.cmd(["echo", "x"]).detached().run()`.

This is a JIT/AOT lens gap of the kind D-LENS-RUN1 forbids: a program must not succeed under AOT and fail under default `jet run`. Found while building card #771 slice 1.

Prove the repro passes under default jet run and under jet build with identical output, and keep the shrink-only gap ratchet from growing. blockedBy: none.

cards.title: Tier-0 deopt target runs only a pure subset, so jet run fails where jet build succeeds
cards.body:
D-LENS-RUN2=A says missing tier-1 coverage deopts per function to the canonical tier-0 interpreter with identical observable behavior. It does not hold. The tier-0 target is the comptime evaluator, which by its own diagnostic evaluates only a pure subset of Jet. Any construct Cranelift cannot compile and comptime does not implement fails under default jet run while jet build succeeds.

Two live repros, both exit 0 under jet build and exit 1 under jet run:

examples/features/crypto/crypto_suite.jet — trace shows 'run tier0 interp (body stmt 6: Let[0] init=OtherExpr)', then E0956 'jet.crypto.sha512_bytes() at comptime can't run at compile time yet'.

examples/features/types/generic_constructor_inference.jet — E0956 'static Box.new can't run at compile time yet'. AOT prints '7 jet 2 9'.

The diagnostic text is also wrong for this path. A user who typed jet run is told the work cannot happen at compile time, and is advised to compute the value at runtime, which is what they asked for.

Both examples reached the compile attempt only after frontend fixes landed on 2026-07-28, so the defect was previously masked rather than introduced.
cards.plan: Decide the correct law first: either the tier-0 deopt target must cover every executable construct, or deopt must route to a full runtime interpreter rather than the comptime evaluator. Then close the gap so a program that succeeds under jet build succeeds under default jet run with byte-identical output. Separate the user-facing diagnostic fix: E0956 must not tell a jet run user that their work cannot happen at compile time. blockedBy: none.

cards.title: JIT: ProcessSpec env, env_remove and cwd missing or silently ignored
cards.body:
The JIT host table has no working entry for the argument-taking ProcessSpec builders. `env` and `env_remove` are absent. `jet_jit_process_spec_cwd` exists but silently ignores its argument.

The silent case is the worse one. A program that sets a working directory under `jet run` runs in the wrong directory and reports no error, so the failure surfaces later as a missing file or a wrong result. A missing entry at least fails loudly.

Same lens-gap class as #1253, which fixed the zero-argument builders `env_clear`, `detached` and `terminal`. These need real environment and path storage on JitProcessSpec, so they did not fit that card.

Found while building #1253.
cards.plan: Follow the pattern proved by c485d5f17 and 534a49fbd: a ProcessSpec method needs an entry in the safety.rs residency list and in the lower_ctx.rs dispatch, plus a host shim that reuses the existing launch behavior. Store the environment edits and the working directory on JitProcessSpec and apply them at launch exactly as jet_process_command does. Reuse the existing runtime; never a second copy. Prove a program that sets cwd and edits the environment gives byte-identical stdout, stderr and exit under jet run and jet run --release, and add a test that fails if either table entry is removed. Do not grow tests/jit_gaps.txt. blockedBy: none.

cards.title: Codegen panics during jet check on a sema-rejected program
cards.body:
`jet check` on `ui_fixed_dynamic_size.E0103.jet` reaches `unreachable!()` at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/method_calls.rs:944 and panics.

Sema reports E0103 correctly, so the program is already rejected. A lowering path still runs afterwards and crashes on it. The user sees a compiler panic instead of the diagnostic that sema already produced.

The underlying question is ordering: why does lowering run at all on a program sema has rejected? That is a design call, not a guess, which is why the worker who found it did not patch it.

Present since b30168788 (2026-07-17), which added the fixture. Found while building #1210.
cards.plan: Establish the correct ordering law first: lowering must not run on a program sema rejected. Fix the ordering rather than adding a guard at the panic site, unless the ordering is deliberate and the panic site is genuinely reachable for a valid reason. Prove it with the existing fixture, and add the case to the checking tests so a rejected program can never reach lowering again. blockedBy: none.

The defect is specific to `jet fmt <dir>`: directory formatting takes a different file-walk path that does not apply the payload-file filter and tries to format package manifests as Jet source.

decisions.title: Build a jetdoc generator from the compiler semantic graph?
decisions.gist: Jet has doc comments (`///`, S49) and a live doctest mechanism (D-TEST4, implemented). The open question is whether to build `jet doc` — a tool that generates browsable API docs from parsed/type-resolved compiler output. Two sub-questions are entangled: (a) when does it ship relative to the sema index (D-SEMINDEX1/c96), and (b) what structured doc comment syntax does S49 need to add before generated docs are useful beyond a flat text dump? Doctests are already solved; this decision is about the API documentation generation surface only.
decisions.explainer: A semantic-graph doc generator reads the sema index (types, signatures, trait impls, doc comments) and emits HTML/Markdown API docs with tested examples. It is an E3 testing/docs ergonomics exit criterion. It depends on stable compiler seams (the `jet-sema` seam crate and the semantic index API card). Doctests close the loop: example code in `/// ` blocks is extracted and run as tests. Without this, doc quality decays because examples are untested. This card does not cover the LSP or IDE dossier views (those are D-DOSSIER1).
decisions.story: I publish a Jet library. I want `jet doc` to generate browsable API docs from my doc comments the same way `cargo doc` does — and I want any `/// ` example to fail CI if it stops compiling, not just silently rot.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) The inWild and Option A code use a pre-D-TEST4 doctest format; D-TEST4 is ratified — correct format is ```jet blocks with // => trailing comments. (2) Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4/c51; the open question is API doc generation only. (3) S49 says "plain text v1" — no structured doc section syntax is ratified; jetdoc built on this baseline can only emit a flat text dump. Either ratify S49 sections first or scope jetdoc explicitly to flat text. (4) Options A and C are functionally equivalent in sequencing (both gate on c96); the real decision is whether jetdoc is an E3 exit criterion.

options.name: Phase 1 AST doc now; Phase 2 sema-indexed when D-SEMINDEX1 lands (recommended)
options.detail: Phase 1 (Epoch 3, unblocked): a `jet doc` subcommand reads parsed public items and their raw `///` comments from the AST alone. Emits flat HTML per module: public signatures + doc text. No sema index required. Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4 — this adds browsable API surface only. Phase 2 (when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable): upgrade to cross-linked, type-resolved, trait-impl-inclusive docs. Prerequisite before either phase: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax (currently "plain text v1") so Phase 1 emits structured sections instead of a raw text dump. Raise that as a follow-on ballot.
options.code:
$ jet doc
Building docs for mylib v0.1.0
  Phase 1 (AST): public symbols + raw doc comments
Wrote: docs/api/index.html
  note: type links and trait impls added in Phase 2 (when sema index lands)

$ jet test --doctests   # already live via D-TEST4
running 3 doctests
test mylib::add ... ok

options.name: Defer `jet doc` to Epoch 6 (after sema index + S49 sections)
options.detail: Do not build jetdoc until D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable and S49 structured sections are ratified. Avoids rebuilding Phase 1 when Phase 2 is ready. Doctests (D-TEST4) keep examples honest in the interim. Authors maintain hand-written Markdown. Viable internally but not for a public registry where doc quality is an ecosystem contract.

options.name: Hand-written docs only
options.detail: No generated docs tool. Doctests still run (D-TEST4). No browsable API surface. Keeps toolchain surface smaller. Only viable for small internal libraries; not scalable as the registry grows.
options.code:
// No jet doc. Docs are maintained manually in docs/.
// Examples compiled only when author writes a #Test block by hand.

comparisons.note: Swift DocC builds docs from typed declarations and links symbols across articles and API pages.
comparisons.code: /// Doc comment attached to a symbol

comparisons.note: rustdoc reads HIR/MIR and emits structured HTML. Doc tests (```` ``` ```` blocks in `///` comments) are compiled and run by `cargo test --doc`. This is the gold-standard baseline for jetdoc to match.
DocC compiles doc comments into a structured catalog; examples are verified at build time. Goes further than rustdoc with tutorials and interactive playgrounds.

decisions.recommendation: Phase 1 AST-level `jet doc` now (unblocked); Phase 2 sema-indexed upgrade when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 lands (Option A). Prerequisite: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax before either phase ships.

decisions.title: Should Jet define a generic database driver interface with parameterized-queries-only enforcement?
decisions.gist: Jet already has SQLite support in core.db (c50). The question is whether to define a generic Driver trait that any database backend implements, with the interface enforcing parameterized queries only — making string-concatenated SQL structurally impossible. No generic driver interface exists today; this is the next step above the SQLite-specific API.
decisions.explainer: A Driver trait with a parameterized-only API eliminates SQL injection by construction — you cannot build a raw SQL string and execute it through the driver interface. This is a strong safety guarantee consistent with I1 (safe by default). The SQLite implementation (c50) becomes the first impl of Driver; Postgres, MySQL, and others would follow as stdlib or community packages. The interface design needs to cover: connection lifecycle, transactions (#Transact?), async vs sync, and error types. None of those require new syntax — they use existing Jet markers and the T ? E error type. The main risk is locking in a Driver shape before we know what async looks like in Jet; a sync-only v1 Driver is safe to ship now.
decisions.story: I want to write database code that works with SQLite in tests and Postgres in production, and I want the compiler to make it impossible to accidentally run string-interpolated SQL.

options.name: Define Driver trait + parameterized-only API; SQLite as first impl
options.detail: Specify a Driver trait with query(sql: &str, params: []Param) -> Result<Rows, DbError> and no raw-execute surface. SQLite (c50) is refactored to implement it. Safe by construction against SQL injection. Sync-only for now; async variant deferred until Jet's async story is settled.

options.name: Per-database APIs only; no generic Driver trait
options.detail: Keep core.db as the SQLite-specific API. Each new database gets its own module with its own API. No shared interface. Simpler short-term; loses the cross-backend portability and the injection guarantee at the interface level.

options.name: Defer — design after async story is settled
options.detail: The right Driver shape depends on whether queries are sync or async. Wait until Jet's async/concurrency model is ratified, then design Driver once with the right shape. Risk: blocks any new database backends in the meantime.

comparisons.note: Generic DB interface with parameterized queries via ? placeholders. Drivers register themselves. No string-building API at the interface level — close to what Jet is proposing.
Macro-verified parameterized queries checked against a live DB at compile time. Stronger than Go but requires a live DB in CI — Jet's approach is lighter.

decisions.title: Next-generation FFI: what one structure makes every foreign language near-trivial to wrap, replace in situ, and tap immediately?
decisions.gist: Pick the architecture every foreign language shares: per-language namespaces with pluggable binders, uniform extern blocks, typed projection importers, or runtime-broker sidecars.
decisions.explainer: Jet already speaks two foreign languages, each with its own shape: Rust via extern rust "crate@version" { … } (S50) and C via generated bindings mounted at c.<lib> with a user overlay (S59). JS is sequenced next, Swift later (D-JSWIFTFFI1). The owner's bar: using a library from almost any language should feel almost as easy as using a Jet package — every ecosystem's work immediately usable, and any foreign dependency replaceable later by a native Jet implementation without touching call sites (in-situ replacement). This ballot picks the one structure all languages share. How deep each language's binding goes (shallow declaration binding, full typed projection, or a runtime broker) is a per-language follow-up ballot on top of the winning frame — the frame is what must never vary.
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool in Jet. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package; the best plotting library is on npm; a checksum routine she needs ships as a C header. She wants all three working this afternoon, each behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and when a native Jet plotting package appears next year, she wants to swap it in by changing one dependency line, not rewriting call sites.
decisions.inWild:
use py.h5instrument as h5     // Python package, typed surface
use js.plotly as plot          // npm package (D-NPMTYPE1 stubs)
use "xxhash.h" as xx           // C header, script tier (S59)

fn main() #(Fs, Proc) {
    run := h5.read("run-0142.h5")
    print(xx.hash64(run.raw))
    plot.line(run.times, run.values)
}
decisions.detail: A, C, and D compose rather than exclude: A is the surface law (namespaces, three tiers, overlay, in-situ shadowing, lockfile provenance); C and D are per-language binder strategies BEHIND that surface — projection importers for static languages (C, Swift, Rust), a broker likely right for Python/JS dynamic tails, shallow declaration binding where that's enough. Ratifying A means: the surface ships now; follow-up ballots (D-FFI-PY1, D-FFI-JS1 folding in D-NPMTYPE1, D-FFI-SWIFT1 honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1 sequencing) pick each language's strategy on the common frame. Existing ratifications are preserved, not reopened: S59 is already the C instance of A; S50's extern rust block becomes the rust binder's declaration format inside rust.*; D-DEP1's vendoring/hash-pinning law extends to every language's refs. I8: one FFI structure for all languages is the point — shipping B alongside A would be two spellings for one job. I1/I2 hold in every option: user code is safe unless #Unsafe; no foreign toolchain's errors ever reach the user unlaundered — binder diagnostics are Jet diagnostics with codes and snapshots (I4). Recommendation rationale: A is the only option that is uniform (one structure to learn), immediate (a new language needs only a binder, at whatever depth exists first), deep where it counts (projection strategy per language later), and structurally in-situ-replaceable — rank on beginner experience, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Language namespaces + pluggable binders (recommended)
options.detail: Generalize S59's proven C structure into the law for every language. Each foreign world mounts as a namespace <lang>.<lib> with the same three tiers everywhere: script tier (use "xxhash.h" as xx — bind on first compile), project tier (use py.h5instrument as h5 with the dep pinned in pkg.jet), overlay tier (#Extern module py.h5instrument { … } to refine generated types; overlay wins). `jet bind <lang>` is a per-language binder producing inspectable, committable bindings in .jet/bindings/<lang>/<lib>.jet. Safety: generated bindings are safe wrappers by construction (marshaling internals compiler-vetted like std internals — I1); calling a foreign symbol outside a binding requires #Unsafe("reason"). In-situ replacement is structural: any <lang>.<lib> can be shadowed by a Jet package exporting the same surface — call sites never change. Per-language depth (projection vs broker vs shallow) is chosen behind this surface, one follow-up ballot per language.

options.name: Uniform extern blocks (generalize S50)
options.detail: Every language uses S50's declaration-first shape: extern <lang> "ref@version" { fn … = "path" }. Maximal explicitness — every crossing is written in the file — and one grammar for all languages. The cost is the wall: wrapping a real library means hundreds of declaration lines per library (generated or not, they live in your project), there is no namespace to shadow so in-situ replacement means hand-built wrapper modules, and 'almost trivial' is exactly what it isn't.

options.name: Typed projection importers only
options.detail: Every language gets a full compiler importer (Swift-Clang-importer style): use py.h5instrument elaborates the package's surface — from type stubs and introspection — directly into checked Jet types with effects and ownership mapped; overlays refine (raw pointer -> checked handle). The deepest 'feels native' ceiling, and the right end-state for static languages. As the only mechanism, it makes every new language wait for a full importer before ANY access exists — the opposite of tapping ecosystems immediately.

options.name: Runtime broker sidecars only
options.detail: Foreign runtimes run as supervised sidecar processes with a typed message boundary; py.* calls marshal to a Python worker (Mojo's play). Any language with a runtime works day one and effects are honest (#(Proc) on every call) — but values are serialized at every crossing (no zero-copy, no shared memory), C headers and Rust crates don't fit the model at all, and production binaries grow a process tree. Right as a per-language strategy for dynamic tails; wrong as the only structure.

comparisons.note: @cImport makes C trivial — but only C. The lesson: binder-in-the-compiler is magic; the miss: no structure for a second language.
Clang importer: full typed projection of C/ObjC — foreign APIs feel native. The depth ceiling to aim per-language binders at.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library, arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via a runtime broker — instant ecosystem reach, marshaled boundary. The play for dynamic-language tails.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: P/Invoke plus WinRT projections: two tiers under one runtime — proof that shallow decls and deep projections coexist behind one surface.
Polyglot: many languages, one VM — reach bought with total runtime lock-in; the anti-goal for an AOT language.

decisions.title: Python binder depth: how deep does `use py.<lib>` reach into CPython?
decisions.gist: The D-FFI-UNIFY1 frame is law; this picks Python's binder strategy behind it. Python's ecosystem is C-extension-heavy (numpy, torch), so the binder must reach real CPython. Choose the host model: crash-isolated sidecar broker, in-process libpython embed, Python-on-WASM, or a shallow script shim.
decisions.explainer: The owner's bar (card #180) is tapping any ecosystem immediately. Python is the biggest prize and the hardest: its value lives in native C-extension packages, so a pure reimplementation or a WASM-only path forfeits most of the ecosystem. Two real hosts remain: an in-process libpython embed (zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, but a buggy native extension can take the whole process down and the GIL must be managed) and a supervised sidecar worker (a crashing extension dies with the worker, honest #(Proc)-style effect, but values marshal across a process boundary — no zero-copy of large tensors). Under I1, crash containment argues for the broker as the safe default; the embed is the expert performance tier for hot numeric paths, mirroring how D-PLUGIN1 made the WASM sandbox the default and native the opt-in. One `use py.X` surface either way; the host tier never moves call sites. Adds a `#(Py)` effect to the D-EFF4 set (owner-visible).
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package, and numpy is her numeric stack. She wants both working this afternoon behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and she does not want a segfault in someone's C extension to take down her whole program.
decisions.detail: All options honor D-FFI-UNIFY1: `<lang>.<lib>` namespace, three tiers, `jet bind py` emitting inspectable `.jet/bindings/py/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers by construction, `#Unsafe` only to reach a raw symbol outside a binding. The choice is only the host/depth. Marshalling law (all options): scalars<->Int/Float/Bool, str<->String, bytes/buffer-protocol arrays<->[T] or zero-copy View<T> in embed / copied in broker, dict<->struct or Map, list/tuple<->[T], None<->optional, Python exception->Jet Result + E-code (never a raw traceback). Async: asyncio coroutine -> Jet async task. Distribution: PyPI ref pinned in pkg.jet, wheel fetched + vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); the CPython interpreter/libpython is a native runtime dep provisioned by jetpack/nixpkgs (ballot D-DEP-PY1). I1/I2/I4 hold in every option.

options.name: Sidecar-broker default + opt-in embed tier (recommended)
options.detail: The default host is a supervised CPython worker process (reuse the jetpack `services` supervision seam) with a typed message boundary — a crashing native extension takes down the worker, not your program, and the compiler restarts it. `#(Py)` effect on every call. An opt-in `py@embed` (dep flag or `#Embed` marker on the import) switches to in-process libpython for zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, for hot numeric paths. One `use py.X` surface; the tier is a distribution/perf choice, never a call-site change. Mirrors D-PLUGIN1's sandbox-default / native-opt-in shape.

options.name: Sidecar broker only
options.detail: Every py.* call marshals to a supervised worker; no in-process path ever. Maximum crash isolation and the simplest safety story; large arrays always copy across the process boundary, so a tensor-heavy inner loop pays a serialization cost with no escape hatch.

options.name: In-process libpython embed only
options.detail: Every py.* call runs in-process against linked libpython, GIL-scoped, zero-copy on buffer-protocol types. Fastest and simplest to reason about for numeric code; a faulty native extension segfaults the host process (weaker isolation), which sits uneasily with I1's crash-containment posture as an unconditional default.

options.name: Python-on-WASM sandbox
options.detail: Run CPython compiled to WASM (Pyodide/CPython-wasi) on the already-approved wasmtime runtime. Fully sandboxed and I1-clean by construction, and reuses the #5 runtime — but the C-extension long tail (arbitrary wheels, native torch) does not run under it, so it forfeits the exact packages that make Python worth calling. Right as a niche isolation tier, wrong as the reach story.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p        // sandboxed; native wheels unavailable

options.name: Subprocess script shim (shallow)
options.detail: `jet bind py` emits thin declarations that shell out to `python -c`/script invocations per call. Trivial to stand up; no persistent interpreter, so state does not carry between calls, everything re-imports each time, and rich values degrade to stringly-typed exchange. Below the frame's typed-surface bar.
options.code: use py.h5instrument as h5          // each call = a fresh python process

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via an in-process CPython embed — the reach bar to match. Mojo accepts the embed's coupling; Jet's I1 posture pushes the safe default toward isolation with embed as the opt-in.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: In-process libpython with GIL tokens and typed conversions — the mechanism the embed tier wraps. Shows zero-copy buffer-protocol bridging is a solved shape.
Out-of-process typed boundary with supervision — the broker model. Proven isolation; the cost is marshaling, which is why large-array paths want the embed escape hatch.

decisions.title: Approve a CPython runtime dependency for the Python binder
decisions.gist: The Python binder needs a real CPython interpreter — libpython linked in-process (embed tier) and/or a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. That is a new runtime-side external dependency, an I6 owner decision, exactly parallel to D-DEP-WASM1 for wasmtime.
decisions.explainer: I6 keeps the compiler (Source/) zero-external-crate forever and requires owner approval for any new stdlib/runtime external dependency. D-FFI-PY1's reach depends on real CPython: the sidecar broker needs a CPython executable present, and the embed tier links libpython. This is runtime-side only — never in Source/ — mirroring how D-DEP-WASM1=A approved wasmtime for plugins. The dependency is provisioned per the ratified native-deps policy (nixpkgs interim, jetpack core provider long-term), carries a native-ize obligation (the frozen end-state), and is hash-pinned in .jet/lock. Without this approval the Python binder cannot ship at any depth except the WASM-sandbox tier (which forfeits the C-extension ecosystem).
decisions.story: The build needs numpy to actually run. That means a CPython the compiler can drive — linked or spawned. Before any code assumes libpython is on the link line, the owner decides whether Jet takes that runtime dependency and how it is provisioned.
decisions.detail: Runtime-side only (I6 holds — never in Source/). Provisioning follows the ratified native-deps policy: nixpkgs where the user has Nix, jetpack core provider long-term, with a clear message on machines lacking both. Native-ize obligation recorded (parallel to D-DEP-WASM1's frozen own-runtime end-state). Hash-pinned in .jet/lock (D-DEP1). Only pulled in when a project actually uses py.* — a pure-Jet project never acquires it.

options.name: Approve CPython runtime dep (libpython embed + broker interpreter), provisioned via nixpkgs/jetpack (recommended)
options.detail: Sanction CPython as a runtime-side dependency for the Python binder: libpython on the link line for the embed tier, a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. Never in Source/ (I6 holds). Provisioned by nixpkgs (interim) / jetpack core provider (long-term); hash-pinned; native-ize obligation recorded; acquired only when a project uses py.*. This is the D-DEP-WASM1 precedent applied to Python and unblocks D-FFI-PY1 at full depth.
options.code:
deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // pulls the approved CPython runtime
// pure-Jet projects never acquire it

options.name: Broker interpreter only (no libpython linkage)
options.detail: Approve only a CPython executable for the sidecar worker; never link libpython. Keeps the dependency at arm's length (out-of-process only) and avoids in-process linkage entirely; forecloses the zero-copy embed tier of D-FFI-PY1, so large-array numeric paths always marshal.
options.code: deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // worker process only; no embed tier

options.name: No CPython dep — WASM-sandbox Python only
options.detail: Decline the CPython runtime dependency; the Python binder is limited to the Python-on-WASM tier on the existing wasmtime. No new dep at all, fully sandboxed — but the native C-extension ecosystem (numpy/scipy/torch) does not run, gutting the reason to call Python.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p    // native wheels unavailable

comparisons.note: The exact precedent: a runtime-side external dep approved for a capability (plugins), never in Source/, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Option A is the same shape for Python.
comparisons.code: // wasmtime approved runtime-side for target: plugin

comparisons.note: Both bundle or link a CPython to reach the ecosystem — the accepted cost of real Python interop.
comparisons.code: // libpython embedded in the distributed binary

decisions.title: npm / PyPI / SwiftPM as jetpack registry providers
decisions.gist: `use js.lodash` / `use py.numpy` / `use swift.Alamofire` must fetch from foreign registries. This decides whether jetpack gains npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers (like the Nix bridge U16), and the network/trust/vendoring policy for them.
decisions.explainer: The FFI binders are only 'trivial' if the dependency is fetched as easily as a Jet package. That means jetpack reaching npm, PyPI, and SwiftPM registries. D-DEP1 already fixes the mechanics (fetch -> vendor -> hash-pin -> lock), and U16 already set the precedent of jetpack consuming a foreign ecosystem (Nix). What is an owner call is the policy: do foreign registries become first-class providers resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"` in pkg.jet, and how do they obey the ratified jetpack laws — U29 offline guarantee (no network when the lock is satisfied, `--offline` makes any fetch a loud error), U21 channels (a floating `@latest` npm ref resolves only during update, never in CI), U28 no-daemon, and trust/provenance on fetched artifacts. Recommended: first-class providers under the existing provider seam, every foreign artifact vendored + hash-pinned into the hangar exactly like a Jet package, subject to the same offline/lock/trust laws. This is one gate shared by all three per-language ballots' distribution stories.
decisions.story: Doris types `use js.plotly`, `use py.h5instrument`, `use swift.Alamofire` and expects `jet build` to fetch each from its home registry, lock it exactly, and rebuild offline forever after — the same contract she gets from a Jet package.
decisions.detail: Extends D-DEP1 (vendor + hash-pin every language's refs) and the U16 foreign-ecosystem-provider precedent. Must obey the ratified jetpack laws: U29 (offline/lock), U21 (channel refs resolve only on update, exact in lock, unlocked ref in CI = error), U28 (no daemon), U24 (provenance envelope on fetched objects), U23 (honest message on machines that cannot reach a registry). Foreign artifacts land in the hangar like Jet objects and GC per U22. Trust: fetched artifacts are hash-verified on arrival; a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build.

options.name: First-class npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers under the jetpack provider seam (recommended)
options.detail: Each foreign registry is a provider resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"`, fetching into the hangar, vendored + hash-pinned to .jet/lock, obeying every ratified jetpack law (U29 offline, U21 channels, U28 no-daemon, U24 provenance, U23 honest fallback). Foreign artifacts are hash-verified on arrival so a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build. One uniform distribution story across all three binders.
options.code:
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4", numpy: py@">=1.26" }
// resolved by the npm / pypi providers; locked exactly; offline-safe after

options.name: Manifest-declared registry endpoints only (no built-in providers)
options.detail: No first-party providers; the user declares each foreign registry endpoint and credentials in pkg.jet and jetpack fetches generically. Maximum control for private registries; every project re-specifies boilerplate and there is no curated default, so `use js.lodash` does not just work out of the box.
options.code:
registries: { npm: "https://registry.npmjs.org", pypi: "https://pypi.org/simple" }
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4" }

options.name: Vendor-only, no live registry fetch
options.detail: jetpack never contacts a foreign registry; users vendor foreign packages into the repo by hand (or via an external tool) and jetpack only hash-pins what is already present. Strongest supply-chain posture and zero network policy to design; but it forfeits the 'trivial to use any library' bar — adding a package is a manual vendoring chore.
options.code: // user vendors node_modules / wheels by hand; jetpack only locks them

comparisons.note: Already-ratified precedent: jetpack consumes a foreign ecosystem as a provider with honest gating. Option A applies the same model to npm/PyPI/SwiftPM.
comparisons.code: jet run nixpkgs@tool   // foreign provider, gated, locked

comparisons.note: Fetch npm/PyPI into a hermetic, hash-locked store obeying an offline/repro contract — the shape of option A under Jet's U29/U21 laws.

decisions.title: What a change must pass before it lands
decisions.gist: How much of the test suite (and which extra gates) run on every pull request versus nightly.
decisions.explainer: Today CI runs 5 of the ~70 test files: unit tests, truthfulness, diagnostic snapshots, golden examples, cross-compile. The other 65 — LSP, formatter, REPL, jetpack, workspace, web build, ownership, debugger, everything else — only run when a developer remembers to run them locally. CI also still calls the frozen old board path (tools/Tower/Tower.mjs). 'Sharded' = split the suite across parallel CI machines so the wall-clock stays short. 'Ratchet' = a number (coverage, binary size, compile time) that may improve but never regress.
decisions.story: A contributor's PR goes green in 12 minutes and merges. It broke jet fmt's round-trip, two REPL commands, and a jetpack flow — none of which CI ran. The breakage surfaces days later on someone else's machine, bisecting costs an afternoon, and 'CI is green' quietly stops meaning anything. For a language whose examples are the executable spec (I5), the suite that isn't run is a spec that isn't enforced.
decisions.inWild:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — the entire test gate today:
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --lib
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test truthfulness
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test cross
# not run on any PR, ever: lsp, fmt, repl, jetpack, workspace, web_build,
# ownership, debug, modules, generics, effects ... (65 files)
# also: - run: nix develop -c node tools/Tower/Tower.mjs status   # frozen dir, per MOVED.md
decisions.detail: Recommend A. The suite is the spec (I4/I5); a gate that skips 65 of 70 files lets the spec be broken silently, and this repo has already paid that bisect tax. Whichever option wins, the frozen tools/Tower CI step is corrected as part of it.

options.name: Everything on every PR; nightly adds the slow science
options.detail: PR gate = the full cargo test suite, sharded across parallel jobs, plus grammar-drift and docs-build checks. Nightly = multi-OS matrix (Linux/macOS), perf-regression harness (tools/perf) with ratchets, fuzzing cadence, coverage report. Green means green: no change lands without the whole spec passing. Costs more CI minutes; sharding keeps wall-clock near today's.
options.code:
# PR (sharded, ~4 parallel jobs):
test-shard-1: lexer parser fmt grammar ui...
test-shard-2: sema ownership generics effects...
test-shard-3: golden examples, codegen, cross
test-shard-4: lsp repl debug jetpack workspace web...
gates: grammar-drift, docs-build, tower status (new path)
# nightly: macOS + Linux, perf ratchet, fuzz 30min, coverage

options.name: Two lanes: fast PR, full suite gates the merge
options.detail: PR lane stays fast (today's five targets + build + lint), and the full suite runs in a merge queue / on master after merge, auto-reverting or red-flagging on failure. Cheap PRs, but a window exists where broken code is on master and someone else pulls it.
options.code:
PR:     12 min — compile, golden, snapshots, lint
merge:  full suite on the merge commit; failure -> auto-revert + card
# the gap: between merge and full-suite result, master may be broken

options.name: Full suite nightly only
options.detail: PRs unchanged; one nightly run of everything files a card on failure. Minimal CI spend; a full day of changes can land between a breakage and its discovery, and the bisect cost returns.
options.code: nightly: cargo test (all) -> on failure: tower card add --kind bug ...

comparisons.note: Nothing merges without the full suite: bors merge queue, every PR fully tested on the merge commit. This is why 'rustc is green' is trusted absolutely.
comparisons.code: @bors r+ -> full CI on the exact merge -> only then master moves

comparisons.note: TryBots on every CL run the broad suite; slower builders complete post-submit. Two-lane, but the fast lane is already broad.

decisions.title: Warning and style policy for the compiler codebase
decisions.gist: Whether the Rust codebase must build warning-free, and how work-in-progress code marks itself so cleanup never amputates a feature.
decisions.explainer: The workspace currently builds with warnings allowed (one live dead-code warning in jet-jit today). Rust's `#[expect(lint, reason = "...")]` is a lint gate that also fails when the lint stops firing — so an exception can't outlive its cause. `-D warnings` in CI = any new warning is a red build. rustfmt/clippy = the standard Rust formatter and lint suite; both are configurable and neither touches this repo's PascalCase file naming.
decisions.story: An agent sweeping the codebase sees `fn scrutinee_bool` flagged dead and deletes it — not knowing it's the next stage of the JIT, mid-build on another card. The reverse also happens: genuinely dead code survives for months because nobody can tell it from in-progress work. This repo has hit both. The policy question: does 'dead code' explain itself, or does every reader have to guess?
decisions.detail: Recommend A. It resolves the standing tension between 'keep the build clean' and 'dead code may be an unbuilt feature' by making the code say which it is — and the expect self-expires when the feature lands.

options.name: Warning-free gate + card-referenced expects
options.detail: CI adds `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, and a curated clippy set (correctness + suspicious lints on; style lints that fight house conventions off). Every intentional exception must be `#[expect(dead_code, reason = "#125: JIT tier-1a, wired in next stage")]` — self-documenting, and when the code goes live the expect itself errors and gets removed. Dead code without a card reference is deletable on sight, by rule.
options.code:
#[expect(dead_code, reason = "#125: JIT tier-1a scrutinee lowering, next stage")]
fn scrutinee_bool(&mut self, cond: &str) -> Result<Value, String> { ... }

$ cargo build   # clean — zero noise, every exception explains itself
# ...later, when #125 wires it in:
error: this lint expectation is unfulfilled  // <- expect must be deleted: self-expiring

options.name: Warning-free except dead_code
options.detail: `-D warnings` for everything else; dead_code stays advisory so in-progress features need no annotation. Keeps builds mostly clean but preserves exactly today's ambiguity for the one lint where ambiguity has already caused damage.
options.code:
$ cargo build
warning: method `scrutinee_bool` is never used   // still: delete or feature?

options.name: Status quo — warnings advisory
options.detail: No gate. Warnings accumulate until someone sweeps; sweeps risk deleting in-progress work; the build output slowly stops being read.
options.code: $ cargo build 2>&1 | wc -l   # a number that only grows

comparisons.note: Unused variable is a compile error, full stop — the language forces option A's discipline with no escape hatch.
comparisons.code: declared and not used: x   // does not compile

comparisons.note: `#[expect]` (stable 1.81) was added precisely for this: exceptions that expire themselves.

decisions.title: Game asset handles
decisions.gist: Choose how game assets are declared, loaded, and diagnosed.
decisions.story: Lena makes a platformer. She wants a typed `player_sprite` handle everywhere and a Jet diagnostic if a PNG is missing or used as a sound.
decisions.inWild: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Scene asset registry with typed handles
options.detail: Assets load through `scene.assets`, returning typed handles tied to scene identity.
options.code:
player :: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?
jump :: scene.assets.sound("assets/jump.wav")?

options.name: Top-level loaders
options.detail: Flexible, but weakens scene-owned diagnostics and editor identity.
options.code: player :: game.asset.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Manifest asset catalog
options.detail: Strong packaging provenance, more ceremony for one-file games.
options.code: targets: { game: { assets: { player: "assets/player.png" } } }

comparisons.note: Resource handles are editor-friendly; Jet should keep them typed and source-owned.

decisions.title: ECS over Scene
decisions.gist: Choose the component and query API that layers over `Scene`.
decisions.story: Omar starts with a simple scene, then adds hundreds of enemies. Components and queries should be another view over the same scene data, not a second engine.
decisions.inWild:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.query(Position, Velocity)

options.name: `component` declarations plus `scene.query`
options.detail: Components are typed declarations; queries are scene methods, preserving one scene identity.
options.code:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
loop item in scene.query(Position, Velocity) { }

options.name: Struct marker components
options.detail: No new declaration form, but component intent is less visible.
options.code:
struct Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.component<Velocity>()

options.name: System functions over query parameters
options.detail: Concise for experts, but puts scheduler vocabulary before the beginner scene story.
options.code: system move(pos: Position mut, vel: Velocity, frame: Frame) { }

comparisons.note: Typed queries are strong; Jet should hide scheduler complexity until needed.

decisions.title: Game input bindings
decisions.gist: Choose how input bindings and per-frame snapshots are named.
decisions.story: Aya wants keyboard today and gamepad later. Replay files should store actions, not raw device quirks, so logic is deterministic across dev, CI, and builds.
decisions.inWild:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Scene bindings plus frame snapshot
options.detail: Bindings live on `scene.input`; frame logic reads deterministic `frame.input` snapshots.
options.code:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Global input map
options.detail: Short, but weak multi-scene/editor isolation.
options.code: game.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])

options.name: Typed action enum
options.detail: Explicit and replay-friendly, more ceremony for tiny games.
options.code:
enum Action { jump }
frame.input<Action>().pressed(Action.jump)

comparisons.note: Action maps are beginner-friendly and replayable.

decisions.title: Game replay contract
decisions.gist: Choose the replay API, file format, and determinism contract.
decisions.story: Ben gets a physics bug report. The player sends one replay file; Ben runs it under `jet dev` and compiled mode and gets the same frame transcript.
decisions.inWild: game.Replay.record("runs/bug-142.jreplay")

options.name: `game.Replay` API plus `.jreplay` artifact
options.detail: First-party typed artifact contains input actions, seeds, fixed-step timing, backend identity, and budget events.
options.code:
game.run(scene, replay: game.Replay.record("run.jreplay"))
game.Replay.play("run.jreplay", scene)?

options.name: CLI-only replay
options.detail: Keeps source clean, weakens tests that need replay facts.
options.code: jet game record game.jet --out run.jreplay

options.name: User serialization hooks
options.detail: Expert control, but no shared deterministic contract.
options.code: scene.on_snapshot((frame) => writer.write(frame.input))

comparisons.note: Input-stream replay is proven; Jet should type and version the artifact.

decisions.title: Game backend selection
decisions.gist: Choose how renderer, audio, and editor backends are selected.
decisions.story: Sana starts with a no-op CI backend, develops on raylib, and later targets wgpu. Gameplay code should not change when backend changes.
decisions.inWild: game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Typed `game.Backend` value
options.detail: Backends are explicit typed values passed to `game.run`; beginners can omit for the default headless/no-op path.
options.code:
game.run(scene)
game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Manifest target backend
options.detail: Fits packages, but single-file games need hidden defaults or a second path.
options.code: targets: { game: { backend: { renderer: core.raylib } } }

options.name: CLI-selected backend
options.detail: Useful for CI, harder to audit from source.
options.code: jet run game.jet --game-renderer=core.raylib

comparisons.note: Plugins are flexible; Jet should keep one stable Core scene API above replaceable backend packages.

decisions.title: Game budgets
decisions.gist: Choose how frame, memory, asset, and draw-call budgets attach and report diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nico ships a handheld build with strict frame, memory, and draw-call ceilings. Violations should be Jet diagnostics with replay context.
decisions.inWild: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Scene/package budgets, same model
options.detail: Budgets attach to scenes for one-file games and package targets for projects; sema/runtime treat both as one fact model.
options.code: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Package-only budgets
options.detail: Clean for CI, but one-file games lose budget diagnostics unless packaged.
options.code: targets: { game: { budgets: { frame: 16.ms } } }

options.name: Runtime watcher API
options.detail: Dynamic control, weaker build/dossier/CI facts.
options.code: budget_watch.attach(scene)

comparisons.note: Budgets work best when CI can fail deterministically.

decisions.title: Proof and replay surface
decisions.gist: Choose the exact command and artifact shape for proof and replay.
decisions.story: Omar receives a production panic trace for payment code. He wants one command to replay the failure, check contracts and budgets, and hand CI a stable JSON report.
decisions.inWild:
jet prove src/payments.jet --replay traces/panic.jreplay
jet prove src/payments.jet --json > proof.json

options.name: jet prove umbrella (recommended)
options.detail: One command with --replay, --lens, --json, and typed .jreplay/.jproof artifacts.
options.code: jet prove src/payments.jet --replay traces/panic.jreplay

options.name: Separate prove and replay
options.detail: Clear verbs, but users learn two entrypoints for one correctness report.
options.code: jet replay traces/panic.jreplay --target src/payments.jet

options.name: Test-runner integration
options.detail: Familiar, but hides effects, budgets, and replay behind a testing-only mental model.
options.code: jet test --prove --replay traces/panic.jreplay

options.name: Dossier-only proof lens
options.detail: Good for inspection, weak for CI action and beginner prove-this workflow.
options.code: jet dossier proof src/payments.jet --json

comparisons.note: Strong proof commands, heavier proof language.
Practical confidence, usually separate from replay/effects.

decisions.title: Budget declaration surface
decisions.gist: Choose where performance budgets are declared.
decisions.story: Mei owns an HTTP service and a small game. She wants service latency, startup, binary size, and frame budgets checked in CI without teaching every new contributor benchmark internals.

options.name: Role modules (recommended)
options.detail: module perf.* declarations attach budgets to packages, envs, services, and scenes as typed facts.
options.code: module perf.server { budgets: { startup: 20ms } }

options.name: pkg.jet target fields
options.detail: Clear for packaged builds, but one-file and scene/service budgets need extra ceremony.
options.code: targets: { server: executable { budgets: { startup: 20ms } } }

options.name: @Budget markers
options.detail: Local and visible, but poor for package/service budgets and statistical baselines.
options.code:
@Budget(p99_latency: 5ms)
fn handle(req: Request) -> Response { ... }

options.name: External policy file
options.detail: Easy to generate, but creates split-brain state.
options.code: perf-budget.jetpolicy

comparisons.note: Lighthouse-style tooling uses budget config files.
Frame/memory budgets live in project settings.

decisions.title: Statistical baseline policy
decisions.gist: Choose how statistical budgets avoid flaky CI.
decisions.story: Mei's p99 latency shifts by machine. CI should catch regressions without failing every time a runner has background load.
decisions.inWild:
jet budget update --baseline ci/linux-x64
jet bench --budget ci/linux-x64

options.name: Pinned baseline artifact (recommended)
options.detail: Hardware/toolchain identity, trend window, confidence policy, and explicit update command.
options.code: jet budget update --baseline ci/linux-x64

options.name: Absolute thresholds only
options.detail: Simple, but noisy for latency and throughput.
options.code: budgets: { p99_latency: 5ms }

options.name: Advisory-only statistical budgets
options.detail: Avoids flakes, but weakens CI value.
options.code: jet bench --budget ci/linux-x64 --warn-only

comparisons.note: Stores baselines and compares distributions.
Distinguishes budgets from lab variance.

decisions.gist: Choose how users open jetos Studio.

decisions.inWild: jetos studio

options.name: jetos studio (recommended)
options.detail: Studio belongs to the OS engine and keeps package-manager verbs out of OS UX.
options.code: jetos studio

options.name: jet studio --os
options.detail: One Jet umbrella command, but blurs engine boundary.
options.code: jet studio --os

options.name: Editor command only
options.detail: Friendly inside IDEs, weak for docs, CI repro, and support.
options.code: Jetos: Open Studio

comparisons.note: Discoverable but not scriptable; jetos needs both.

decisions.title: jetos Studio default editing view
decisions.gist: Choose Studio's default editing view.
decisions.story: Ren enables Steam and SSH. They want safe toggles first, then the exact module diff before saving.

Studio -> Services -> SSH -> Enable
Diff: module system.laptop { services.ssh.enable: true }

options.detail: Panels for common tasks, source and provenance always one click away.
options.code: Services -> SSH -> Enable -> Diff

options.name: Source-first IDE
options.detail: Powerful and honest, but weak beginner onboarding.
options.code: edit system.jet

options.name: Graph/canvas-first
options.detail: Strong visual consistency with #182, but OS settings are usually forms and provenance trees.
options.code: canvas

comparisons.note: Declarative review is strong; beginner settings UI is weak.

decisions.title: jetos Studio local state boundary
decisions.gist: Decide what Studio may persist outside Jet source.
decisions.story: Priya arranges panels and filters proof logs. She does not want those UI choices to become semantic config or noisy PR diffs.
decisions.inWild:
.jet/studio/cache.json
system/laptop.jet

options.name: Generated cache only (recommended)
options.detail: Studio may persist view prefs under .jet, never semantic settings.
options.code: .jet/studio/cache.json

options.name: Committed .studio.jet metadata
options.detail: Reviewable UI metadata, but another source-like artifact.
options.code: .studio.jet

options.name: No persistence

options.code: none

decisions.title: jetos Studio activation proof gate
decisions.gist: Choose how Studio blocks risky activation.
decisions.story: Mara changes kernel and filesystem settings. Studio must tell them whether VM boot and rollback proof are required before switch.
decisions.inWild:
Risk: boot + filesystem
Required: plan, VM boot, rollback proof
Switch: disabled until proof passes

options.name: Plan-only warning
options.detail: Always allow switch after diff approval. Fast, weaker than D-WD8 proof intent.
options.code: warning only

options.name: Risk-based hard gate (recommended)
options.detail: Boot/kernel/filesystem/service-risk changes require VM and rollback proof; low-risk changes require plan/diff unless policy says more.
options.code: switch disabled until proof passes

options.name: Always VM proof
options.detail: Simple and safe, but over-applies proof to trivial edits.
options.code: VM required for every switch

comparisons.note: Offers VM/build tools but leaves policy to user habit.

decisions.title: jetos Studio plan/proof schema stability
decisions.gist: Decide whether Studio proof/diff artifacts are public schemas in v1.
decisions.story: Owen wants CI to show the same plan, risk, and proof result that Studio shows before activation.
decisions.inWild:
jetos plan @laptop --json > plan.json
jetos prove @laptop --json > proof.json

options.name: Public schemas from first write flow
options.detail: Studio and CI share stable JSON immediately.
options.code: jetos plan --json

options.name: Internal GUI schema first
options.detail: Faster GUI iteration, but CI cannot trust the same artifact.
options.code: internal schema

options.name: Public after read-only Studio (recommended)
options.detail: Stabilize once projection fields prove out, before activation handoff.
options.code: public before switch flows

comparisons.note: Plans are useful because CI and humans inspect the same object.

decisions.title: Filesystem watch surface and home
decisions.gist: Where filesystem change notifications live and what the beginner surface looks like.
decisions.explainer: A: discovery beats taxonomy — the person with a path in hand is already in core.files; normalize per-OS quirks and debounce by default.
decisions.story: Lena writes a static-site tool in Jet and wants rebuild-on-save. Today she loops fs.list_dir + mtimes on a timer — wasteful, laggy, and subtly wrong on renames. jet dev itself watches files internally; users deserve the same primitive.

options.name: files.watch in core.files
options.detail: One more capability on the module that owns paths: watch(path) returns a WatchHandle whose events() iterate typed changes (Created/Modified/Removed/Renamed). Debounced by default (beginner-safe); raw stream behind an option.

options.name: New core.watch module
options.detail: Separate module name for the whole watching domain (files now; maybe processes/ports later). Cleaner if watching grows beyond files, but today it is one function and a new top-level name to learn.

options.name: Decline — polling helper only
options.detail: Ship files.poll_changes(path, interval) sugar over mtime polling. No OS notification backends to maintain, but it bakes the laggy/wasteful pattern in as the blessed answer.
options.code: loop ev in files.poll_changes("site/", time.ms(500)) { rebuild() }

comparisons.note: fsnotify is the de-facto standard everyone pulls in — Go not shipping it in stdlib is a known gap.
fs.watch is stdlib but semantics vary per-OS; chokidar exists to paper over it — the lesson is to normalize events in the library.

decisions.comment: also include processes and ports now, not later

decisions.title: Core filesystem depth surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical shape for deep file and path operations.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A keeps one semantic path model: typed Path is the backbone for composition and audit, while core.files keeps beginner-friendly string entrypoints that immediately coerce into Path. This reconciles D-PATHFS1 with today's core.files docs without creating two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marta writes a static-site publisher. She needs to create nested folders, copy an asset tree, atomically write output, inspect mtimes, skip symlink cycles, and clean a temp directory when the build exits. If Jet gives her only read/write/list_dir, she falls back to brittle string paths and shell commands.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Path-only purity makes beginner scripts noisy; string-only helpers make expert audit and cycle-safe walking weak. The hybrid is one mechanism because every string entrypoint lowers to Path before sema/codegen effects, docs, and audit facts see it. No aliases: names are stable once ratified.

options.name: Path backbone plus string entrypoints (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify typed Path as the internal and expert surface, and keep core.files string helpers as the beginner facade. Add Stat, FileKind, WalkEntry, TempDir, FileLock, and one canonical operation set: stat, create_dir_all, remove_dir, remove_all, glob, walk, symlink/read_link, hard_link, temp_dir/temp_file, lock, canonicalize, absolute, copy_dir, read_at/write_at/seek, fsync, write_atomic.
options.code:
use core.files as files

p :: Path.from("site").join("posts")
files.create_dir_all(p)?              // Path accepted
files.create_dir_all("site/posts")? // String accepted by same coercion

stat :: files.stat(p)?
if stat.kind == .Dir {
    loop ent in files.walk(p)? { print(ent.path.to_string()) }
}

tmp :: files.temp_dir()?              // RAII cleanup
lock :: files.lock("build.lock")?   // advisory, scoped
files.write_atomic(p.join("index.html"), bytes)?

options.name: String-only core.files
options.detail: All operations are module functions over String paths. Very easy to type, but path composition, relative roots, symlink-cycle handling, and audit output stay stringly typed.

options.name: Path-only methods
options.detail: Every deep operation hangs off Path methods. Strong audit and discoverability from a Path value, but beginner one-file scripts must learn Path before simple tasks like mkdir -p or remove_all.
options.code:
root :: Path.from("site")
root.join("posts").create_dir_all()?
root.walk().filter((e) => e.stat.kind == .File)

options.name: Decline depth for now
options.detail: Keep read/write/list_dir/open and document shell/core.process workarounds. This leaves Jet worse than Python pathlib, Go os, and Rust fs for everyday scripting and build tools.
options.code:
process.run(["mkdir", "-p", out])?
process.run(["cp", "-R", src, out])?

comparisons.note: pathlib gives a pleasant Path object, but many APIs still accept strings. Jet can keep that ergonomics while making audit facts typed.
os and filepath are robust but split path values into strings. Jet can be more discoverable with typed Path plus module helpers.
std::path and std::fs have strong types and broad coverage, but error copy is not beginner-facing. Jet keeps the front-end diagnostic contract.

decisions.title: Unified watch surface for files, processes, and ports
decisions.gist: Choose how watch-style change notifications cover files, processes, and ports.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A honors the owner's D-FSWATCH1 comment now: one Watch/Event model, with constructors in the domain where the thing lives. Beginners find files.watch(path); experts compose typed watchers across files, process exit, and port readiness without polling.
decisions.story: Earl builds a dev runner in Jet. It rebuilds when source files change, restarts a child server, waits until port 3000 is accepting connections, and exits cleanly if the child dies. Today he needs three different polling loops and timing guesses.
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as files
use core.process as process
use core.net as net

watch :: WatchSet.new()
watch.add(files.watch("src")?)
child :: process.spawn(["jet", "run", "server.jet"])?
watch.add(process.watch(child))
watch.add(net.watch_port(3000))

loop ev in watch.events() { handle(ev) }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a single core.watch module looks clean, but it becomes a taxonomy drawer and steals discovery from the domain APIs. Domain constructors plus one shared WatchSet/Event type preserve one mechanism while keeping entrypoints where users already are.

options.name: Domain constructors plus shared WatchSet (recommended)
options.detail: files.watch(path), process.watch(child_or_pid), and net.watch_port(port_or_addr) return typed Watch handles with one shared WatchEvent enum and WatchSet multiplexer. Debounced file events are the default; raw event streams are explicit options.

options.name: One core.watch module
options.detail: watch.files, watch.process, and watch.port live under one top-level module. Easy to enumerate, but the common beginner case imports a taxonomy module instead of the file/process/net module already in use.
options.code:
use core.watch as watch

w :: watch.set([
    watch.files("src")?,
    watch.process(child),
    watch.port(3000),
])

options.name: Only files in Epoch 3
options.detail: Implement D-FSWATCH1 literally and defer process/port watching. This ignores the owner ratification comment and leaves dev-runner tooling polling process/port state.

options.name: Callback watchers
options.detail: Each watch call takes a lambda callback. Good for tiny examples, but harder to compose, cancel, test, and replay than event values.
options.code:
files.watch("src", (ev) => rebuild())?
process.watch(child, (ev) => stop())?
net.watch_port(3000, (ev) => ready())?

comparisons.note: Node has fs.watch and child process events, but port readiness is hand-rolled. Jet can unify these as typed event values.
comparisons.code: fs.watch('src', cb); child.on('exit', cb); net.createConnection(port).on('connect', cb)

comparisons.note: Go pushes file watching to fsnotify and process/port readiness to ad hoc goroutines/channels. Jet can ship the channel-like composition in Core.
notify plus tokio process/net can compose, but through external crates and async runtime choices. Jet keeps a blocking beginner surface and explicit expert control.

decisions.comment: a & b - instead of putting file watcher in file module/lib, put all watcher methods in a core.watcher lib. ALSO, support callback/event triggers with our new event system

decisions.title: Socket layer surface
decisions.gist: Choose the socket API beneath HTTP and services.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Go-like simple networking with explicit expert hooks for readiness/cancellation/performance.
