options.detail: Canonical `module workspace { policy: Policy.{...} }` declares maximum/requested cache roles and trust. Stricter user/org policy may refuse or narrow it; repositories cannot force cache use, add trust roots, choose credentials, or weaken sandbox/trust. Host config binds names to endpoints and scoped keychain/provider pipes.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ cache_read_roles: ["release"] } }
# host config: release -> endpoint + credential pipe

options.name: User config only
options.detail: Every cache URL, priority, key, and write rule is machine-local; repositories cannot demand a trust posture.
options.code: ~/.config/jet/caches.toml

options.name: Environment variables and flags
options.detail: Cache URLs/keys/order are supplied per command or environment.
options.code: JET_CACHE=https://... jet build --cache-write

options.name: Role trust in one policy namespace, bound mirrors, verified-first-hit (hybrid)
options.detail: Workspace `policy:` declares requested/maximum cache roles and trust posture in the same single ratified policy namespace; stricter user/org policy may narrow or refuse, and repositories never name endpoints, keys, or credentials. `jet cache bind` manages the one host config mapping roles to ordered mirror endpoints and typed credential providers (OS keychain or scoped pipe); no environment variable or flag may introduce an endpoint or key, and secrets never enter URLs, argv, environment, logs, or locks. Read law: mirrors are tried in bound order, the first hit that verifies digest and signature against the role's trust roots wins regardless of location (Law 3), negative-cache hints stay mirror-local, misses fall back to source build, and `--offline` (D-JPK-OFFLINE1) beats everything. Writes require the separate D-BUILDREMOTE1/D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 grant; zero-config beginners get the ratified default read set with pinned trust roots and never see cache jargon, and `jet explain <pkg> --lens cache` shows every decision.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ cache_read_roles: ["public", "release"], cache_write_role: "release" } }
$ jet cache bind release https://cache.corp.example --credential keychain:jet/release
$ jet build                                # ordered mirrors, verify, miss -> source build
$ jet explain package:foo --lens cache     # role, mirror, verification, fallback

comparisons.note: Substituters and trusted keys are nix.conf settings.
Build cache endpoints and push policy are configured separately.

decisions.title: Store endpoint interoperability scope
decisions.gist: Choose which native and Nix store endpoints Jetpack must speak.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A contradicts the plan's JP5 card, which already requires daemon/SSH/file/HTTP/S3 endpoints, and abandons real air-gap and builder workflows; C adopts Nix URI vocabulary as canon, violating Law 7 (compatibility is not canon). B has the right scope but is vague on write authority, credential handling, NAR fingerprint round-tripping, mirror ordering, and failure UX. The hybrid pins those down with typed capability records, dual identity for exact re-signing, D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 write grants, typed credential providers, and deterministic mirror-to-source fallback.
decisions.story: Earl copies a locked closure among a laptop, an SSH builder, an air-gapped file cache, and S3-backed CI cache. One store abstraction should preserve integrity everywhere.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to builder-arm
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to file:///mnt/airgap
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to s3://release-cache/prefix
decisions.detail: Native design stays canonical while interoperability covers real Nix/cache/air-gap workflows.

options.name: Jetpack-native endpoints only
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP, and native remote executor; Nix caches only through NAR HTTP import.
options.code:
local://
https://jet-cache/...

options.name: Native plus Nix-compatible endpoint adapters
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP, SSH, file, S3-compatible cache, and Nix daemon/SSH/file/HTTP adapters. All lower to verified Jetpack object/closure APIs.
options.code:
hangar://local
ssh://builder
file:///cache
s3://bucket
ssh-ng://nix-host

options.name: Nix store URI semantics everywhere
options.detail: Adopt Nix store URL vocabulary/protocol as Jetpack's primary store abstraction.
options.code:
daemon
ssh-ng://host
https://cache.nixos.org

options.name: Native plus Nix adapters with typed capabilities and dual identity (hybrid)
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP cache, SSH, file, S3-compatible, and Nix daemon/SSH/file/HTTP adapters; every endpoint declares a typed capability record (read, write, remote-execute, trust domain, credential provider) and all transfers lower to verified Jetpack object/closure APIs — no trust by location. Objects crossing a Nix endpoint record dual identity — canonical Jetpack digest plus NarHash/signed fingerprint — so round-trips re-verify and re-sign exactly. Write access is a separate grant under D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1; credentials come only from typed providers and never enter URLs, argv, logs, or locks. Mirrors are ordered with deterministic fallback to source build; a capability gap fails with one E-code naming the endpoint, the missing capability, and the nearest supported path. Nix store URI spellings are accepted as endpoint addresses only, never as Jetpack's canonical vocabulary (Law 7).
options.code:
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to ssh-ng://nix-host
endpoint: nix-daemon adapter [read+write, trust: team]
verified: canonical digest + NarHash fingerprint
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to s3://release-cache
E13xx: endpoint grant is read-only
fix: jet trust cache --write s3://release-cache

comparisons.note: Store backends include local, daemon, SSH, file, HTTP, and S3 binary caches.
CAS/remote execution normally use HTTP/gRPC services.

decisions.title: Dependency update and verification modes
decisions.gist: Choose how users request conservative, latest, lowest, and cross-platform resolution.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: C is expert-hostile and cannot satisfy the plan's binding lowest/latest resolver lane without manual constraint surgery. A and B are artificially siloed halves of one mechanism: A leaves CI matrices as unreviewable copy-pasted flags with no default-strategy or lock-mutation law; B buries the standard vocabulary behind mandatory policy ceremony. The hybrid merges them — fixed vocabulary with conservative default, optional source-declared profiles that can only bundle that vocabulary, non-mutating typed proof artifacts, and tested byte-stability of unrelated lock records.
decisions.story: Betty updates one HTTP library, then CI proves the workspace works at lowest-direct constraints and on Linux/macOS/Windows without rewriting unrelated locks.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet update http --strategy conservative
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct --platform linux,macos,windows
lock: unrelated records unchanged
decisions.detail: Common default stays simple; explicit strategies make compatibility proof discoverable and reproducible.

options.name: Explicit update/verify strategies
options.detail: One resolver exposes conservative/default/latest/lowest/lowest-direct strategies. `jet update` may write the selected closure; the ratified `jet prove` umbrella evaluates dependency matrices without mutating the canonical lock unless asked.
options.code:
jet update http --strategy conservative
jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct

options.name: Source-defined resolution profiles
options.detail: Named strategies and platform matrices live only in workspace policy; commands select a profile.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ resolution_profiles: { oldest: ... } } }
jet prove --lens dependencies --profile oldest

options.name: Fixed policy only
options.detail: `jet update` is always conservative; CI users edit constraints to test latest/lowest manually.
options.code: jet update http

options.name: One strategy vocabulary, source profiles, non-mutating proof artifacts (hybrid)
options.detail: One resolver exposes the fixed vocabulary conservative/latest/lowest/lowest-direct; `jet update <pkg>` defaults to conservative and may move only the named subtree, writing strategy and command into lock rationale (D-JPK-CHANNEL1 intact; realize verbs never resolve). Workspace policy may declare named profiles that only bundle vocabulary strategies plus platform matrices, so CI runs are source-reviewable. `jet prove --lens dependencies` never mutates the canonical lock; it emits typed .jproof matrix artifacts per D-PROVE-REPLAY1. Byte-stability of unrelated lock records is a tested guarantee.
options.code:
$ jet update http                    # conservative: only http subtree moves; rationale logged
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct --platform linux,macos,windows
proof: .jet/proofs/deps-lowest-direct.jproof
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --profile ci-floor   # profile declared in workspace.jet
lock: unrelated records byte-identical

comparisons.note: Supports highest, lowest, and lowest-direct resolution strategies.
Conservative updates limit changes around named gems.

decisions.title: Cache policy for unreproducible outputs
decisions.gist: Choose what happens when independent builders produce different bytes for one action.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A discards the divergent bytes teams need to debug the mismatch at all; option C is trust-by-annotation — a tag that policy engines will eventually ignore, blessing a single builder's bytes against Law 3. Option B has the right namespace split but never requires evidence retention, defines the consumer opt-in, propagates taint downstream, or states how a fixed package re-earns trust. The hybrid keeps B's visible split and adds diff+provenance retention, explicit opt-in with taint propagation, and rebuild-only promotion.
decisions.story: George's package embeds the wall clock. Two approved builders disagree. Jetpack must not bless either result as a trusted shared cache hit.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet prove --lens reproducibility package:foo
mismatch: bin/foo offset 0x2a1 (timestamp)
shared cache promotion: denied
decisions.detail: Debugging remains practical without letting non-deterministic bytes satisfy trusted policy.

options.name: Reject all caching
options.detail: Unreproducible outputs remain local build results and are never uploaded to any cache.
options.code: cache publish: denied

options.name: Separate visibly untrusted namespace
options.detail: Trusted shared namespaces reject them. An explicit private/untrusted namespace may store bytes for debugging, but can never satisfy trusted/release policy.
options.code:
cache write private/unreproducible: accepted
cache promote shared: denied

options.name: Allow trusted cache with metadata tag
options.detail: Store one result in the trusted namespace if metadata says reproducibility is not guaranteed.
options.code: shared cache: accepted, reproducible=false

options.name: Untrusted evidence namespace, taint propagation, rebuild-only promotion (hybrid)
options.detail: Trusted shared namespaces accept only outputs whose action satisfied reproducibility policy. Divergent results are preserved — both builders' bytes, both provenances, and the structured first-difference diff — in a visibly untrusted `private/unreproducible` namespace, so `jet prove --lens reproducibility` can name the first differing path and producer action. Untrusted objects never satisfy trusted or release policy and are fetched only with an explicit `--untrusted-namespace` opt-in that taints every downstream output as untrusted too. Promotion happens only by fresh independent rebuilds that agree after the fix — never by relabeling stored bytes — and every denial prints the differing path plus the fix hint.
options.code:
$ jet prove --lens reproducibility package:foo
mismatch: bin/foo offset 0x2a1 (timestamp) — builders b1,b2 disagree
stored: private/unreproducible (both results + diff + provenance)
shared promotion: denied — fix determinism, rebuild independently
$ jet build --untrusted-namespace   # expert: outputs tainted untrusted

comparisons.note: `guix challenge` compares substitute results with independent builds.
Provenance describes build process but does not make differing outputs reproducible.

decisions.title: Canonical ownership of native scientific and accelerator computing
decisions.gist: Choose the public architectural owner for arrays, optimization, automatic differentiation, and accelerator execution without creating a second language runtime.
decisions.explainer:
This umbrella chooses product ownership only. It does not pre-ratify a Tensor type, placement policy, user kernels, autodiff rules, or backend behavior; the linked ballots decide those independently. All execution still lowers beneath executable TIR and obeys AOT/dev parity.

Fable hybrid review: A names one vocabulary but leaves the physical layer unspecified, so devices/buffers/kernels risk arriving as a bolt-on second model; B inverts the priority order by making the beginner path kernel-shaped; C forecloses the expert kernel reach the owner direction and D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1 require. The hybrid keeps A's single operation family and ratifies B's substrate as the expert tier of that same family, so I8 sees one mechanism with two entrypoints.
decisions.story: Priya starts with a small CPU calculation, scales it to a GPU, differentiates a loss, and later writes one specialized kernel. She wants one Jet vocabulary and one ownership model instead of switching among NumPy, JAX, CUDA, and deployment glue.
decisions.inWild:
use core.compute

scores :: compute.array(rows).matmul(weights).softmax()
trained :: compute.optimize(loss, model) ?? panic("optimization failed")
decisions.detail: The selected owner must compose existing lists, fixed arrays, View, Vec, Matrix, columnar data, SIMD, Gpu effects, and audited Unsafe regions. Internal graph or kernel forms are implementation stages beneath TIR, not public execution seams. Provider roots such as gpu.cuda remain explicit compatibility bridges, never the native canonical model.

options.name: One first-party compute operation family
options.detail: Core owns one public operation family spanning eager use, optimization, differentiation, and expert acceleration. Separate ballots define its types and policies. Libraries and bridges integrate through the same operations and semantic facts.
options.code:
y :: compute.array(x).matmul(w).relu()
// the same operation names survive eager execution, fusion, autodiff, and explicit device policy

options.name: Kernel-first native substrate
options.detail: Core owns portable kernels, devices, buffers, and scheduling. Arrays, autodiff, ML, and dataframes are first-party libraries built above that substrate rather than one Core operation family.
options.code:
kernel :: compute.kernel(map_relu) ?? panic("kernel is not portable")
y :: kernel.launch(input, output) ?? panic("kernel launch failed")

options.name: Array-graph compiler only
options.detail: Core owns typed array operations, fusion, and autodiff. Users cannot author native Jet kernels; specialized work uses generated operations or explicit foreign providers.
options.code: y :: tensor.graph((x) => x.matmul(w).relu()).run(input) ?? panic("compute failed")

options.name: One Core operation family layered on an expert substrate tier (hybrid)
options.detail: Core owns a single public core.compute operation family spanning eager use, fusion, differentiation, and placement; the same operation names and semantic facts survive every execution stage. Beneath it Core also owns the device/buffer/stream/kernel substrate, but that substrate is the expert tier of the same family — reached through compute.* builders under the existing ownership/effect/Unsafe law, never a second public execution model. Arrays, autodiff, ML, and dataframes integrate through the operation family; graph and kernel forms remain internal stages beneath executable TIR. Provider roots such as gpu.cuda stay explicit bridges that must differentially match native semantics, never the canonical model.

comparisons.note: NumPy established a compact array vocabulary; JAX adds transformation and accelerator compilation. Jet should preserve that ergonomic progression without tracer surprises or a Python host.
CUDA gives experts direct kernels, memory, streams, and profiling. Jet must preserve that reach behind its existing ownership/effect/Unsafe law.

decisions.title: Multidimensional compute type and existing collection relationship
decisions.gist: Choose how ranked, shaped, strided, mutable, and borrowed compute values relate to existing Jet lists, fixed arrays, View, Vec, Matrix, and columnar data.
decisions.explainer:
One type cannot erase ownership or shape facts, and two types cannot perform the same job under I8. Every option must handle compile-time and runtime dimensions, rank, mutation, non-contiguous views, broadcasting, and source compatibility with existing math/data code.

Fable hybrid review: B cannot state high-rank ownership, broadcasting, or accelerator layout coherently; C imports the PyTorch/JAX track/detach boundary — a beginner trap and an I8 hazard of two overlapping array types; A is right but its 'specializations/adapters' wording is vague enough to permit hidden copying seams between Matrix and Tensor. The hybrid pins Vec/Matrix to the ratified shared substrate (zero-copy by law), unifies host and device views under one alias/residency law, and makes autodiff a transform rather than a type.
decisions.story: Elena loads a runtime-sized image batch, slices a strided view, passes a fixed 4x4 transform to existing Matrix code, and sends the batch to an accelerator without copying by accident.
decisions.inWild:
pixels :: Tensor<Float>.from(rows).reshape([batch, height, width, 4]) ?? panic("bad image shape")
crop :: pixels.view([all, 8..72, 8..72, all])
decisions.detail: Static dimensions participate in sema shape checks; runtime dimensions produce typed fallible shape operations before execution. Mutable access obeys exclusive ownership, views carry lifetime/stride/alias facts, and device views retain the same law. Conversion that can allocate or copy is explicit and auditable.

options.name: Tensor owner with View borrows and math specializations
options.detail: Tensor<T> owns ranked multidimensional storage with optional static shape facts. View<T> is the borrowed strided projection. Existing Vec and Matrix become fixed-rank specializations/adapters with source-compatible operations. Lists and fixed arrays convert explicitly when rank/storage changes; columnar tables remain relational, not tensors.
options.code:
image :: Tensor<Float>.zeros([height, width, 4])
tile: View<Float> :: image.view([0..32, 0..32, all])
m: Matrix<4, 4> :: transform
mt :: Tensor.from_matrix(m)  // explicit representation conversion

options.name: Extend lists, fixed arrays, Vec, Matrix, and View only
options.detail: No Tensor type is added. Nested lists/fixed arrays express rank; Vec/Matrix keep static shapes; a generalized View carries runtime shape and strides. This minimizes types but makes high-rank ownership, broadcasting, and accelerator layout harder to state coherently.
options.code:
image: [[[Float]]] :: load_image()
batch :: View.from_nested(images) ?? panic("ragged image batch")
result :: batch.broadcast([n, h, w]) ?? panic("shape mismatch")

options.name: NDArray storage plus differentiable Tensor values
options.detail: NDArray owns general numeric storage, shape, strides, and mutation. Tensor is a distinct immutable value only when computation history/gradients are required; it wraps or views an NDArray with explicit conversion. The jobs are non-overlapping but users cross a boundary when enabling autodiff.
options.code:
x: NDArray<Float> :: NDArray.zeros([batch, 784])
tracked: Tensor<Float> :: Tensor.track(x.view())
plain: NDArray<Float> :: tracked.detach()

options.name: One Tensor owner with unified View and zero-copy math aliases (hybrid)
options.detail: Tensor<T> is the single owner of ranked multidimensional storage with optional static shape facts checked in sema; runtime shapes go through typed fallible operations before execution. View<T> (D-DYNARRAY1) is the one borrowed strided projection for host and device memory alike, carrying identical lifetime/stride/alias/residency facts under the existing exclusive-mutation law. Vec<N> and Matrix<M,N> remain fixed-shape forms over the same substrate (D-MATHLIB1, #293), so passing them to tensor operations is zero-copy and adapter-free; only rank- or layout-changing conversions exist, each explicitly named and flagged as allocating in plan and dossier output. Differentiability is a property of the compute.grad transform, never a second type — no track/detach seam exists — and columnar tables stay relational with an explicit, audited to_tensor.
options.code:
image :: Tensor<Float>.zeros([height, width, 4])
tile: View<Float> :: image.view([0..32, 0..32, all])
m: Matrix<4, 4> :: transform
y :: tile.matmul(m)   // zero-copy: Matrix shares the substrate
flat :: image.reshape([height * width, 4]) ?? panic("bad shape")  // named, auditable when it copies

comparisons.note: Separate dynamic ndarray and statically-shaped math types preserve useful facts but create conversion seams. Jet needs an explicit law for that seam.
One Tensor carries shape, device, strides, mutation rules, and optional gradients. It is ergonomic but many failures remain runtime-only; Jet can move static facts into sema.

decisions.title: Compute placement, transfer visibility, effects, and fallback
decisions.gist: Choose when Jet selects CPU or accelerator execution and how experts audit placement, transfers, missing backends, and fallback.
decisions.explainer:
Placement never changes language semantics. Static effect inference is mandatory: any execution policy allowed to choose a GPU carries the existing Gpu effect; a CPU-pinned operation remains pure when its operations are pure. Copies and fallbacks must appear in the plan and trace.

Fable hybrid review: B hands beginners a CUDA-shaped surface; C makes #(Gpu) inference depend on an external policy file, breaking local reasoning about effects; A is the right core but omits the deployment layer services need and understates receipt stability for CI. The hybrid keeps A's call-site law, admits C's policy strictly as a narrowing overlay so effect inference stays sound, and makes every transfer and fallback a stable, diffable receipt.
decisions.story: Sam wants a notebook to use the best available device automatically, a service to require one exact GPU class, and CI to prove that no hidden CPU fallback or host-device copy changed the result or budget.
decisions.detail: The selected policy must cover allocation limits, transfer lifetime, backend absence, remote devices, multi-device placement, deterministic/reproducible profiles, cache identity, and stable audit output. A fallback may vary capability or performance only within an explicit policy; it never silently changes precision, effects, failure, or observable results.

options.name: Automatic safe placement with explicit pins and receipts
options.detail: Beginners choose .Auto and Jet plans placement and transfers. Because .Auto may select an accelerator, the call carries Gpu. Experts pin device, memory, precision, and transfer policy. Missing required capability fails before execution. Any allowed fallback is policy-controlled and emits a stable receipt; no silent fallback exists.
options.code:
// enclosing function carries #(Gpu) because .Auto may choose a GPU
y :: compute.on(.Auto).run(() => model(x)) ?? panic("compute failed")
z :: compute.on(cpu).run(() => pure_model(x))  // remains pure
q :: compute.on(cuda(0), fallback: .Deny).run(job) ?? panic("CUDA required")

options.name: Fully explicit devices and transfers
options.detail: Every device allocation, copy, stream, and launch is authored. This maximizes auditability but makes the beginner path resemble CUDA and prevents safe automatic whole-graph placement.
options.code:
dx :: cuda(0).allocate<Float>(x.shape) ?? panic("allocation failed")
cuda(0).copy_from_host(dx, x) ?? panic("transfer failed")
dy :: kernel.launch(on: cuda(0), input: dx) ?? panic("launch failed")

options.name: Policy-selected backend with visible fallback
options.detail: A project or deployment policy selects preferred backends and an ordered fallback list. Call sites do not pin devices, but dossier/trace records the selected backend and fallback reason. Gpu is inferred whenever the policy permits a GPU. Strict policy can require an exact backend.

options.name: Auto placement with receipts, pins, and narrow-only deployment policy (hybrid)
options.detail: compute.on(.Auto) is the beginner default: Jet plans placement and transfers, and the call carries Gpu because an accelerator may be chosen; CPU-pinned work with pure operations stays pure. Experts pin device, memory, precision, and transfer policy at the call site; a deployment or project policy may only narrow a call site's allowance (pin, deny, cap budgets) and never widen it, so inferred effects remain sound without reading any config file. Every transfer, over-budget allocation, and fallback emits a stable machine-readable receipt in plan, trace, and dossier; fallback exists only where policy names it and never changes precision, effects, failure shape, or observable results. Missing required capability fails at plan time as ComputeBackendMissing.
options.code:
y :: compute.on(.Auto).run(() => model(x)) ?? panic("compute failed")   // carries #(Gpu)
q :: compute.on(cuda(0), fallback: .Deny).run(job) ?? panic("CUDA required")
// deployment policy may narrow train() to cuda-class; it cannot widen cpu-pinned code
$ jet dossier train --compute
placement: CUDA:0; transfers: host->device 64 MiB; fallback: none

comparisons.note: Automatic placement is ergonomic, but device transfer and recompilation can surprise users. Jet should make every transfer and fallback inspectable.
Explicit devices, streams, and copies maximize control. Jet keeps that expert reach through the same ownership/effect model.

decisions.title: Safe Jet kernel authoring and audited raw-device tier
decisions.gist: Choose whether experts can author accelerator kernels in ordinary Jet and where the proof boundary lies.
decisions.explainer:
This ballot proposes no keyword or marker. A safe kernel is an ordinary typed function passed to a Core builder. Sema must prove bounds, address spaces, alias/race freedom, capture legality, barrier uniformity, supported control flow, and backend portability. Raw pointers, vendor intrinsics, or unproved synchronization require the existing #Unsafe("reason") gate.

Fable hybrid review: B gates routine parallel loops behind #Unsafe, making ordinary compute expert-only; C denies the expert reach the owner direction requires; A is directionally correct but leaves the raw boundary contract and kernel determinism unstated — exactly where CUDA-class unsoundness and run-to-run drift leak in. The hybrid types the unsafe boundary, ties race-freedom proof to deterministic execution, and forbids silent proof-to-runtime-check degradation.
decisions.story: Ari uses fused built-in operations for most work, then needs a domain-specific stencil. They want a short safe Jet function first and an audited vendor escape hatch only for the one instruction the portable model cannot express.
decisions.detail: Unsupported safe-kernel constructs fail during sema with the exact proof that is missing. Runtime bounds checks are permitted only when the backend contract preserves them. New syntax, markers, address-space spellings, or external compiler dependencies require follow-up ballots. Raw kernels remain within user-written audited regions and cannot leak unsafe handles into safe code.

options.name: Checked safe kernels plus raw #Unsafe tier
options.detail: Ordinary Jet functions become portable kernels when sema proves memory, race, bounds, capture, and barrier rules. Experts use #Unsafe only around raw device operations or vendor intrinsics, with explicit address spaces and audit output.

options.name: All user-authored kernels require #Unsafe
options.detail: Built-in operations remain safe, but any custom kernel is an audited raw-device region. This keeps compiler proof scope smaller at the cost of making routine parallel code expert-only.

options.name: No user-authored native kernels
options.detail: Jet exposes only safe built-in operations, fusion, and foreign provider calls. Custom native kernels are outside the first-party model. This is coherent only if D-COMPUTE1 does not promise expert kernel authoring.
options.code:
y :: x.zip(other).map((a, b) => a * scale + b)
// compiler may fuse; user cannot name or author the physical kernel

options.name: Proven safe kernels plus contract-bounded #Unsafe raw tier (hybrid)
options.detail: Ordinary Jet functions become portable kernels when sema proves bounds, alias/race freedom, capture legality, barrier uniformity, and supported control flow; a missing proof fails during sema naming the exact obligation and smallest supported rewrite, and never degrades to unproven runtime checking. A proven race-free kernel executes deterministically under the selected backend profile; atomics or reorderable reductions require an explicit policy opt-in recorded in the receipt. Raw device code, vendor intrinsics, or unproved synchronization live only inside #Unsafe("reason") with a typed boundary contract — shapes, address spaces, read/write sets, effects — that sema enforces at entry and exit, so unsafe handles cannot leak into safe code. Raw kernels appear in the dossier unsafe audit, and strict/release profiles reject raw kernels lacking a declared differential test against a reference implementation.

comparisons.note: Full control comes with manual bounds, address spaces, barriers, and race discipline. Jet can prove the common subset and gate the remainder.
comparisons.code: __global__ void saxpy(...) { int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; ... }

comparisons.note: Typed host code helps, but kernel ecosystems often impose separate subsets/toolchains. Jet should keep one language and surface unsupported proof obligations directly.

decisions.title: Automatic differentiation modes, transform validity, and custom derivatives
decisions.gist: Choose Jet's canonical differentiation model, including mutation/control flow limits and the meaning of a custom derivative.
decisions.explainer:
The compiler can prove type, shape, ownership, effect, and transform validity; it cannot prove that a user-supplied derivative is mathematically correct. Optional numerical validation can detect discrepancies but remains evidence, not proof. Unsupported control flow or mutation must fail loudly.

Fable hybrid review: B forces rewriting ordinary simulations into a pure subset (expert-hostile) and C abandons exact differentiation entirely; A is the right shape but silent on gradient determinism, RNG semantics, nondifferentiable-operation policy, and open-world rule patching — the recurring JAX/Julia failure modes. The hybrid pins definition-site rules, an explicit subgradient law, seed-fixed randomness, and policy-inherited deterministic gradients.
decisions.story: Lin differentiates a scalar training loss, computes forward sensitivities for a simulation, and supplies one stable derivative for a custom operation. CI must distinguish exact transformation from numerical approximation.
decisions.inWild:
result :: compute.value_and_grad(loss, at: model.parameters()) ?? panic("gradient failed")
tangent :: compute.jvp(simulate, inputs, directions) ?? panic("JVP failed")
decisions.detail: Every option defines higher-order derivatives, nondifferentiable operations, integer/boolean paths, captured state, randomness, side effects, mutation, loops/branches, checkpointing, complex numbers, sparse values, custom gradients, and deterministic validation. Gradient failures carry source spans and the smallest supported rewrite.

options.name: Reverse default, forward API, checked custom rules
options.detail: Reverse mode is the ergonomic scalar-loss default; forward mode and mixed composition are explicit APIs. Sema accepts mutation/control flow only when the transformation remains valid and rejects unsupported forms. Custom derivatives are type/shape/effect checked and may request numerical validation with stated tolerances; Jet never labels them mathematically proven.
options.code:
grads :: compute.grad(loss, at: params) ?? panic("gradient failed")
tangent :: compute.jvp(step, state, direction) ?? panic("JVP failed")
compute.derivative(custom_op, rule: custom_rule, validate: .Numerical(tolerance: 1e-5)) ?? panic("bad derivative")

options.name: Reverse mode over a pure functional subset
options.detail: Only pure array expressions without mutation, effects, or data-dependent control flow are differentiable. The boundary is simple and predictable; users rewrite simulations and stateful algorithms into the subset.

options.name: Numerical differentiation library
options.detail: No compiler transformation exists. Core evaluates finite differences and returns an ApproxGradient carrying value, estimated error, step, and evaluation count. It never masquerades as exact autodiff.
options.code:
approx: ApproxGradient<Model> :: compute.approx_grad(
    loss, at: params, method: .Central, step: 1e-4
) ?? panic("approximation failed")
print(approx.error_bound)

options.name: Reverse default, composable forward, definition-site checked rules (hybrid)
options.detail: Reverse mode (compute.grad / value_and_grad) is the scalar-loss default; jvp/vjp are explicit APIs that compose for mixed and higher-order derivatives. Sema accepts mutation and control flow only where ownership and the transform proof remain valid; anything else fails as DifferentiationUnsupported with the source span and smallest supported rewrite — never a silently wrong gradient. Integer/boolean paths and nondifferentiable operations are zero-derivative only where an explicit rule declares it, otherwise errors; randomness must flow through injected Rng capabilities (D-DET1) and differentiates with the seed held fixed. Custom derivatives are declared at the operation's definition site — one rule per operation per mode, redefinition is an error — are type/shape/effect checked, and may request .Numerical(tolerance:) validation reported as evidence, never proof. Gradient execution inherits the primal's placement and determinism policy, so a Reproducible profile yields bit-stable gradients.
options.code:
grads :: compute.grad(loss, at: params) ?? panic("gradient failed")
hess_v :: compute.jvp(compute.grad(loss), params, v) ?? panic("HVP failed")
compute.derivative(custom_op, rule: custom_rule, validate: .Numerical(tolerance: 1e-5))?
// unprovable mutation -> DifferentiationUnsupported at the exact span

comparisons.note: Composable grad/jvp/vjp transformations are powerful, but tracer errors and mutation constraints can be obscure. Jet should diagnose the exact unsupported source construct.
Language-integrated derivatives and custom rules demonstrate typed integration; Jet must be explicit about what is mechanically checked versus numerically evidenced.

decisions.title: Accelerator backend portability, precision, determinism, and unsupported behavior
decisions.gist: Choose the contract shared by CPU SIMD, CUDA, Metal, and Vulkan/WebGPU implementations.
decisions.explainer:
A CPU implementation can be the differential conformance oracle, but never a dev-mode substitute for the selected release backend. AOT and dev use the same selected backend and precision/determinism policy. Capability or performance may vary; language semantics, effects, failures, and declared numerical contract may not.

Fable hybrid review: C abandons the native portable model D-COMPUTE1 exists to create; B negotiates capabilities but never names the numerical contract or the conformance oracle; A states the contract but has no typed path for optional hardware features — the WebGPU lesson about the portable floor versus extensions. The hybrid merges both, makes reproducibility the beginner default with fast-math as an audited opt-in, and extends the ratified dev/release byte-parity rule to backend selection.
decisions.story: Omar develops on a Mac GPU, validates on CPU CI, and deploys to CUDA. He needs one declared precision/determinism contract, explicit unsupported diagnostics, and proof that dev did not quietly run a different backend.
decisions.inWild:
policy :: compute.policy(precision: .F32Strict, determinism: .Reproducible)
result :: compute.on(cuda(0), policy: policy).run(job)?
decisions.detail: The selected contract defines supported types/operations, precision and reassociation, reductions, NaN/signed-zero behavior, random streams, atomics, synchronization, memory limits, compilation cache identity, backend/version facts, and tolerance rules for tests. Dossier and traces expose the exact backend and policy.

options.name: Portable semantic contract with loud backend gaps
options.detail: Core defines required semantics and named precision/determinism profiles. Tier backends pass differential suites against the CPU oracle under the selected profile. Unsupported operations fail before launch with alternatives. Dev and release execute the same selected backend/policy; no hidden CPU substitution.
options.code:
$ jet dossier train --compute
backend: CUDA 13.0
policy: F32Strict + Reproducible
unsupported: none
$ jet dev train.jet   # uses the same CUDA backend and policy

options.name: Capability-negotiated backend profiles
options.detail: Each backend publishes a typed capability set. Applications require/prefer capabilities and may select different implementations, but the chosen precision/determinism contract and observable Jet semantics remain fixed. Missing requirements fail during planning.

options.name: Foreign provider bridges only
options.detail: CUDA, Metal, and WebGPU remain explicit gpu.* provider APIs with their own semantics. Core compute is CPU-only. This maximizes honesty but abandons one native portable accelerator model.

options.name: Portable profiles with typed capabilities, CPU oracle, no dev drift (hybrid)
options.detail: Core defines named precision/determinism profiles; the default is F32Strict + Reproducible — same backend, policy, and seeds give identical results, and cross-backend agreement is bounded by the profile's published tolerance. Reassociation, fast-math, and order-nondeterministic reductions exist only as named opt-in profiles recorded in every receipt. Optional features (fp16, subgroups, tensor cores) go through typed capability negotiation that fails during planning with the missing capability named; unsupported operations fail before launch with the nearest supported alternative. Tier backends pass differential conformance suites against the CPU oracle under each supported profile; dev and AOT execute the same selected backend, policy, and compilation cache identity — a dev-time backend substitution is a release blocker per D-DEVMODE1's parity rule — and dossier exposes backend, version, capability proof, and cache identity.
options.code:
policy :: compute.policy(precision: .F32Strict, determinism: .Reproducible)  // default
req :: compute.requires(.Fp16, .Subgroups)
device :: compute.select(req, policy: policy)?   // plan-time proof or ComputeBackendMissing
$ jet dossier train --compute
backend: CUDA 13.0; policy: F32Strict+Reproducible; capabilities: fp16, subgroups; cache: 9f3a
$ jet dev train.jet   # same backend, same policy — divergence is a release blocker

comparisons.note: A portable contract spans vendors but excludes capabilities that cannot be made coherent. Jet should be equally loud about the portable floor and extensions.
CUDA exposes precise device/version/capability facts and deterministic limits. Jet must not hide those facts behind portability.

decisions.title: Canonical application service topology over taskgroups and channels
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet has a first-party service topology and where supervision and deployment facts live, without adding actor syntax or a second scheduler.
decisions.explainer:
This umbrella chooses ownership of service topology only. It does not pre-ratify delivery, durability, identity, workflow, or upgrade policy; linked ballots decide those. Every option reuses typed channels, taskgroups, cancellation, deadlines, and the one runtime. Jetpack continues to own supervised external development processes; JetOS projects deployment facts into system services.

Fable hybrid review: A leaves restart semantics undefined and unreconciled with ratified structured taskgroup lifetimes; B splits application and operational topology into two sources of truth; C loses whole-system checking entirely. The hybrid keeps A's sema-known tree, defines restarts as supervisor-owned child taskgroups with typed budgets and escalation so OTP-style recovery lives inside ratified structured concurrency, and makes deployment projection strictly one-way so the source graph is never contradicted.
decisions.story: Rina grows one in-process API into several workers and then a cluster. She wants the same typed request and stream contracts, structured lifetimes, and diagnostics locally and in production, without learning an actor language or maintaining separate deployment truth.
decisions.detail: A service topology is semantic metadata over ordinary Jet functions, taskgroups, and channels; executable bodies remain TIR. The selected model must define local execution, typed endpoint generation, cancellation/drain, observability, deployment projection, topology inspection, and collision diagnostics. No option permits unbounded mailboxes or ambient authority.

options.name: Sema-known supervised service tree
options.detail: Core builders create a typed service tree. Sema validates endpoints, lifetimes, cycles, effects, and topology; the runtime realizes it with taskgroups/channels. The same graph projects into Jetpack/JetOS deployment and audit without importing those engines into the compiler.

options.name: Typed request and stream graph; deployment owns supervision
options.detail: Core knows endpoint types and call/stream edges but not restart or placement topology. Local code uses taskgroups; Jetpack/JetOS deployment source adds supervision and placement. This keeps compiler semantics smaller but splits application and operational topology.
options.code:
api :: service.graph().endpoint("orders", orders)
// deployment module separately attaches api.orders to a supervised process group

options.name: First-party library-only services
options.detail: Services are ordinary library wrappers over tasks and channels. Explicit deployment descriptors reference them, but the compiler has no topology model. This is flexible and simple, with weaker whole-system checking and explanation.

options.name: Sema-known tree, structured restarts, one-way deployment projection (hybrid)
options.detail: The sema-known tree is the single topology authority: builders promote ordinary functions into named workers and groups; sema validates names, cycles, endpoint types, effects, and lifetimes; the runtime realizes each group as a supervisor task owning a child taskgroup so restarts stay inside structured lifetimes (D-NURSERY1/D-TASKSCOPE1). Restart policy is typed and defaulted — OneForOne with a bounded restart budget and escalation to the parent group on exhaustion — so root.worker(name, fn) is a complete beginner service. Jetpack/JetOS projection is strictly one-way: deployment may place and scale the declared graph but never adds, renames, or supervises children the source does not declare. The same builders are the library API; no second untyped service mechanism exists (I8).

comparisons.note: Supervision trees make failure topology explicit and observable. Jet can preserve that strength through taskgroups rather than a second process language.
Goroutines and channels are simple, but application supervision, lifecycle, and deployment conventions fragment across libraries. Jet can make them one checked product.

decisions.title: Service delivery, retry, idempotency, ordering, and backpressure
decisions.gist: Choose the default message/request delivery contract and the explicit path to durable retries without claiming impossible exactly-once execution.
decisions.explainer:
All mailboxes are bounded. Full queues either wait under a deadline/cancellation context or return a typed Full/Timeout result; they never silently drop. The compiler can check that an idempotency key and transaction/dedup contract exist, but cannot prove an arbitrary handler is semantically idempotent.

Fable hybrid review: A picks the right default but leaves FIFO scope, post-send ambiguity, dead letters, and dedup retention undefined; B makes invisible retry the remote default — a retry-storm and partition-amplification footgun that violates the no-opt-out-footgun rule; C fragments the durable path into external systems and loses uniform receipts. The hybrid keeps A's honest default, imports B's sema enforcement only where retries actually exist, and closes the gaps with typed Ambiguous results, Enqueued/Executed receipts, declared retention, and mandatory dead-letter handling.
decisions.story: Diego submits an order while a worker restarts and the network retries. He needs to know whether the request ran, may run again, or was rejected, and he needs overload to become backpressure rather than memory growth.
decisions.inWild:
receipt :: orders.call(
    PlaceOrder(order),
    delivery: .DurableAtLeastOnce(key: order.id),
    deadline: ctx.deadline
)?
decisions.detail: The chosen law must define FIFO scope, concurrent handlers, cancellation after send, timeout ambiguity, reply loss, retry budget, dedup retention, transactional side effects, poison messages, dead letters, overload metrics, and partition behavior. Exactly-once is rejected as a product claim; durable behavior exposes receipts and ambiguity explicitly.

options.name: At-most-once live default; explicit durable idempotent retry
options.detail: Local/live calls never retry invisibly. A full mailbox waits within the caller context or returns a typed failure. DurableAtLeastOnce requires a typed idempotency key plus a declared dedup/transaction contract and returns a receipt. Handlers may still fail; Jet never claims arbitrary idempotence or exactly-once side effects.
options.code:
now :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .AtMostOnce, on_full: .Wait(ctx.deadline))?
durable :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .DurableAtLeastOnce(
    key: cmd.id, dedup: order_store.transaction
))?

options.name: Automatic at-least-once remote delivery
options.detail: Remote calls retry by default after transport failure. Every remotely callable mutating endpoint must declare an idempotency key and dedup/transaction contract; otherwise sema rejects it. Reads may retry under a bounded policy. Full mailboxes still wait or fail explicitly.

options.name: At-most-once Core only
options.detail: Core provides bounded at-most-once request and stream delivery with explicit timeout ambiguity and no retry. Durable queues, deduplication, and replay are external packages or databases. Lossy delivery exists only as an explicitly named telemetry API, never the service default.
options.code:
result :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .AtMostOnce, on_full: .Fail)?
metrics.lossy().try_emit(sample)  // separate telemetry-only opt-in

options.name: At-most-once default; sema-checked durable retry and dead letters (hybrid)
options.detail: Live calls are at-most-once with per-sender FIFO to a given endpoint; a full mailbox waits under the caller's context deadline or returns typed Full, and a timeout after send returns typed Ambiguous — never a silent retry. DurableAtLeastOnce is the only retry path: sema requires a typed idempotency key, a declared dedup/transaction contract, and a retention window, and the call returns a receipt distinguishing Enqueued from Executed. Retry-budget exhaustion routes the message to a typed dead-letter endpoint the tree must handle; drops exist only in the separately named lossy telemetry API. Exactly-once is never claimed: dedup guarantees at most one committed effect per key within retention only when the handler commits through the declared transaction.
options.code:
now :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .AtMostOnce, on_full: .Wait(ctx.deadline))?  // timeout after send -> typed .Ambiguous
receipt :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .DurableAtLeastOnce(
    key: cmd.id, dedup: order_store.transaction, retain: time.days(7)))?  // receipt: .Enqueued | .Executed
// durable endpoint missing key/dedup -> sema diagnostic; retry budget exhausted -> orders.dead_letters (must be handled)

comparisons.note: At-least-once delivery requires idempotent processing, offsets, and transactional boundaries. Jet should make those facts typed rather than imply exactly-once magic.
Per-sender ordering is clear, but unbounded mailboxes can turn overload into failure. Jet keeps channel backpressure structural.

decisions.title: Service state: ephemeral, snapshots, and event logs
decisions.gist: Choose the first-party persistence relationship for supervised services, excluding durable workflow execution semantics.
decisions.explainer:
This decision covers service state only. Durable workflows, replayed timers, and effectful activities are a separate D-SERVICE-WORKFLOW1 choice. State schemas, migration, consistency, recovery, and storage authority must remain explicit; an in-memory field never becomes durable by accident.

Fable hybrid review: A is directionally right but silent on commit points, corruption, rollback reading newer state, and reuses none of the ratified D-MIGRATE3/4 machinery; B abandons uniform snapshot/recovery tooling; C forces event-sourcing semantics on transactional domains. The hybrid keeps the ephemeral default, gives both adapters a single commit-point law plus the existing migration chain, and converts corruption and version skew into typed refusals instead of silent data loss.
decisions.story: Mei has a cache that should restart empty, an order projection that should restore from a snapshot, and an audit stream that should rebuild from events. She wants those modes visible in the service declaration and dossier.
decisions.inWild:
root.worker("catalog-cache", cache, state: .Ephemeral)
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .Snapshot(order_store, schema: OrderState.v3))
decisions.detail: The selected model defines state ownership, snapshot consistency, event ordering, schema/version identity, migrations, corruption, recovery point, backup, encryption, retention, compaction, transaction scope, and what happens when a rollback cannot read newer state.

options.name: Ephemeral default with typed snapshot or event-log opt-ins
options.detail: Services restart empty unless they explicitly select a typed state adapter. Snapshot and event-log adapters share schema/version/migration/recovery facts but preserve their different semantics. Storage authority is injected, never ambient.
options.code:
root.worker("cache", cache, state: .Ephemeral)
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .Snapshot(store, schema: OrderState.v3))
root.worker("audit", audit, state: .EventLog(log, event: AuditEvent.v2))

options.name: Services are stateless; databases own all durability
options.detail: Core services have no persistence contract. Handlers use typed database clients and rebuild in-memory state explicitly. This keeps runtime semantics small but loses uniform snapshot/migration/recovery tooling.
options.code:
root.worker("orders", (ctx) => orders_from_database(ctx, db))
// database schema and migration remain outside service topology

options.name: Event log is the only durable service state
options.detail: Any durable service records typed events and rebuilds by replay; snapshots are only event-log accelerators. This gives one audit model but imposes event-sourcing semantics on domains better served by transactional snapshots.
options.code:
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .EventLog(order_log, event: OrderEvent.v4))
// snapshots contain log position and are never independent truth

options.name: Ephemeral default; adapters share one commit and migration law (hybrid)
options.detail: Services restart empty unless they declare a typed .Snapshot or .EventLog adapter; both adapters share one schema/version contract that reuses ratified migration{} chains and decode_traced provenance (D-MIGRATE3/4). Durability has exactly one commit point — state.commit() for snapshots, event append for logs — with no ambient mid-handler persistence, and recovery restores the last committed point, reporting applied migrations. Corruption and newer-than-code state are typed refusals: the worker fails start naming the required migration or forward recovery, and quarantine-then-restart-empty exists only as an explicit supervisor policy, never a silent reset. Storage authority is an injected capability; plain database clients remain first-class for state the service does not own.

comparisons.note: Processes commonly keep ephemeral state while durable truth lives elsewhere. Jet can preserve that default and make optional recovery contracts explicit.
Integrated state persistence is ergonomic but can hide storage and consistency boundaries. Jet should expose adapters, schema, and authority in source.

decisions.title: Durable workflow execution, replay, timers, and effectful activities
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet ships a first-party durable workflow layer and how it separates deterministic replay from real-world effects.
decisions.explainer:
A durable workflow is execution semantics, not merely service storage. Replayable code must be deterministic; time, randomness, I/O, and external calls occur through recorded activities. History and version markers must survive code upgrades without silently re-running effects.

Fable hybrid review: A claims deterministic replay but never states the enforcement mechanism despite Jet owning a ratified effect tree; B defers determinism to runtime checks so divergence surfaces in production replay, the exact Temporal failure mode; C outsources the hardest correctness problem to FFI. The hybrid enforces replay purity at sema, adds the lessons A omits — continue-as-new history bounds, per-activity idempotency keys, deploy-time history-compatibility refusal — and keeps workers on the single service substrate.
decisions.story: Ava runs a month-long fulfillment workflow with timers, human approval, payment, retries, and deployment during execution. A crash or upgrade must resume from history without charging twice or inventing a different branch.
decisions.detail: The selected model defines deterministic workflow code, recorded activities, durable timers, retry, cancellation, compensation, history identity, version markers, schema migration, long-lived code upgrades, worker loss, observability, test-time time travel, and effect diagnostics. Ordinary service handlers remain ordinary tasks; workflow restrictions apply only inside the explicit workflow API.

options.name: First-party deterministic workflows over service infrastructure
options.detail: Core provides explicit workflow and activity APIs. Workflow bodies replay deterministically; activities own recorded effects and idempotency. Version markers and compatibility checks protect in-flight histories. The same service deployment and observability substrate runs workers.

options.name: First-party package, not Core/runtime semantics
options.detail: A blessed package implements workflow history and workers over normal service endpoints, timers, and storage. The compiler enforces only ordinary effects; the package performs replay checks and versioning at runtime.
options.code:
use jet.workflow as workflow
flow :: workflow.define(fulfill).activity(charge).timer(wait).activity(ship)

options.name: No first-party durable workflow layer
options.detail: Services, queues, state adapters, and schedulers ship, but long-running durable workflows remain external systems accessed through typed FFI/provider bindings.
options.code:
use js.temporal as temporal
temporal.start("fulfill", order)?

options.name: Effect-checked deterministic workflows, versioned bounded histories (hybrid)
options.detail: Core ships workflow/activity APIs whose bodies sema checks as replay-deterministic through the ratified effect tree (D-EFFTREE1): ambient time, randomness, I/O, channels, and free task spawn are rejected with a deterministic-replay diagnostic naming the recorded equivalent (w.now, w.random, w.activity, w.sleep, w.all). Activities own effects, a typed idempotency key, and retry policy; history identity is workflow id plus run id, and unbounded histories are cut by an explicit w.continue_as law. Version markers gate every branch change, and deploying code incompatible with live histories is refused with the affected history set, feeding D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1 compatibility checks. Workers, durable timers, and observability run on the one service substrate, and the test runtime replays histories under a deterministic clock.

comparisons.note: Deterministic workflow replay plus recorded activities and durable timers is the production bar. Jet can integrate those rules with its effect system and source diagnostics.
Long-lived systems need explicit version compatibility. Workflow histories make the compatibility boundary even stricter than process restart.

decisions.title: Service identity, discovery, cluster authority, and partition semantics
decisions.gist: Choose how typed service endpoints acquire identity and reach local or remote instances without ambient global authority.
decisions.explainer:
A service reference is a typed capability, not a string URL. Local development and production use the same identity contract. Deployment may project placement and discovery facts, but callers cannot discover undeclared services or bypass authentication. Partitions and stale discovery are typed outcomes.

Fable hybrid review: A's own recommended sample panics on unavailability and leaves discovery staleness, rotation overlap, and non-projected endpoints undefined; B repeats operational wiring by hand with no rotation story; C's signed table is auditable but cannot follow dynamic placement. The hybrid delivers A's capabilities through C's signed generational directories with a max-staleness law, dual-generation rotation, typed partition outcomes, and B's explicit connect retained as the audited expert escape.
decisions.story: Tariq calls the same Orders endpoint in a local process and a three-region cluster. He needs mutual authentication, key rotation, explicit authority, and a clear partition result rather than a hidden retry or ambient DNS name.
decisions.detail: The selected model defines logical identity, instance identity, endpoint typing, trust-root ownership, certificate/key issuance and rotation, local-dev projection, discovery freshness, placement constraints, load balancing, authorization, encryption, revocation, partitions, split brain, topology privacy, and audit output.

options.name: Typed capability endpoints with deployment-projected discovery
options.detail: Callers receive only declared typed endpoint capabilities. Jetpack/JetOS deployment projects logical identities to authenticated instances; a project/organization trust module owns roots and rotation. Local dev injects loopback capabilities from the same graph. Partitions, revocation, and stale discovery return typed failures.

options.name: Explicit typed addresses and manual configuration
options.detail: Endpoint types are checked, but applications construct them from explicit addresses, certificates, and policies. There is no first-party discovery or placement projection. This is transparent but repeats operational wiring.

options.name: Injected static deployment name table
options.detail: Build/deploy generates a signed typed table of logical names to endpoints; the application receives that table explicitly at startup. There is no dynamic discovery. Updates require a new table generation and controlled reload.

options.name: Typed capability endpoints over signed generational directories (hybrid)
options.detail: Callers hold only declared typed endpoint capabilities; discovery material arrives as signed, generation-versioned directory snapshots projected by Jetpack/JetOS from source trust policy (D-JPK-PROVIDERAUTH1 roots), and local dev injects loopback capabilities from the same graph with zero configuration. Every resolution carries directory generation and a max-staleness bound; partitions, revocation, expired directories, and stale generations return typed results — never a hidden retry or ambient DNS fallback. Key rotation is dual-generation: old and new credentials overlap for a declared window so no correct caller observes an authentication gap. Explicit service.connect with address and trust root remains the audited expert escape for endpoints outside the projected graph, gated by an explicit trust grant.

comparisons.note: DNS names are convenient but ambient and weakly typed. Jet should project deployment topology into explicit typed capabilities.
Possession of an unforgeable typed reference carries authority. This matches Jet's explicit-grant direction better than global names.

decisions.title: Service generation upgrade, drain, state migration, and rollback
decisions.gist: Choose how running services move between code generations while exposing mixed-version and rollback truth.
decisions.explainer:
No distributed switch is globally atomic under partition. The contract must name its atomic scope and convergence behavior. State rollback is permitted only with reversible migration, dual-write compatibility, or a proven snapshot; otherwise Jet refuses rollback and reports the required forward recovery.

Fable hybrid review: A is the strongest option but is silent on work that outlives the drain deadline and on in-flight workflow histories; B's two-version hot code imports a second runtime and memory model for marginal gain over shard pinning; C accepts downtime and has no mixed-version story. The hybrid keeps A's shard-scoped handoff, adopts B's typed migrate function with plan-time reversibility classification, adds an explicit pin-or-cancel drain-overrun law, and reconciles partitions through the already-ratified staged fleet rollout.
decisions.story: Grace deploys Orders v3 while v2 requests are in flight across three regions. One region partitions after migrating state. She needs bounded mixed-generation behavior, compatible routing, exact health proof, and an honest rollback decision.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet deploy orders --generation v3
plan: validate endpoint/state compatibility -> start v3 -> drain v2 -> switch each routing shard -> retain rollback proof
decisions.detail: The selected model defines compatibility checks, protocol/schema versions, drain deadlines, long streams, health gates, routing-shard atomicity, convergence, partition isolation, mixed-generation visibility, state migration, reversible/forward-only classification, dual writes, rollback window, failure recovery, and audit receipts.

options.name: Generation handoff with scoped switches and proven rollback
options.detail: Jet starts the new generation, validates endpoint and state compatibility, drains old work, and switches traffic atomically per declared routing shard. Global convergence is observable, not claimed atomic. Partitions retain an allowed generation or isolate. Rollback requires reversible migration, dual-write compatibility, or snapshot proof; otherwise deployment exposes forward-recovery state and refuses rollback.
options.code:
use core.time
plan :: service.upgrade()
    .compatible(OrdersV2, OrdersV3)
    .switch_scope(.RoutingShard)
    .migration(service.dual_write(v2_store, v3_store))
    .rollback_window(time.minutes(30))
// dossier lists shards on v2/v3 and convergence deadline

options.name: In-place two-version hot code
options.detail: A runtime process may hold old and new code concurrently and migrate live state through an explicit code-change function. Calls select by generation until old frames drain. This minimizes restart but expands runtime and memory-model complexity.

options.name: Restart-only generations
options.detail: Services stop or drain, state migration runs offline, and the new generation starts. There is no mixed-version routing or hot handoff. Rollback restores only a proven compatible snapshot.
options.code:
$ jet deploy orders --strategy=restart
drain v2 -> stop -> migrate snapshot -> start v3 -> health -> route

options.name: Shard-scoped handoff; classified migrations, typed drain overrun (hybrid)
options.detail: Deployment starts the new generation, validates endpoint and state compatibility, drains, and switches atomically per declared routing shard; global convergence is observed, never claimed atomic. State moves through a typed migrate function classified .Reversible(inverse), .DualWrite, or .ForwardOnly at plan time; a ForwardOnly migration prints a zero rollback window before the switch, and rollback without reversible, dual-write, or snapshot proof is refused with the forward-recovery plan. Work exceeding the drain deadline — long streams and live workflow histories — follows a declared on_exceed policy (.PinShard keeps it on the old generation; .Cancel is explicit), never a silent kill, with pinned shards and mixed generations visible alongside a convergence deadline. Partitioned shards retain their last allowed generation and reconcile on rejoin through the same staged, proof-gated rollout object ratified for fleets (D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1).
options.code:
plan :: service.upgrade()
    .compatible(OrdersV2, OrdersV3)
    .migrate(v2_to_v3, class: .Reversible(v3_to_v2))
    .drain(time.seconds(30), on_exceed: .PinShard)
    .switch_scope(.RoutingShard)
    .rollback_window(time.minutes(30))
$ jet deploy orders --generation v3
// 2 shards pinned on v2 (live streams); rollback proven until 14:32; convergence deadline shown

comparisons.note: Two code versions and code_change support live upgrade, but require strict compatibility discipline. Option B imports that deeper runtime model explicitly.
Rolling replacement and health gates are common, but mixed versions and database rollback remain application concerns. Jet should type and audit those facts.

decisions.title: Cross-platform executable lease security
decisions.gist: Which existing promise changes so executable packages can work safely on macOS and Windows.
decisions.explainer: Jetpack verifies a package, copies its output into a lease snapshot, and must keep every executable name bound to those verified bytes while a child and its descendants run. Linux does this with a private read-only mount. An unprivileged macOS process has no equivalent immutable named PATH view; Windows file handles can block replacement of files but do not alone protect every descendant name lookup. Today the non-Linux backend returns an error for every lease, even data-only outputs; that empty-output bug is ungated and will be fixed. Executable outputs expose a real conflict among three ratified promises: hostile same-user swaps fail before handoff, Linux/macOS/Windows are tier-1 native, and Jetpack uses no root or daemon. No known design keeps all three. The owner must choose which promise changes.
decisions.story: Mira uses one committed lockfile on Linux, macOS, and Windows. She runs a formatter directly and through jet env. Another same-user process swaps the original package path after verification. Jetpack must execute the verified bytes or refuse; it must never follow the replacement. Beginners need one ceremony-free workflow, while experts need exact audit proof of the native protection used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files

# A same-user process renames the verified output and replaces it with a malicious symlink tree.
# Jetpack must execute the leased bytes or refuse, never follow the replacement.

options.name: Protected native lease service
options.detail: Keep tier-1 usability and the hostile-race guarantee by narrowly amending the no-root/no-daemon law. Linux keeps its unprivileged private mount. This option also ratifies new macOS/Windows distribution-installer behavior: official Jet installers register a root-owned macOS LaunchDaemon or Windows LocalSystem service after one explicit admin approval; no new Jet command is added. The service independently re-verifies the locked digest and copies executables into an OS-protected lease directory the caller cannot rewrite. It authenticates the local caller, then impersonates that caller and launches the child under the caller UID/session/token with no root/SYSTEM privileges or inherited service handles. The child PATH puts protected lease bins first, followed by the caller's approved inherited/system PATH; privilege-sensitive service variables and handles are removed, and package executable names can resolve only through protected lease dirs. A jet env lease lives through the shell and all descendants, then deletes after the process tree exits. The service has no network access, never resolves packages, and fails closed if stopped, mismatched, or unverifiable. Ordinary run/env use remains ceremony-free and offline.
options.code:
# During the new official macOS/Windows installer flow ratified by A:
Install protected executable lease service? [yes/no] yes
installed jet-lease-service 1.0.0

$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
[jet:dev] $ formatter --check src/
checked 18 files
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  protected
service            1.0.0, toolchain-matched
request identity   nate, authenticated
child identity     nate, no service privileges
handles/env        service authority removed
PATH                protected lease bins, then approved caller/system bins
network             denied
handoff             root-protected verified lease
same-user redirect blocked

$ jet env  # service stopped or version mismatched
error E1292: protected executable lease service is unavailable
fix: repair the Jet installation; no child or shell was started

options.name: Relax the hostile same-user guarantee
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and tier-1 usability, but explicitly weaken the security law on macOS and Windows. Jetpack uses a private snapshot, restrictive native handles where available, and digest validation immediately before launch. This catches corruption and non-racing swaps, but a hostile process running as the same user can race the final validation and a descendant PATH lookup; post-exit detection cannot undo executed code. Doctor and audit output name the weaker guarantee. This option is an intentional safety downgrade, not an equivalent backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
warning L1292: this host cannot exclude a same-user executable PATH race
why: macos has no unprivileged immutable named PATH view
fix: audit local same-user processes before running executable packages
formatted 18 files

$ jet env
warning L1292: commands in this environment have the weaker macos lease guarantee
[jet:dev] $ sh -c 'formatter --check tests/'
checked 7 files  # a hostile same-user final-lookup race is not excluded

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  guarded, weaker than linux
same-user redirect not excluded

options.name: Fail closed for non-Linux executables
options.detail: Keep no-root/no-daemon and the full hostile-race guarantee. Fix data-only leases on every platform, but reject leases containing executables on macOS and Windows before any child starts. A new registered diagnostic explains that the platform cannot provide the required immutable handoff. This narrows D-JPK-PLATFORM1: macOS and Windows remain native for data libraries and non-executable package operations, but executable packages are Linux-only until an equally safe unprivileged primitive exists.
options.code:
$ jetpack run tools:formatter -- src/
error E1292: executable leases are unavailable on macos
why: Jetpack cannot create an immutable PATH view without a protected service
fix: run this executable package on Linux; mutable cache paths are never used

$ jet env  # project declares formatter executable
error E1292: this environment needs an executable lease unavailable on macos
no shell was started

$ jetpack doctor
executable leases  unavailable
policy             fail closed

$ jetpack build data:unicode-tables
completed  # data-only leases still work

comparisons.note: Nix protects immutable store objects through privileged ownership and a daemon. Option A uses the same concrete authority boundary, but scopes it to verified executable handoff: no resolution, builds, cache networking, or general store ownership.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-store --verify --check-contents
# protected store paths remain outside user write authority

comparisons.note: Linux supplies a private read-only mount view inside an unprivileged user namespace. Jetpack already uses it to map stable PATH names to inherited descriptors.
CreateFile sharing flags can prevent replacement or deletion of opened executables, but a complete PATH solution must also protect directory/name resolution and child handoff.

decisions.title: jetos user-data backup and snapshot declaration
decisions.gist: How a jetos system declares backup/snapshot coverage for /home and other user data — generations (#327) only cover the system store, so there's no restore path for a user's own files today.
decisions.story:
Glossary: a generation is an atomic, versioned record of a full system build/switch (jet os generations, jet os rollback). A snapshot is a captured copy of file data at one point in time. A workload (D-JOS-CONTAINER1) is jetos's existing managed-thing mechanism: pick a backend, get shared image/mounts/secrets/health/resources/proof/rollback fields. Retention is how long old backups are kept before they're pruned.

Alex is editing ~/Documents/report.docx, fat-fingers a find-replace, saves over the good version, and closes the laptop. Ten minutes later Alex wants yesterday's copy back — no git repo, no cloud sync, just "give me my file from before." Priya, on the same jetos machine, wants more: her whole home directory backed up weekly to an offsite bucket, encrypted, in case the laptop is stolen or the disk dies — borgbackup-class protection she already runs on her old distro. Today jetos has no declaration surface for either need.

options.name: Fold backup into the existing generation/rollback engine
options.detail: Backup becomes a scoped extension of the system-generation source: a backup { ... } block inside system.<host> or user.<name>, walked by the same jet os generations / jet os rollback engine already ratified in D-JPK-OSGEN1/D-JOS-USERAPPLY1. No new CLI verb. Rejected: generations were designed for atomic whole-system state transitions triggered by jet os build/switch; backups are periodic captures of mutable data on their own clock. Mixing the two in one history list means a system-config rollback and a file-restore look like the same operation when they aren't — a real safety and long-term-correctness problem, not just an ergonomic one: jet os rollback on a mixed timeline risks reverting unrelated system state when the user only meant to recover a file.
options.code:
# config.jet
system.laptop {
  backup {
    hourly: paths(["~/Documents"])
    weekly_offsite: paths(["~"], encrypted: true, remote: "s3://alex-backup/home")
  }
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42 (system, 2026-07-10 14:00)
backup scope armed: hourly(~/Documents), weekly_offsite(~, encrypted)

$ jet os generations
  42  2026-07-10 14:00  system   switch (kernel bump)
  41  2026-07-10 13:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  40  2026-07-10 12:00  backup   hourly snapshot (~/Documents)
  39  2026-07-09 09:00  backup   weekly_offsite snapshot (~, encrypted)
  ...

$ jet os rollback --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from generation 17 (2026-07-07 14:00)

options.name: Standalone top-level `backup.<name>` mechanism
options.detail: A new declaration kind, independent of generations and of workload: backup.<name> { source, schedule, backend } with its own backend enum (.LocalSnapshot / .EncryptedRemote) and its own CLI surface (jet os backup snapshot|restore|list|verify|prune). Clean separation of concerns, but it duplicates the exact field spine — secrets, health, proof, rollback, resources — that D-JOS-CONTAINER1 already built for workload. That's a second mechanism doing a job ("declared thing with a backend enum, health checks, and a rollback path") the platform already has one mechanism for, which is the I8 violation the workload precedent exists to prevent: the next managed-thing need after this one faces the same fork (extend workload, or mint backup.<name>-style #3), fragmenting the surface further over time.
options.code:
# config.jet
backup.documents {
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  backend: .LocalSnapshot
}

backup.home_offsite {
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  backend: .EncryptedRemote {
    remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
    encryption: .AgeKey(secrets.backup_key)
  }
}

$ jet os backup list documents
  2026-07-10 14:00  snapshot 118
  2026-07-10 13:00  snapshot 117
  2026-07-09 14:03  snapshot  94
  ...

$ jet os backup restore documents --file ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
restored ~/Documents/report.docx from snapshot 94 (2026-07-07 14:03)

options.name: `workload.<name>`-style backend enum, backup as a managed workload
options.detail: Reuses the exact mechanism D-JOS-CONTAINER1 ratified for Container/MicroVM: one workload.<name> declaration, a backend enum that now also includes .Snapshot and .EncryptedRemote, and the same shared fields — mounts (what to capture), secrets (encryption key), health (did the last capture/restore succeed), resources, proof, and rollback. Restore goes through jet os rollback, the exact verb users already know from generations and other workloads — no new CLI surface to learn, and the proof/health machinery already gating container and microVM workloads (partial-write detection, post-action health check) applies to backups automatically instead of needing its own copy. One declaration shape covers 'run a container,' 'run a microVM,' and 'protect this data' — genuinely the same underlying question (what backend manages this, and how do I roll it back) asked three ways.
options.code:
# config.jet
workload.documents_backup {
  backend: .Snapshot
  source: paths(["~/Documents"])
  schedule: .Hourly
  rollback: .Enabled
}

workload.home_offsite {
  backend: .EncryptedRemote
  source: paths(["~"])
  schedule: .Weekly
  secrets: [secrets.backup_key]
  remote: "s3://alex-backup/home"
}

$ jet os build && jet os switch
switched to generation 42
workload documents_backup: healthy (last capture 14:00, 118 snapshots, 3d retention)
workload home_offsite: healthy (last capture 2026-07-09 09:00, encrypted, verified)

$ jet os rollback --workload documents_backup --path ~/Documents/report.docx --at "3 days ago"
