decisions.title: Debugger diagnostics, exits, and recovery
decisions.gist: Choose how debugger failures are named, translated, exited, and recovered.
decisions.explainer:
Scope and dependencies. D-DBG1/2/3 and D-OBS2 remain law. Live open D-DBG-DAP1 owns framing, states, lifecycle, and message ids 22031..22038. Live open D-DBG-NATIVE1 owns E2205 missing/incompatible/untrusted tool and E2206 unsupported host. D-DBG-AUTH1 is live, open, and unratified; its proposed authority law grants nothing until the owner selects an outcome. D-DBG-EDITOR1 is live, open, and unratified; its proposed registration/configuration law grants nothing until the owner selects an outcome. If AUTH1 and EDITOR1 are ratified compatibly, AUTH uses E2240 approval, E2241 environment, E2242 path, E2243 attach authority, E2244 backend authority, E2245 remote; EDITOR contributes E2236 variants below. DIAG1 never changes their authority or UI policy.

Canonical terminal frame for every selected option is exactly four LF-terminated UTF-8 lines, with no headline outside What: `Error [<code>] [<class>]\n What: <what>\n Why: <why>\n Fix: <fix>\n`. Class is exactly `user`, `tool`, or `internal`; brackets, capitalization, one leading space on What/Why/Fix, colon placement, and field order are invariant. ANSI may wrap tokens only in TTY mode and stripping ANSI must reproduce these exact bytes. Related diagnostics follow as separate complete frames; no duplicated headline, `Class:` line, or class suffix after the Fix.

Common laws for every option. Every user/tool failure has a stable Jet E-code, What/Why/Fix, class, redaction, I4 snapshots, and exit/lifecycle truth. A CLI parse failure before a debug request exists is exit 2 and uses existing usage diagnostics. A terminal debug request failure after valid CLI parsing is exit 1. A terminal user cancellation before effect is 0; E2204 remains current interpreted early-quit law. A debuggee completion is not an adapter/request failure: terminal returns existing 0 or runtime 70, DAP emits exited with the real debuggee code then terminated, and a clean adapter exits 0. A failed correlated DAP request receives exactly one failure response but does not by itself exit the adapter; state/lifecycle below decides whether it remains usable. Fatal unsynchronized protocol loss exits adapter 1. Internal invariant failure exits terminal/adapter 101 after fail-closed cleanup. No option turns backend/editor prose into source truth or acknowledges failure as success.

Option A only — specific codes and exact copy. E2230 launch: class user for build/drift/process-create variants and tool for first-frame loss. What `debug launch could not start the selected Jet program`. Why exactly one: `the debug build failed with the Jet diagnostic above`; `the verified program disappeared or changed before launch`; `the operating system denied process creation`; `the program stopped before the debugger established its first Jet frame`. Fix respectively: `fix the earlier Jet diagnostic, then run jet debug <file> again`; `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild and revalidate the program`; `allow this user to start the program, then retry`; `run jet debug <file> again; if it repeats, rerun with --audit <filename> and report E2230`.
E2231 tool attach-after-authority: What `debugger could not attach to the authorized process`. Why `the verified process exited before attach completed`, `the operating system revoked process-control permission`, or `the debugger engine rejected the verified target`. Fix `choose the process again; Jet will revalidate identity and ask for new authority`.
E2232 user protocol: What `debug adapter received an invalid protocol message`. Why `the DAP header or JSON body is malformed`, `request <command> is not legal while the session is <state>`, or `request sequence <seq> was duplicated or invalid`. Fix `restart the debug session; update the editor extension if the message repeats`.
E2233 tool timeout: What `debug operation <operation> did not finish within <duration>`. Why `the debugger engine stopped responding while the session was <state>`. Fix after proved restoration `retry <operation>; if it repeats, restart the debug session`; after unproved attached cleanup `check the target process before retrying; Jet could not prove detach completed`.
E2234 tool backend: What `native debugger stopped speaking Jet's supported protocol`. Why `the verified backend exited unexpectedly`, `the backend returned malformed or unsupported output`, or `the backend executable changed after verification`. Fix `restart jet debug; if it repeats, run jet doctor and report E2234 with the redacted audit`. Discovery remains E2205.
E2235 user map: What `debug map does not match the selected program`. Why `.jetmap is missing`, `.jetmap schema <found> is not supported by Jet <version>`, `.jetmap build id <map-id> does not match program build id <program-id>`, `source hash for <workspace-relative-file> changed after the debug build`, or `a requested Jet line has no stoppable mapped span`. Fix first four `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild both artifacts`; last `move the breakpoint to a Jet statement on a mapped line`.
E2236 user editor/config incorporates latest EDITOR artifact. What `Jet debug configuration is invalid`. Why/Fix pairs: `field <field> <constraint>` / `correct <field> in the editor's Jet debug configuration`; `no runnable Jet file is active` / `open a runnable .jet file or choose Jet: Debug package entry`; `package entry selection is ambiguous: <workspace-relative entries>` / `choose one package entry explicitly`; `Jet extension protocol <editor-version> is incompatible with Jet <jet-version>` / `update Jet and the Jet editor extension to compatible versions`; `the private editor bridge could not authenticate the installed extension` / `reinstall the Jet extension and restart the editor, then retry`; `target path cannot be represented by jet.editor.debug-targets/v1` / `move the Jet source to a UTF-8 path, then retry`.
E2237 tool lost session: What `debug session connection was lost`. Why `the editor, adapter, or debugger control channel closed while the target was <state>`. Fix after proved cleanup `start a new debug session`; unproved `check the target process before starting another session; Jet could not prove <terminate|detach|continue> completed`.
E2238 user stale object: What `debug view is from an earlier stop`. Why `frame, scope, or variable reference <id> expired when execution resumed`. Fix `refresh the editor's stack and variables after the next stop`.
E2239 internal: What `internal debugger error <incident-id>`. Why `Jet could not preserve its debugger invariant; this is a Jet bug, not a problem in your program`. Fix `restart without reusing the session; report <incident-id> and the redacted audit if it repeats`. Exit 101.

Retry semantics. `retryable` is a strict response-field boolean meaning the receiver may automatically repeat the request after receiving this DiagnosticRecord/ErrorResponse. Every emitted debugger diagnostic sets retryable=false. For timeout_read only, Jet may perform one internal identical replay before emitting any DiagnosticRecord or failure response, after proving the same held process and stop generation. It may emit an un-coded DAP progressUpdate `retrying timed-out read once` or equivalent terminal progress, but that progress is not a diagnostic, has no E-code/class/What/Why/Fix, and is absent in non-progress JSON mode. One original request permits at most one replay total; replay cannot recursively replay. Success yields the original request's single success response and no timeout diagnostic. Only a failed replay emits timeout_read with retryable=false. Retry after fixing/changing/choosing/approving/restarting is a new deliberate request, never retryable=true.

Option B/C complete closed reason registry. The following entries are the entire allowed set. Each terminal projection uses the canonical four-line frame above with the stated code/class/What/Why/Fix; there is no hidden table or fallback reason. B uses phase code; C always uses E2230. Every DAP ErrorResponse also carries the stated Jet code, class, reason, and retryable value.
launch_build — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `launch_build: the debug build failed with the Jet diagnostic above`; Fix `fix the earlier Jet diagnostic, then run jet debug <file> again`; retryable false; cleanup `kill only owned child and close owned pipes`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
program_drift — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `program_drift: the verified program disappeared or changed before launch`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild and revalidate the program`; retryable false; cleanup `close owned build/adapter handles; no child exists`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
process_create — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `process_create: the operating system denied process creation`; Fix `allow this user to start the program, then retry`; retryable false; cleanup `close owned pipes and remove owned temporary artifacts`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
program_first_frame — class tool; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `program_first_frame: the program stopped before the debugger established its first Jet frame`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again; if it repeats, rerun with --audit <filename> and report E2230`; retryable false; cleanup `reap owned child and close backend`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee exited(real code)`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
map_missing — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `map_missing: .jetmap is missing`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild both artifacts`; retryable false; cleanup `remove unverified breakpoints; no process effect`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.mapMismatch/22037`.
map_schema — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `map_schema: .jetmap schema <found> is not supported by Jet <version>`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild both artifacts`; retryable false; cleanup `remove unverified breakpoints; no process effect`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.mapMismatch/22037`.
map_build — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `map_build: .jetmap build id <map-id> does not match program build id <program-id>`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild both artifacts`; retryable false; cleanup `remove unverified breakpoints; no process effect`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.mapMismatch/22037`.
map_source — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `map_source: source hash for <workspace-relative-file> changed after the debug build`; Fix `run jet debug <file> again to rebuild both artifacts`; retryable false; cleanup `remove unverified breakpoints; no process effect`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee not-started`; DAP `jet.mapMismatch/22037`.
map_unmappable — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `map_unmappable: a requested Jet line has no stoppable mapped span`; Fix `move the breakpoint to a Jet statement on a mapped line`; retryable false; cleanup `remove only that unverified backend breakpoint`; lifecycle `setBreakpoints request succeeds, response entry stays in request order with verified=false, adapter/state/debuggee unchanged`; DAP `no ErrorResponse and no numeric error id; A Breakpoint.message is exactly E2235: no stoppable Jet statement at <workspace-relative-file>:<line>; B/C Breakpoint.message is exactly E2230: no stoppable Jet statement at <workspace-relative-file>:<line>`.
config_field — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_field: field <field> <constraint>`; Fix `correct <field> in the editor's Jet debug configuration`; retryable false; cleanup `no process effect`; lifecycle `request failed or pre-adapter exit1; adapter state unchanged/not-started`; DAP `jet.invalidArguments/22032 when adapter exists`.
config_no_target — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_no_target: no runnable Jet file is active`; Fix `open a runnable .jet file or choose Jet: Debug package entry`; retryable false; cleanup `no process effect`; lifecycle `pre-adapter exit1; adapter absent; debuggee not-started`; DAP `no DAP message`.
config_ambiguous — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_ambiguous: package entry selection is ambiguous: <workspace-relative entries>`; Fix `choose one package entry explicitly`; retryable false; cleanup `no process effect`; lifecycle `pre-adapter exit1; adapter absent; debuggee not-started`; DAP `no DAP message`.
config_version — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_version: Jet extension protocol <editor-version> is incompatible with Jet <jet-version>`; Fix `update Jet and the Jet editor extension to compatible versions`; retryable false; cleanup `close private bridge; no process effect`; lifecycle `pre-adapter exit1; adapter absent; debuggee not-started`; DAP `no DAP message`.
config_bridge_auth — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_bridge_auth: the private editor bridge could not authenticate the installed extension`; Fix `reinstall the Jet extension and restart the editor, then retry`; retryable false; cleanup `close every received handle and bridge; no process effect`; lifecycle `pre-adapter exit1; adapter absent; debuggee not-started`; DAP `no DAP message`.
config_path_encoding — class user; B terminal `E2230` What `debug setup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `config_path_encoding: target path cannot be represented by jet.editor.debug-targets/v1`; Fix `move the Jet source to a UTF-8 path, then retry`; retryable false; cleanup `close path handles; no process effect`; lifecycle `pre-adapter exit1; adapter absent; debuggee not-started`; DAP `no DAP message`.
attach_exit — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `attach_exit: the verified process exited before attach completed`; Fix `choose the process again; Jet will revalidate identity and ask for new authority`; retryable false; cleanup `prove held target exited; release handle`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee exited(real code)`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
attach_permission — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `attach_permission: the operating system revoked process-control permission`; Fix `choose the process again; Jet will revalidate identity and ask for new authority`; retryable false; cleanup `detach+continue temporary-stop target when applicable and prove it`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee detached-continued`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
attach_backend — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `attach_backend: the debugger engine rejected the verified target`; Fix `choose the process again; Jet will revalidate identity and ask for new authority`; retryable false; cleanup `detach+continue and prove it; unproved becomes detach_unproved`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue; debuggee detached-continued`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
timeout_read — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `timeout_read: idempotent read operation <operation> timed out twice while the session was <state>`; Fix `Jet already retried this read once; restart the debug session or reconnect the editor`; retryable false; cleanup `before replay, send one bounded cancel and prove the identical held process and stop generation`; lifecycle `before any DiagnosticRecord/failed response, replay the identical request once maximum; success gives one success response and no diagnostic; second timeout gives one failed response and leaves adapter at last proved state; debuggee unchanged`; DAP `jet.timeout/22035 only after the replay fails, with retryable=false`.
timeout_effect — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `timeout_effect: effectful operation <operation> timed out while the session was <state>`; Fix `inspect the reported target state, then issue a new deliberate command`; retryable false; cleanup `send one bounded cancel and prove stopped, running, terminated, or detached state`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter last proved state or cleanup termination; debuggee proved state or unknown`; DAP `jet.timeout/22035`.
backend_exit — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `backend_exit: the verified backend exited unexpectedly`; Fix `restart jet debug; if it repeats, run jet doctor and report the selected code with the redacted audit`; retryable false; cleanup `terminate owned child or detach+continue attached target and prove it`; lifecycle `request failed if correlatable; adapter exit1; debuggee terminated or detached-continued`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
backend_output — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `backend_output: the backend returned malformed or unsupported output`; Fix `restart jet debug; if it repeats, run jet doctor and report the selected code with the redacted audit`; retryable false; cleanup `terminate/detach as backend_exit; never parse onward`; lifecycle `request failed if correlatable; adapter exit1; debuggee terminated or detached-continued`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
backend_drift — class tool; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `backend_drift: the backend executable changed after verification`; Fix `restart jet debug; run jet doctor before retrying`; retryable false; cleanup `do not spawn changed backend; clean owned target/build state`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Initialized/continue before target, otherwise exit1 after cleanup`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034`.
stale_reference — class user; B terminal `E2231` What `debug control failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `stale_reference: frame, scope, or variable reference <id> expired when execution resumed`; Fix `refresh the editor's stack and variables after the next stop`; retryable false; cleanup `no cleanup; discard stale reference`; lifecycle `request failed; adapter Stopped/continue; debuggee stopped`; DAP `jet.staleReference/22036`.
malformed_frame — class user; B terminal `E2232` What `debug adapter received an invalid protocol message`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `malformed_frame: the DAP header or JSON body is malformed`; Fix `restart the debug session; update the editor extension if the message repeats`; retryable false; cleanup `apply disconnect defaults; prove terminate/detach when target exists`; lifecycle `no response when uncorrelatable; adapter exit1; debuggee per disconnect cleanup`; DAP `no correlatable DAP id`.

invalid_seq — class user; B terminal `E2232` What `debug adapter received an invalid protocol message`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `invalid_seq: request sequence <seq> was duplicated or invalid`; Fix `restart the debug session; update the editor extension if the message repeats`; retryable false; cleanup `no process effect while stream synchronization is proved; otherwise disconnect cleanup`; lifecycle `request failed and state unchanged if synchronized, else adapter exit1`; DAP `jet.invalidArguments/22032 when correlatable`.
lost_<state> — class tool; B terminal `E2233` What `debug cleanup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `lost_<state>: the editor, adapter, or debugger control channel closed while the target was <state>`; Fix `start a new debug session`; retryable false; cleanup `apply disconnect defaults and prove terminate or detach+continue`; lifecycle `no response if channel gone; adapter exit1; debuggee terminated or detached-continued`; DAP `console record then terminated only if channel survives; otherwise none`.

detach_unproved — class tool; B terminal `E2233` What `debug cleanup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `detach_unproved: Jet could not prove detach completed`; Fix `check the target process before retrying`; retryable false; cleanup `close control handles without claiming detach/continue`; lifecycle `adapter exit1; debuggee unknown`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034 if correlatable`.
continue_unproved — class tool; B terminal `E2233` What `debug cleanup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `continue_unproved: Jet could not prove continue completed`; Fix `check the target process before starting another session`; retryable false; cleanup `close control handles without claiming running state`; lifecycle `adapter exit1; debuggee unknown`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034 if correlatable`.
internal_invariant — class internal; B terminal `E2233` What `debug cleanup failed`; C terminal `E2230` What `debug operation failed`; Why `internal_invariant: Jet could not preserve its debugger invariant; this is a Jet bug, not a problem in your program`; Fix `restart without reusing the session; report <incident-id> and the redacted audit if it repeats`; retryable false; cleanup `perform fail-closed owned cleanup; never assert an unproved outcome`; lifecycle `request failure if correlatable; adapter exit101; debuggee proved cleanup state or unknown`; DAP `jet.unavailable/22034 if correlatable`.

B emits no E2234..E2239. C emits no E2231..E2239. Unknown reason is internal_invariant, never free-form text.

Option A DAP mapping and lifecycle, every code/variant. E2230 all variants -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false for every variant; launch failure response, owned child killed, adapter returns Initialized. E2231 all -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false even after verified detach+continue; attach failure response, adapter Initialized; unproved cleanup escalates E2237/E2239 and terminates adapter. E2232 malformed unsynchronized header/JSON -> no correlatable response and adapter exit 1; invalid_state -> jet.invalidState/22031, retryable false, state unchanged; invalid_seq -> jet.invalidArguments/22032, retryable false, stream remains only if synchronization is proved. E2233 -> jet.timeout/22035 only after timeout_read's one internal pre-response replay fails, or immediately for timeout_effect; every emitted response has retryable=false; proved restoration returns the failure response and keeps the adapter at its last proved usable state; only unproved cleanup escalates to E2237/E2239 and terminates the adapter. E2234 all -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false; fail response if correlation survives, launched child terminated or attached target detached+continued, exited/terminated events only when DAP1 lifecycle requires, adapter exits 1 after cleanup. E2235 missing/schema/build/source during launch -> jet.mapMismatch/22037, retryable false, response failure and Initialized; unmappable breakpoint -> setBreakpoints success with that breakpoint verified=false and exact Breakpoint.message `E2235: no stoppable Jet statement at <workspace-relative-file>:<line>`; no ErrorResponse/id, no session exit, state unchanged. E2236 all -> jet.invalidArguments/22032, retryable false; the stated Fix requires a new request, state unchanged; pre-adapter bridge/config failures have no DAP message and terminal/editor process exit 1. E2237 -> no response if channel is gone; if channel survives, console DiagnosticRecord then terminated, retryable false; adapter exit 1. E2238 -> jet.staleReference/22036, retryable false because refresh creates a new request/reference, request fails, session stays Stopped. E2239 -> jet.unavailable/22034 when correlatable, retryable false, terminated after fail-closed cleanup, adapter exit 101.

Inherited AUTH DAP mapping if AUTH later ratifies. E2240 is not an immediate failed launch: original launch/attach remains pending in AwaitingAuthority; approval continues that same request. User cancel -> jet.cancelled/22038, retryable false, one failure response, Initialized, adapter stays; expiry/broker loss -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false, Initialized. E2241 -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false; environment change/new approval creates a new request, original request fails, Initialized. E2242 -> jet.invalidArguments/22032, retryable false; path correction/new approval creates a new request, state unchanged/Initialized. E2243 -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false; new target verification creates a new request, attach request fails, Initialized with proved detach/continue. E2244 -> jet.unavailable/22034, retryable false; restoration/new session creates a new request; request fails, cleanup then Initialized or adapter exit 1 if backend lost. E2245 -> jet.unsupported/22033, retryable false until a remote decision changes capabilities; request fails, state unchanged.

Option B maps setup E2230 to 22032 for config reasons, 22037 for map reasons, otherwise 22034; control E2231 maps timeout reasons 22035, stale_reference 22036, others 22034; protocol E2232 maps as A; cleanup E2233 maps 22034 when correlatable and terminates. Option C maps its reason through the same semantic id; jetCode remains E2230. Thus every option preserves DAP id meaning rather than forcing one id per Jet code.

Request, process, and adapter outcomes are separate fields. DiagnosticRecord is `{schema:"jet.diagnostic/v1",code,class,severity:"error",what,why,fix,operation,reason?,retryable,requestOutcome,adapterOutcome,debuggeeOutcome,state,exit,source?,redactedDetails?}`. requestOutcome is failed/cancelled; adapterOutcome is continue/exit1/exit101; debuggeeOutcome is not-started/running/exited(code)/terminated/detached-continued/unknown. Terminal exit reflects its direct request; DAP response reflects request; exited/terminated reflect debuggee; adapter process exit reflects transport/internal lifecycle. Tests reject conflation.

E2203 collision migration and retirement. Live source uses E2203 both for interpreter debug boundary and Canvas unsafe-span extract; Canvas has no diagnostics-table ownership. Before debugger E2203 can retire, migrate Canvas atomically to E2935. E2935 What `Canvas extract cannot cross an unsafe source span`. Why `moving only part of an #Unsafe region could change its audited authority boundary`. Fix `select the whole #Unsafe region or extract code outside it`. Add diagnostics.md, jet explain, Canvas JSON/UI snapshot and update tests/canvas.rs in the same change; prove no E2203 remains in Canvas. Then, only after compatible NATIVE1 routing ships, remove debugger E2203 docs/explain/fixtures/tests and reserve E2203 forever. Until both gates finish, E2203 remains live and DIAG acceptance must fail.

Recovery common safety. Record last proved state and cleanup obligation. No blind retry. Launch kills only owned child. Attach follows AUTH held-identity detach/continue. Timeout sends one bounded cancel then proves state. Map mismatch never guesses. One internal pre-response replay is allowed once only for timeout_read with identical arguments, same held process, and same stop generation; no diagnostic exists before it and the emitted record after failure sets retryable=false. Never auto-retry launch, attach, resume, step, terminate, approval, evaluate, writes, stale references, or any request whose Fix requires change. Unproved cleanup becomes the selected option's cleanup/internal reason.

Acceptance is option-scoped. A snapshots every E2230..E2239 Why/Fix and mapping above. B snapshots every closed phase reason and confirms E2234..E2239 absent. C snapshots every closed umbrella reason and confirms E2231..E2239 absent. Every selected option adds diagnostics.md, jet explain, terminal TTY/plain/NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR, JSON schema/goldens, DAP response/event/lifecycle goldens, enabled-editor rendering, exit assertions, redaction, spans, hostile backend/path/secret fixtures, cleanup success/failure, and injected internal invariant. AUTH E2240..45 rows run only if live/open AUTH1 is ratified compatibly; until then they are gated and cannot be marked met. EDITOR-only E2236 rows run only if live/open EDITOR1 is ratified compatibly; until then they are gated and cannot be marked met. Dependency gates cannot be marked met early. NATIVE E2205/06 ownership is explicitly tested. E2203/E2935 migration order is tested.

Beginner pass: one plain What and one safe Fix; process state is never hidden behind editor jargon. Expert pass: code, class, reason, operation, retryability, request/adapter/debuggee outcomes, DAP id, state, redacted identities, and cleanup proof are inspectable. Hybrid pass: terminal, JSON, DAP, and enabled editors project the selected one diagnostic law.
decisions.story: Leah presses Debug on a native Jet service. Her backend is missing, then an old map is found, and later the editor loses the adapter while the process is paused. She needs one precise Jet explanation and safe next action each time—not LLDB text, a generic editor popup, or a false success. CI needs stable codes and exits; support needs redacted machine-readable facts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet debug src/server.jet
Error [E2235] [user]
 What: debug map does not match the selected program
 Why: .jetmap build id 41ac… does not match program build id 7bd2…
 Fix: run jet debug src/server.jet again to rebuild both artifacts
$ echo $?
1

# DAP response; adapter remains alive in Initialized:
{"success":false,"command":"launch","message":"jet.mapMismatch",
 "body":{"error":{"id":22037,"format":"debug map does not match the selected program","showUser":true,
 "variables":{"jetCode":"E2235","class":"user","retryable":"false"}}}}
decisions.detail:
Recommend A. One stable Jet code per recoverable debugger failure family, NATIVE and AUTH ownership preserved, one typed record translated across terminal, JSON, DAP, and editors, with proof-driven recovery and no blind retry. Users get a direct fix; automation branches on stable codes, classes, and exits without ever parsing backend text. B collapses those into four phase codes plus an enumerated reason field, so code-plus-reason searches still work but a bare code search loses the family; C uses one code for everything and cannot be distinguished by CI.

Tier compatibility (D-CANVAS-DEBUG-UX1). The axis here — code granularity — is independent of which engine ran. This one diagnostic law is the failure projection for both backends of the ratified tier-aware direction: a native lldb/DAP session for compiled runs and the in-tier session under `jet dev`. Tool-class native-backend failures (E2234 backend, E2231 attach-after-authority, and the E2205 tool-discovery boundary owned by NATIVE1) arise only for the compiled backend; the in-tier session emits only the tier-relevant subset — map, config, protocol, stale-reference, and internal-invariant families — through the identical four-line frame, ids, classes, and exit truth. The E2203 interpreter-boundary migration already recorded here is the same tier seam. No engine turns backend or editor prose into source truth, and no failure is ever reported as success.

options.name: Specific stable debugger diagnostics
options.detail: Recommended. Assign one stable Jet code per recoverable debugger failure family, preserve NATIVE/AUTH ownership, translate one typed record across terminal/JSON/DAP/editors, and require proof-driven recovery. Users get direct fixes; automation gets stable classes and exits without parsing backend text. Timeout-read replay happens internally before any diagnostic; an emitted timeout is final and retryable=false. Acceptance proves exactly two total backend attempts after a timeout. A replay path that makes a third attempt fails the test.
options.code:
$ jet debug src/server.jet
Error [E2234] [tool]
 What: native debugger stopped speaking Jet's supported protocol
 Why: the backend returned malformed or unsupported output
 Fix: restart jet debug; if it repeats, run jet doctor and report E2234 with the redacted audit
$ echo $?
1

options.name: Phase codes with reason fields
options.detail: Use four stable phase codes with the fully enumerated closed reason registry: setup E2230, control E2231, protocol E2232, cleanup E2233. Classes and exact fixes remain reason-specific—not implied by the phase code—and the registry pins each value. DAP semantics, exits, cleanup proof, and strict pre-response single-replay law remain identical to the matching A reason; automation branches on code plus reason. Timeout-read replay happens internally before any diagnostic; an emitted timeout is final and retryable=false. Acceptance proves exactly two total backend attempts after a timeout. A replay path that makes a third attempt fails the test.
options.code:
Error [E2230] [user]
 What: debug setup failed
 Why: map_build: .jetmap build id 41ac… does not match program build id 7bd2…
 Fix: run jet debug src/server.jet again to rebuild both artifacts

{"code":"E2230","class":"user","reason":"map_build","requestOutcome":"failed","adapterOutcome":"continue","retryable":false}

options.name: Single typed debugger diagnostic
options.detail: Use E2230 for every debugger failure with mandatory class, phase, closed reason, lifecycle outcomes, and reason-specific What/Why/Fix. This minimizes codes without leaking tool/editor prose or weakening I4, but code-only searches and CI cannot distinguish failures. Timeout-read replay happens internally before any diagnostic; an emitted timeout is final and retryable=false. Acceptance proves exactly two total backend attempts after a timeout. A replay path that makes a third attempt fails the test.
options.code:
Error [E2230] [tool]
 What: debug operation failed
 Why: control: backend_output
 Fix: restart jet debug; if it repeats, run jet doctor with the redacted audit

{"code":"E2230","class":"tool","operation":"control","reason":"backend_output","adapterOutcome":"exit1","retryable":false}

comparisons.note: Rust assigns stable diagnostic codes to user-actionable compiler failures, while crashes are explicit internal errors. A applies that separation to debugger orchestration and keeps external tool text subordinate.
comparisons.code:
error[E0382]: use of moved value
internal compiler error: unexpected panic

comparisons.note: DAP standardizes request failures and lifecycle events but leaves adapter-specific copy and ids. A preserves DAP1's ids while carrying the stable Jet code and recovery class.
Native debuggers often emit command-oriented text tied to engine state. A treats that text as untrusted evidence and reports a Jet operation, state, and safe fix.
comparisons.code:
error: process attach failed
# becomes E2231 with Jet attach recovery

decisions.title: DNS resolver trust and platform contract
decisions.gist: Choose how ordinary DNS lookups use the host, validate replies, and fall back.
decisions.story: Mira runs the same service on Linux, macOS, Windows, a VPN, and a corporate split-DNS network. A lookup must honor each host's resolver policy, never silently send private names to a public resolver, reject forged packets, and still allow an expert to query a named DNS server.
decisions.inWild:
use core.net as net

addrs :: net.resolve_ip("db.corp.example")?
records :: net.DnsResolver.at("10.20.0.53:53").txt("_policy.corp.example")?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: the host resolver is automatic. Expert pass: one typed resolver handle controls server, deadline, and audit-visible behavior. Hybrid pass: both return the same record types and NetError law. Security law: unpredictable IDs; source, ID, QR, opcode, question, class, RCODE, bounds, compression-loop, and truncation validation; UDP TC retries over TCP; no invented public fallback. Platform law: native resolver configuration on Linux, macOS, Windows, BSD; search domains and hosts-file behavior belong only to the system path. Dependency law: std/OS APIs or an owner-approved runtime bridge outside compiler seam crates; never a compiler dependency; any bootstrap bridge carries native-ize ownership.

options.name: System default plus strict first-party wire resolver (recommended)
options.detail: Ordinary calls delegate to the platform resolver and preserve VPN, search-domain, hosts-file, and enterprise policy. `DnsResolver.at` is the single expert escape hatch and uses a strict first-party UDP/TCP DNS client. Missing/invalid host configuration is an error, never a public fallback.

options.name: Strict first-party resolver for every lookup
options.detail: Every call parses platform resolver configuration, then sends validated DNS itself. This gives uniform packet behavior but partially reimplements platform policy and can diverge from VPN, mDNS, hosts files, NSS, and Windows resolver behavior.

options.name: Approved resolver bridge for every lookup
options.detail: A vetted runtime resolver bridge owns platform policy and DNS parsing. It may be bootstrapped behind the Core FFI boundary only after separate dependency approval; the compiler remains dependency-free and the bridge must expose Jet's exact errors and deadlines.

comparisons.note: `net.Resolver` uses system or Go resolution depending on platform/config and offers an explicit resolver hook; Jet should keep one typed result/error law.
`ToSocketAddrs` follows the platform but does not expose TXT/SRV; ecosystem DNS clients add explicit wire resolution.

decisions.title: Socket bytes, text helpers, and close law
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical payload and shutdown model for TCP, UDP, and Unix sockets.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a database driver whose frames contain arbitrary bytes and half-closes its request side before reading the reply. He also writes a beginner echo server that should remain pleasant for UTF-8 text.
decisions.inWild:
conn :: net.Tcp.connect("127.0.0.1:5432")?
conn.write_all(frame)?
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
reply :: conn.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: `read_text` and `write_text` make the echo case obvious. Expert pass: bytes preserve every protocol, partial reads/writes, limits, peer EOF, half-close, local close, and UDP truncation metadata. Hybrid pass: text helpers are checked projections over the same byte operations, not a second transport; the same byte operations are the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` stream contract (D-IO2 `FileReader`/`FileWriter`, D-ENCSTREAM1 codec stream modes), so stream sockets and a wrapped TLS stream compose with the same generic middleware as files and codecs. Datagram law: UDP is packet-oriented, never a byte stream, so it keeps `receive` with source, original length, and `truncated`, and does not implement the stream contract. Socket-only facts (half-close, peer address, readiness) stay first-class inherent methods, never trait-probed capabilities. Unix sockets are available on Unix; unsupported targets reject at compile time when target is known, otherwise return `.Unsupported(.UnixSocket)`. Close law: `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Option D subtlety: conformance reuses the reserved `Reader`/`Cursor` core names under D-IO2's user-type-wins guard and adds no new trait or transport; a socket read through generic `Reader` middleware and a direct `conn.read` are the identical byte operation, so there is one canonical mechanism, not two.

options.name: Bytes canonical, checked text helpers
options.detail: TCP/Unix `read(limit)` returns bytes and empty bytes means EOF; `write` returns count; `write_all` loops. UDP packets contain bytes, source, original length, and `truncated`. `read_text` validates UTF-8. `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Sockets carry these operations as their own methods only, so generic buffering, framing, or codec middleware cannot compose over them without a socket-specific adapter.
options.code:
chunk :: conn.read(64.kib)?
if chunk.is_empty() { print("peer closed") }
conn.write_all(chunk)?
line :: conn.read_text(8.kib)? // invalid UTF-8 => .InvalidText
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
conn.close()?

packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?
if packet.truncated { return .PacketTooLarge(packet.original_len) }

options.name: Generic readable/writable stream trait
options.detail: Sockets expose bytes through shared `Reader`/`Writer` traits; text uses Core codecs. This unifies files, TLS, and sockets, but makes socket-only facts such as datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness additional capability methods.
options.code:
chunk :: io.read(conn, 64.kib)?
io.write_all(conn, frame)?
net.shutdown(conn, .Write)?
packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?

options.name: Keep String payloads
options.detail: TCP, UDP, and Unix operations remain UTF-8-only. Arbitrary protocols fail with invalid-text errors and UDP cannot safely represent all datagrams, so Core cannot meet the raw-socket mandate.
options.code:
text :: conn.read()?
// binary frame => error: tcp read: invalid UTF-8

options.name: Byte-canonical sockets that also conform to the shared Reader/Writer contract (recommended)
options.detail: Recommended. Keep every byte and close rule of A, and additionally make stream sockets (TCP, Unix) and the wrapped TLS stream implement the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` core contract (D-IO2, D-ENCSTREAM1) so files, codecs, TLS, and sockets all compose with one generic middleware set. `read_text`/`write_text` stay checked UTF-8 projections over the same bytes. Socket-only facts stay first-class inherent methods, so datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness are never capability probes. UDP stays datagram-only and does not implement the stream contract. This dominates A by adding generic composition at no cost to socket richness, and dominates B by keeping datagram and half-close facts concrete instead of trait-probed and text a checked projection instead of a separate codec step.

comparisons.note: Connections read/write byte slices and expose half-close on TCP; text is layered above.
`Read`/`Write` are byte-oriented; `shutdown` selects read, write, or both.

decisions.title: Typed network error law
decisions.gist: Choose what callers can reliably inspect when networking fails.
decisions.story: Asha retries timeouts, reports DNS not-found without retrying, and removes a Unix-socket feature on unsupported targets. String matching would make those decisions depend on OS wording.
decisions.detail: All fallible core.net operations return `? NetError`; stable cases include InvalidInput, PermissionDenied, AddressInUse, AddressUnavailable, ConnectionRefused, ConnectionReset, NotConnected, Closed, Timeout, Cancelled, Unsupported, Dns, Tls, Protocol, and Other. Each carries operation plus relevant address/name and a display message; raw OS code is optional expert audit data, never control-flow law. Compiler diagnostics cover statically known target/API misuse; runtime failures remain values.

options.name: One structured NetError family (recommended)
options.detail: One exhaustive top-level network error with nested DNS/TLS/protocol detail. Stable variants drive logic across platforms; `message`, `operation`, `address`, `os_code` support reporting/audit. Deadline and cancellation are distinct.

options.name: Per-operation error enums
options.detail: ConnectError, ReadError, DnsError, and TlsError precisely enumerate each call. Callers gain narrow types but generic middleware must repeatedly translate them and the same OS event can acquire divergent names.
options.code:
conn: TcpStream ? ConnectError :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)
chunk: Bytes ? ReadError :: conn.read(64.kib)

options.name: Keep String errors
options.detail: Every operation preserves human-readable strings only. This is easy to print but unsafe for retry, fallback, metrics, and cross-platform control flow.

comparisons.note: `net.Error` exposes timeout/temporary behavior while concrete errors retain operation and address.
comparisons.code: if ne, ok := err.(net.Error); ok && ne.Timeout() { ... }

comparisons.note: `io::ErrorKind` gives stable categories plus optional raw OS codes.

decisions.title: Socket deadlines, cancellation, and readiness
decisions.gist: Choose how one socket model serves scripts and high-concurrency tasks.
decisions.story: Leo writes a simple health check, then grows it into ten thousand concurrent probes. The same socket calls must honor the surrounding task budget, permit an explicit per-operation deadline, cancel promptly, and expose readiness without creating async-only socket types.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: blocking-looking calls automatically observe current #Context. Expert pass: named `deadline:` override, cancellation token/context, readiness interest, and scheduler integration use the same handle. Hybrid pass: no AsyncTcpStream type. Precedence: earliest of current context deadline and explicit deadline; cancellation returns `.Cancelled`; expiry returns `.Timeout`; manual socket timeout is persistent configuration and cannot extend a context budget.

options.name: Context-aware calls plus readiness on same handles (recommended)
options.detail: Every blocking-looking operation yields through the shared runtime where available, checks cancellation, and obeys the earliest budget. Experts call `ready` or pass named deadlines on the same Tcp/Udp/Unix/DNS handles. Native-thread fallback preserves semantics without claiming multiplexing.

options.name: Context-only blocking calls
options.detail: Operations observe #Context but expose no readiness or per-call override. Simple and coherent, yet expert event loops cannot integrate sockets without a second lower-level API.

options.name: Separate async socket types
options.detail: Blocking sockets remain simple while AsyncTcp/AsyncUdp own cancellation and readiness. This splits semantics and violates the ratified one-handle hybrid direction.
options.code:
conn :: await net.AsyncTcp.connect(host)
chunk :: await conn.read(64.kib)

comparisons.note: Blocking-looking operations are runtime-polled; context is commonly passed to dialing and DNS while connection deadlines interrupt I/O.
Structured cancellation applies through coroutine context while sockets remain resources.

decisions.title: TLS layering over socket streams
decisions.gist: Choose how TLS wraps sockets without creating a second I/O model.
decisions.story: Noor connects through a preconfigured TCP socket, sets SNI and verification policy, reads binary protocol frames, and needs the same deadline, cancellation, close, and audit behavior before and after TLS.
decisions.inWild:
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
tls :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: "api.example.com")?
tls.write_all(frame)?
reply :: tls.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: D-TLS1 remains law: safe HTTPS defaults use rustls and system roots; advanced client TLS configuration lives in core.tls. This ballot only fixes stream composition. Default verification cannot be disabled outside the audited expert/unsafe policy already governing TLS. ALPN, roots, client identity, SNI, protocol versions, handshake deadline, peer identity, and close-notify are explicit expert controls. Runtime rustls bridge remains outside compiler seam crates under the existing approved dependency/native-ize law.

options.name: core.tls wraps the canonical byte stream (recommended)
options.detail: `tls.client` consumes a connected TcpStream and returns TlsStream implementing the same byte/readiness/deadline/close law. Safe defaults verify hostname with system roots. `TlsClientConfig` adds roots, ALPN, identity, and version bounds; insecure verification is unavailable here.
options.code:
cfg :: tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_alpn(["h2", "http/1.1"])
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
secure :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: host, config: cfg, deadline: 3.seconds)?
secure.write_all(frame)?
secure.close()? // sends close-notify, then closes transport

options.name: TLS methods remain inside core.net
options.detail: `net.tls_connect` consumes TcpStream and returns a separate TlsStream API. This keeps current placement but mixes transport and security policy, duplicates read/write functions, and conflicts with core.tls ownership of advanced configuration.
options.code:
secure :: net.tls_connect(tcp, host)?
net.tls_write(secure, text)?
net.tls_close(secure)?

options.name: TLS only through core.http
options.detail: Raw TLS is hidden; HTTPS works but database, mail, messaging, and custom protocols cannot securely compose over sockets.
options.code:
response :: http.Client.get("https://api.example.com")?
// no raw TLS stream for another protocol

comparisons.note: A TLS connection wraps transport I/O while configuration owns roots, SNI, ALPN, and protocol versions.
TLS wraps `net.Conn`, preserving deadline and address behavior while adding handshake/peer state.

decisions.title: Represent the shared byte-stream Reader and Writer contract
decisions.gist: Choose the real generic contract that lets one middleware implementation consume files, TCP, Unix, and TLS streams.
decisions.story: Mina writes a length-prefixed protocol reader against a file capture, then points the same code at a TCP connection and a TLS connection in production. D-NETIO1 promises that this is one generic middleware path, but Jet currently has only concrete FileReader/FileWriter methods and an unrelated binary.Reader cursor; there is no contract a generic parameter can name.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO1=D ratified generic composition while also saying to add no new trait and reuse the existing D-IO2 FileReader/FileWriter law. Repository truth has no generic Reader/Writer law to reuse: FileReader/FileWriter are concrete opaque handles, while core.binary.Reader is a consuming in-memory parser. This ballot clarifies representation without changing byte-canonical I/O, checked text projection, UDP exclusion, or socket-only inherent methods.

options.name: Public io.Reader and io.Writer traits (recommended)
options.detail: Amend the no-new-trait sentence and define two ordinary nominal core.io traits. FileReader, FileWriter, TcpStream, UnixStream, and TlsStream receive real implementations; codecs can implement or wrap them. Beginners keep calling inherent read/write methods with no ceremony. Experts can name bounds and write normal reusable middleware. The compiler uses the existing trait system, so there is no second structural dispatch mechanism.

options.name: Compiler-known structural stream contracts
options.detail: Keep the no-new-trait wording. The compiler treats any approved core handle with matching read/write signatures as Reader/Writer for generic bounds, without a user-declarable trait implementation. Beginner calls remain unchanged and built-in middleware composes, but experts cannot implement the contract for their own safe stream type; Jet gains a second, privileged conformance system beside nominal traits.

options.name: Closed core Stream sum type
options.detail: Keep concrete handles and make middleware accept a core-owned Stream value constructed from file, TCP, Unix, or TLS handles. This supplies one implementation for built-in transports but moves/boxes handles into a closed wrapper and prevents third-party stream participation. Socket-only operations require recovering the concrete handle before use.
options.code:
source :: io.Stream.from(file)
target :: io.Stream.from(tls)
io.copy(&source, &target)?

// peer_addr is unavailable until the TCP handle is recovered

comparisons.note: std::io::Read and Write are nominal traits implemented by files, TCP streams, Unix streams, and TLS wrappers; generic middleware names those bounds directly.
comparisons.code: fn copy<R: Read, W: Write>(r: &mut R, w: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64>

comparisons.note: io.Reader and io.Writer are structural interfaces; files, network connections, TLS connections, and user types compose through the same tiny contracts.
comparisons.code: func Copy(dst Writer, src Reader) (written int64, err error)

decisions.title: Exact Reader and Writer contract law
decisions.gist: Define the exact error, receiver, EOF, partial-write, close, and codec laws for the ratified core.io Reader and Writer traits.
decisions.story: Mina writes one bounded frame relay, tests it against a file capture, then runs it over TCP and TLS. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A chose public nominal traits, but did not say whether the relay preserves NetError versus IOError, whether reads and writes borrow mutably, what zero bytes mean, or whether closing belongs to generic middleware. Those details decide whether one safe implementation really works across every stream.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A remains binding direction: public nominal traits under core.io. Clarification is required because its worked example assumed one IOError even though files, sockets, TLS, and codecs currently expose distinct typed failures. Every option below fixes exact namespace, error law, receivers, EOF/limit behavior, partial writes, write_all, close ownership, and codec conformance. All preserve D-NETIO1=D: bytes canonical, UDP excluded, socket-only facts inherent, checked text layered over bytes.

options.name: Associated Error per stream
options.detail: Exact namespace: core.io.Reader and core.io.Writer. Each has associated type Error. read(&self, limit) and write(&self, bytes) use mutable-borrow receivers because cursor/transport state advances without consuming the handle. limit must be positive; read returns at most limit bytes; empty bytes alone means clean EOF; failures retain the concrete FileError/NetError/TLSError/EncodingError. write may return any positive prefix count and zero for nonempty input is an error; write_all is one default trait method that loops until complete or returns Error. close and socket shutdown are not trait members: resource handles own inherent idempotent close, RAII remains fallback, generic middleware never steals ownership. Codecs conform only through explicit Reader/Writer adapter types whose Error is EncodingError and which delegate to one underlying stream; direct encoders/decoders do not claim byte-stream conformance.

options.name: One core.io.IOError for every stream (recommended)
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but both traits return core.io.IOError. File, TCP, Unix, TLS, and codec adapters convert their native failures into one closed IOError tree carrying operation, source category, address/path, OS code, and cause. This makes Reader-to-Writer middleware use one error type, but callers lose direct NetError/TLSError/EncodingError matching at the generic and inherent byte-operation boundary. Close remains inherent and idempotent; codecs conform only through explicit byte-stream adapters.

options.name: Universal Error at contract boundary
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but trait methods return universal Error through the ratified Fallible conversion path. Concrete inherent methods keep NetError/TLSError/etc.; only calls through a Reader/Writer bound erase to Error. write_all remains the sole default looping implementation. Close remains inherent and idempotent. Explicit codec adapters implement the traits and erase EncodingError only at the generic boundary.

comparisons.note: Read and Write use mutable receivers, empty successful read means EOF, write may be partial, write_all loops, and Close is outside both traits; Rust unifies failures as io::Error.
comparisons.code:
fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize>
fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize>

comparisons.note: Protocols can preserve concrete associated types, matching Jet's existing associated-type feature and retaining transport-specific failures.

decisions.title: Attach option priority without colliding with real option keys
decisions.gist: Choose the typed source form that attaches Default, Force, or Priority(n) to one option contribution without reserving ordinary dotted keys such as filesystem.swap.fast.priority.
decisions.story: Two reusable modules choose different display managers. The baseline should be overridable, the site policy should normally win, and an emergency module may force a value. Separately, a swap device legitimately has an option named priority. Jet must distinguish precedence metadata from that real setting, show every contender in explain output, and never silently reinterpret a user's option key.

options.name: Typed contribution record
options.detail: An ordinary value remains the beginner path. An expert wraps only the contribution that needs precedence in OptionValue.{ value, priority }, where priority is .Default, .Force, or .Priority(n). The record is structurally distinct from dotted option keys, so filesystem.swap.fast.priority remains ordinary data. Explain output projects the wrapper fields but the option consumer receives only value.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: OptionValue.{ value: "sddm", priority: .Default },
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: true,
]

options.name: Priority value wrapper
options.detail: Default(value), Force(value), and Priority(n, value) wrap one contribution directly. This is compact and unambiguous, but the named tiers look like general calls and mix policy with value construction. Every supported value type must pass through the wrapper unchanged.
options.code:
options: [
  services.displayManager: Default("sddm"),
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  services.audio.enable: Force(true),
  kernel.package: Priority(2500, packages.cachyos),
]

options.name: Contribution attributes
options.detail: Attributes attach policy before one option entry. The relationship is visually clear and does not consume dotted keys, but it creates new attribute vocabulary and makes list-entry formatting carry semantic state outside the value expression.
options.code:
options: [
  #[Default] services.displayManager: "sddm",
  filesystem.swap.fast.priority: 5,
  #[Force] services.audio.enable: true,
  #[Priority(2500)] kernel.package: packages.cachyos,
]

comparisons.note: Nix wraps a value with mkDefault, mkForce, or mkOverride. The wrapper is unambiguous, but Jet can keep its expert form typed instead of relying on dynamically interpreted functions.
CSS attaches !important to one declaration, not to a separate property named priority. This preserves unrelated property names but provides only one override tier.

decisions.lesson:
A declarative system builds one final configuration by combining contributions from many modules. Two modules can set the same option, so the system needs a precedence rule: which contribution wins, and why? A default is a weak suggestion meant to lose to ordinary configuration. A normal value is the usual choice. A forced value is an explicit override meant to beat ordinary choices. Numeric priority adds finer ordering when three tiers are not enough.

This priority is metadata about a contribution, not part of the configured value itself. For example, the value may be the text gdm while the metadata says this is only a default. The final service receives gdm, not a wrapper or priority number. Explain output should still retain every contender and its source so a user can understand the winner.

The naming collision matters because real configuration paths may themselves end in priority, such as a swap device priority. Jet must distinguish that ordinary option key from merge metadata without guessing from its spelling. This ballot chooses the source form that makes that distinction explicit while keeping simple values simple.

decisions.title: Retire benchmark budget prototypes
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet removes the old benchmark helper without losing meaning.
decisions.story: Mina has old benchmark calls. Some only run a workload, while others use the returned true-or-false value. Jet must remove the old helper without inventing performance rules or silently changing control flow.

options.name: Narrow mechanical source migration
options.detail: Jet converts only calls whose meaning is fully clear. It preserves the workload when a matching typed budget already exists, and refuses every uncertain case.
options.technical: Before deleting the prototype, the repository migration pass may transform a call only when all of these AST conditions hold: it is a direct expression statement whose value is discarded; callee resolves exactly to core.testing.bench_budget; arguments are exactly a static string literal name, nonnegative integer literal max_ns, and a zero-parameter lambda; the lambda captures no local binding and references only package-visible functions/constants/imports; exactly one #Bench with the same name is absent; and exactly one existing BudgetSpec in the same package already has scope .Bench(name), metric .BenchTime(percentile), provider .BenchMeasurement(name), comparison .AbsoluteFrom(baseline), and limit .AtMost(max_ns ns). The pass lifts the lambda body byte-semantically into #Bench(name), deletes only the expression statement, and changes no BudgetSpec. It refuses rather than inventing a percentile, baseline, sampling policy, role, or module location. Any call used as an argument, return, condition, binding initializer, interpolation, operator operand, assertion value, or other value-producing expression is not transformed. After the repository migration, delete the Core item, sema signature, TIR/prelude helper, JET_BENCH_VERBOSE behavior, fixed 3/10 sampling, mean/stddev output, Bool result, and enforcement. All remaining calls receive the canonical unresolved Core-member diagnostic already used for absent members; no special old-syntax diagnostic remains. jet bench measures #Bench through the shared engine only.

options.name: Delete without source transformation
options.detail: Jet deletes the old helper and converts nothing automatically. Every user must rewrite the workload and performance policy by hand.
options.code:
#Bench("parse-large") { parse(large_fixture) }
Budget.{ name: "parse-large-time", scope: .Bench("parse-large"), metric: .BenchTime(.P95), comparison: .AbsoluteFrom("ci/linux-x64"), limit: .AtMost(5000000ns) }
options.technical: Keep #Bench and BudgetSpec exactly as ratified and mechanically remove every first-party prototype use during implementation. The retirement ledger maps name to Bench identity, body to #Bench body, and max_ns to the user's typed AtMost Duration intent; it records fixed warmups/trials, floating mean/stddev, stderr, environment-controlled rendering, and Bool as removed semantics with no equivalent. Delete the complete helper path. External remaining calls receive the normal unresolved-member diagnostic and require explicit user-authored percentile, baseline, and policy.

options.name: Transform workloads only, never thresholds
options.detail: Jet converts safe workloads but always drops the old time limit. Users must recreate every performance limit by hand, even when an exact typed match already exists.
options.technical: Apply A's exact discarded-result, literal, zero-capture, no-existing-#Bench AST conditions but do not require or create a matching BudgetSpec. Lift only the workload to #Bench and explicitly retire max_ns plus all old sampling/output/Bool semantics. This preserves executable benchmark coverage while forcing every performance policy choice to be authored explicitly under GRAMMAR1. Value-consuming calls are refused and later receive the canonical unresolved-member diagnostic.

comparisons.note: Mechanical migrations apply only where meaning is fixed and reject context-sensitive rewrites; A uses that same boundary without shipping a user command.
A named benchmark defines workload while the harness owns measurement; no Bool-returning threshold helper survives.

decisions.lesson:
A benchmark workload and a performance budget answer different questions. The workload says what code to measure. The budget says what metric matters, how samples are summarized, what baseline or absolute limit applies, and whether failure blocks the build. Keeping these separate lets one benchmark support different policies without hiding measurement rules inside a helper call.

The old bench_budget prototype mixed both jobs: it named and ran a lambda, chose fixed warmups and trials, computed a floating mean, printed its own report, compared nanoseconds, and returned Bool. The newer design uses #Bench as the sole workload declaration and BudgetSpec as the sole typed policy. Percentile, units, baseline, sampling, and enforcement become explicit and shared with canonical reports.

Retirement must not pretend old data means more than it did. A source migration may safely lift a clearly identified, capture-free workload, but it cannot invent a percentile or baseline the user never chose. Calls whose Bool result affects control flow also cannot be deleted mechanically. This ballot chooses the exact boundary between narrow automatic conversion and explicit removal, while ensuring no second benchmark evaluator survives.

recommendation.why: A preserves work and policy only when Jet can prove the result is the same. It removes the old evaluator without guessing about missing rules.

whyNot.reason: B is honest but discards conversions that are mechanical and fully provable.
C preserves more workloads than B, but still throws away a limit when Jet can prove an exact typed replacement.

recommendation.tradeoff: A has strict conversion rules, so many unusual calls still need manual edits. Refusing uncertain cases is safer than inventing meaning.

hybrid.synthesis: A combines strict honesty with safe workload conversion and preserves a limit only when an exact typed budget already exists.

harvest.use: Keep these narrow checks as the conversion gate.

harvest.aspect: Migration must not invent missing policy.
harvest.use: Refuse every call whose policy is not already explicit.
Lift the workload whenever the narrow checks prove it safe.

decisions.title: Retire game budget prototype
decisions.gist: Choose which old game limits become real measured performance budgets.
decisions.story: Jo wrote limits for frame time, memory, assets, and draw calls. The old object only stored those numbers. Jet must decide which limits become real measurements and which are retired.

options.name: Add exact scene asset and draw metrics
options.detail: Jet adds precise asset-size and draw-call measurements. It then converts all four old limits into budgets backed by a fixed scene test.
options.technical: Atomically amend GRAMMAR1 with SceneAssetBytes (Bytes; Scene + SceneProbe; lower better) and DrawCalls(percentile) (Count; Scene + SceneProbe; lower better). Map frame_ms to FrameTime(.P99) AtMost value*1,000,000ns; memory_mb to MemoryHighWater AtMost value*1,048,576 bytes (MiB, explicitly resolving the old ambiguous label); asset_kb to SceneAssetBytes AtMost value*1,024 bytes (KiB); draw_calls to DrawCalls(.P99) AtMost Count. Every metric uses AbsoluteFrom because backend/device/replay policy supplies statistical evidence. One SceneProbe run pins backend build, target/device, named replay/input bytes, scene-ready event, 120 warmup frames, 600 measured frames, and identical viewport/settings. FrameTime samples one integer nanosecond duration per measured frame; DrawCalls samples renderer submissions per measured frame; SceneAssetBytes samples total decoded resident bytes at the ready boundary and after each measured frame, with the run maximum as its estimator; MemoryHighWater samples process resident bytes after each measured frame, with the run maximum. REPORT1 then applies its statistical/confidence law. Old Game.Budgets construction/set/show only represented desired thresholds, never evidence; migrate the four intents and explicitly retire its stored object and GameBudgets(...) display. Delete all sema/TIR/JIT/prelude slots and paths. Remaining old calls/types receive ordinary unresolved member/type diagnostics, not performance-budget diagnostics.

options.name: Map frame and memory; retire asset and draw
options.detail: Jet converts frame time and memory because those measurements already exist. It retires asset size and draw calls, so those two limits are lost.
options.code:
migrated: frame_ms 16 -> FrameTime(.P99) AtMost(16ms)
migrated: memory_mb 128 -> MemoryHighWater AtMost(128MiB)
retired without equivalent: asset_kb, draw_calls
options.technical: Use the same pinned SceneProbe, frame samples, memory samples, old ms-to-ns and mb-to-MiB mappings as A. Explicitly retire asset_kb and draw_calls because GRAMMAR1 has no truthful metric for them. Migration refuses to claim those thresholds survived and reports both removed intents. Delete the entire Game.Budgets API and all results; no alias or second enforcement path remains.

options.name: Retire all four decorative limits
options.detail: Jet removes the old object and converts nothing. Users must write new budgets themselves, and asset size plus draw calls remain unavailable.
options.code:
$ jet migrate perf-budgets game.jet --check
Game.Budgets stored four thresholds but produced no evidence or policy result; all four require explicit typed replacement.
options.technical: Record that the old object never measured or enforced any field, delete it completely, and migrate nothing automatically. Users may author any currently ratified FrameTime or MemoryHighWater BudgetSpec explicitly. SceneAssetBytes and DrawCalls remain unavailable until separately ratified. This preserves GRAMMAR1 and removes the facade without asserting false continuity.

comparisons.note: Unity treats frame time, memory, loaded assets, and draw calls as facts from a specific test session and device.
Unreal fixes the map, replay, device, warmup, and capture window before comparing performance numbers.

decisions.lesson:
A limit written in configuration is only an intention until a real measurement proves it. The old Game.Budgets object stored numbers such as frame_ms, memory_mb, asset_kb, and draw_calls and displayed them, but did not measure a running scene or enforce those limits. Treating those numbers as historical evidence would be false.

A real scene performance budget needs a metric, unit, sampling rule, workload, and execution context. Frame time varies from frame to frame, so a percentile such as P99 asks how slow the worst one percent are. Memory high-water means the largest observed resident memory. Asset bytes need a precise boundary such as decoded resident bytes. Draw calls need a renderer-defined count. Results are only comparable when backend, device, replay input, viewport, warmup, and measured frames are pinned.

Migration can preserve threshold intent only where the new typed model can state and measure the same thing. Unit labels also matter: MB may ambiguously mean decimal megabytes or binary mebibytes. This ballot decides whether to add exact missing scene metrics, migrate only already-supported metrics, or retire every decorative field and require fresh explicit policy.

recommendation.why: A turns every old intention into a real, repeatable measurement. It keeps all four user goals while removing the decorative object.

whyNot.reason: B loses the asset and draw-call goals even though both can be defined and measured precisely.
C is truthful about the old object, but it discards all four goals and leaves two useful measurements unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds two metrics to the performance system. They belong there because they have clear units, sampling rules, and real game uses.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps only truthful old intent, uses exact existing mappings, and adds real measurements for the two useful missing metrics.

harvest.aspect: All four user goals survive as measured budgets.
harvest.use: Keep the complete measured replacement.

harvest.aspect: Frame and memory already have exact mappings.
harvest.use: Reuse those mappings unchanged.

harvest.aspect: The old object was never evidence.
harvest.use: Retire its stored display and never present old numbers as measurements.

decisions.title: Measurement provider protocol
decisions.gist: Choose how measurement code sends trusted samples to the performance budget engine.
decisions.story: Priya measures builds, benchmarks, services, and game scenes. Jet must accept complete samples, reject damaged data, and clearly distinguish a missing measurement from a broken provider.
decisions.inWild: Budget.{ name: "ready-p95", scope: .Service("api"), metric: .ServiceReadiness, provider: .ServiceProbe("api-ready"), comparison: .AbsoluteFrom("ci/linux-x64"), limit: .AtMost(2s) }

options.name: In-process typed provider registry
options.detail: Trusted Jet code gathers samples inside the main process through a typed registry. One central engine checks the data and decides every budget result.
options.code:
Error [E2906]: performance budget api-ready has no usable evidence
Why: ServiceProbe api-ready completed with insufficient-samples after 12 of 20 required trials.
Fix: restore the service probe and run `jet budget check` again.

Error [E2908]: performance budget operation failed
Why: SceneProbe level-one emitted sequence 8 after sequence 10 for request 4a….
Fix: repair the provider; no report was accepted.
options.technical: The driver owns a closed ProviderRequest and ProviderRecord API; there is no user command protocol. ProviderRequest is exactly {schema:"jet.perf-provider-request",version:1,request_id:Hex64,provider:{kind,identity},context_key:Hex64,budget_spec_hashes:[Hex64],metrics:[MetricCanonical],workload:{identity,digest},policy:MeasurementPolicy}. Arrays sort by canonical bytes; request_id hashes the remaining canonical object plus LF. Records are exactly Sample{request_id,sequence:Int,metric,budget_spec_hash,unit,value:Quantity,captured_at:RFC3339UTC}, Unavailable{request_id,reason_kind:"unsupported-host"|"missing-runtime"|"probe-not-ready"|"insufficient-samples",detail:Text}, and Complete{request_id,sample_count:Int,records_sha256:Hex64}. Sequence starts at 0 and is contiguous; Complete is last. Maximum 1,000,000 samples, 16 MiB canonical record bytes total, 4096 budget specs, and 512 UTF-8 scalars in detail; excess is E2908 before report creation. BuildArtifact resolves the one artifact target identity from the loaded package graph and reads its no-follow published file. CompilerFacts resolves the checked target and reads front-end facts. BenchMeasurement(name) resolves exactly one #Bench of that canonical package-qualified name. ServiceProbe(name) and SceneProbe(name) resolve exactly one existing named service/scene probe registered by their owning runtime subsystem; no PATH/environment command discovery. AllocationProbe(name) resolves exactly one allocation workload registered on the attached Bench/Service/Scene; absent or ambiguous identities are compile-time E2905. Runtime registries carry the pinned workload contract required by GRAMMAR1 and are hashed into workload.digest. Provider adapters may collect samples only; engine owns direction, statistics, policy, report, and baseline. A valid Unavailable or valid Complete with too few samples becomes E2906. Malformed ordering/schema/unit/context/hash, adapter panic, timeout, or registry invariant failure is E2908. Unsupported metric/provider pairs remain E2903; unresolved identity remains E2905.

options.name: Versioned subprocess protocol
options.detail: Runtime measurements run in a child process and send framed messages back. A crash is isolated, but the process protocol adds more failure cases.
options.technical: Use the same request, record variants, resolution rules, limits, ordering, hashes, E2906/E2908 boundary, and centralized evaluator as A, but registered runtime probes execute in an isolated child. stdin is one A-canonical ProviderRequest followed by LF. stdout is frames of four-byte unsigned big-endian length followed by exactly that many A-canonical JSON bytes without LF; zero length and frames over 1 MiB reject, aggregate remains 16 MiB. stderr is bounded to 1 MiB diagnostic log and never parsed. EOF before Complete, bytes after Complete, nonzero exit, timeout, or invalid UTF-8/JSON is E2908. BuildArtifact and CompilerFacts remain in-process trusted adapters. Registry entries select a compiled Jet provider target, never arbitrary PATH commands.

options.name: Signed evidence-file handoff
options.detail: Providers write signed evidence files for later reading. This supports other devices, but cross-machine trust cannot work until Jet has an attestation rule.
options.code:
.jet/perf/provider-inbox/<request_id>.json
# Canonical, create-new, local-only until attestation is ratified.
options.technical: Use the same schemas, resolution, limits, ordering, and evaluator as A. A provider writes one no-follow, create-new canonical container {request,records,complete}; the engine verifies request_id, context, record hash, ownership, mode, size, and atomic completion before reading. Missing compatible evidence is E2906; malformed, replaced, oversized, or protocol-invalid evidence is E2908. This supports remote/device capture but requires the separately gated attestation law before evidence can be trusted across machines; without attestation it is local-only.

comparisons.note: Cargo keeps machine-readable records separate from human logs.
Bazel workers use bounded request and response messages for long-running helper processes.

decisions.lesson:
A performance engine needs raw measurements before it can decide whether a budget passes. A measurement provider is the component that runs or inspects the relevant workload and emits those raw samples. The central evaluator should still own units, statistics, limits, baseline comparison, and the final report; otherwise each provider could quietly apply different rules.

The provider boundary is also a trust boundary. Every sample must belong to the requested metric, budget, workload, target, and run. Canonical encoding means the same facts always serialize to the same bytes, making hashes and replay checks reliable. Sequence numbers and a final record detect truncation or reordering. Size and sample limits prevent a faulty provider from exhausting memory. Unavailable means a valid provider cannot measure here, such as a missing runtime.
