Malformed means the provider violated the protocol. Those states require different diagnostics.

Provider identity must resolve deterministically; silently searching PATH could run unrelated or hostile code. In-process providers are simplest and trusted. Subprocesses add crash isolation. Evidence files help remote devices but need attestation before another machine can trust them. This ballot chooses the canonical transport while keeping one evaluator and one evidence meaning.

recommendation.why: A gives Jet one typed, deterministic path with the fewest moving parts. Providers only gather samples; the central engine keeps all policy consistent.

whyNot.reason: B adds process startup, message framing, timeouts, and crash handling before Jet needs that isolation.
C is valuable for remote devices, but Jet cannot yet prove that another machine produced trustworthy evidence.

recommendation.tradeoff: A runs trusted providers in the main process, so a provider bug can affect that process. Strict typed limits and validation reduce this risk.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps the simple typed in-process path while borrowing strict message bounds, completion records, and hashes from the transport-heavy options.

harvest.aspect: One typed registry keeps collection simple and deterministic.
harvest.use: Keep it as the primary provider boundary.

harvest.aspect: Bounded records and explicit completion expose broken output.
harvest.use: Apply those checks to in-process records without starting a child process.

harvest.aspect: Context hashes prevent evidence from being reused in the wrong run.
harvest.use: Keep the same hashes in every in-process record.

decisions.title: Performance budget integration contract
decisions.gist: Choose when commands gather performance evidence and when proof may reuse it.
decisions.story: Alex builds, runs benchmarks, starts a development service, proves a release, and opens editor views. Jet must gather measurements without surprising side effects or repeating work that is still valid.
decisions.inWild:
jet build app.jet --release
jet bench app.jet
jet dev app.jet
jet budget check
jet prove app.jet
jet inspect dossier app.jet

options.name: Intent-owned refresh with compatible slice reuse
options.detail: Each command measures the work it already owns. Proof may reuse a matching result for one exact budget, while missing results stay visibly incomplete.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
build budgets: 2 passed · report 8bdb1120b90a
$ jet prove app.jet
# Existing #240 rendering/status law applies. No budget-specific prove flag or receipt surface is added.
options.technical: jet budget check measures every applicable BudgetSpec for the current target/profile and writes the whole-policy report; update reuses that run. Every successful artifact-producing build always evaluates applicable deterministic BuildArtifact and CompilerFacts Fail budgets after atomic artifact publication and before success; failure exits 1, preserving the hard gate. jet bench measures all applicable BenchMeasurement specs whose Bench scope exists in the package, through the shared evaluator and report model. jet dev measures StartupTime on the first transition to runnable, ServiceReadiness from named service start to its declared ready event, and Scene metrics only when the existing scene/replay is explicitly started. Dev refreshes once per provider context, then only when source, BudgetSpec, workload, target, or profile digest changes; Warn never blocks, Fail blocks readiness. Dossier, Canvas, and LSP never measure and project freshness/context/report identity only. CI runs jet budget check. Prove never measures and introduces no flag, receipt type, status, field, or output. It translates each latest compatible budget result into #240's existing ProofReport Evidence representation and lets #240's existing aggregation decide pass, fail, or pass_incomplete and its existing exit behavior. A compatible passing deterministic build slice may satisfy the matching Evidence fact; statistical command slices may satisfy only the exact same BudgetSpec/context/workload fact and never imply whole-policy completion. Missing, stale, incompatible, unavailable, or unmeasured applicable evidence becomes incomplete Evidence under #240; a failed Fail budget becomes failed Evidence. Warn remains evidence detail and does not change #240 status.

options.name: Intent-owned refresh, whole-report proof reuse
options.detail: Commands still gather their own results, but proof ignores them. Only a full budget-check report can satisfy performance evidence.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
build budgets: 2 passed · slice report 8bdb1120b90a
$ jet prove app.jet
# #240 sees performance Evidence incomplete until `jet budget check` writes a compatible whole report.
options.technical: Use A's mandatory deterministic build gates, bench/dev timing, read-only projections, and prove-never-measures rule. Command slices are visible in build/dev/bench/dossier/Canvas/LSP but never satisfy ProofReport Evidence. Only a compatible whole-policy report from jet budget check contributes performance Evidence to #240; otherwise existing #240 aggregation yields pass_incomplete. Failed deterministic build budgets still prevent a successful artifact and therefore cannot be bypassed by proof.

options.name: Eager statistical refresh at owning command boundaries
options.detail: Build, development, and benchmark commands eagerly refresh every statistical measurement they can reach. This produces fresher data but makes normal commands do extra work.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
deterministic budgets: 2 passed
target statistical budgets: 1 warning
# Service, Scene, and Bench providers were not started by build.
options.technical: Keep A's hard deterministic build gates, one evaluator, read-only dossier/Canvas/LSP, and exact #240 Evidence/pass_incomplete/exit law. In addition, build refreshes applicable statistical Target scopes after deterministic gates, dev refreshes all applicable Service/Scene scopes at the same explicit start/ready boundaries, and bench refreshes all Bench scopes. Compatible slices may satisfy matching #240 Evidence exactly as A. No command runs a provider outside the target/service/scene/bench it already owns, so build does not launch services/scenes and editor views remain side-effect free.

comparisons.note: Editors show saved test state and wait for an explicit run action. All options keep editor views read-only.
Bazel reuses command facts only when their build graph and context still match.

decisions.lesson:
Performance budgets become useful only when the right commands measure them at the right time. Deterministic evidence, such as artifact size or compiler facts, should be identical for the same build inputs and can hard-gate every artifact-producing build. Statistical evidence, such as startup time or frame time, varies between runs and needs repeated samples in the runtime context that owns the workload.

Refresh means collecting new evidence. Reuse means accepting existing evidence only when its context still matches: budget definition, source, workload, target, profile, device, and provider facts. Stale or mismatched evidence must never silently pass. Read-only views such as an editor, dossier, or Canvas should display freshness and results without launching benchmarks or services as a side effect. Commands such as bench or dev already own those workloads and are natural refresh points.

Proof aggregation is separate from measurement. A proof command can reuse compatible recorded facts, mark missing required evidence incomplete, and preserve an existing failed result without becoming another hidden benchmark runner. This ballot chooses whether matching command-specific slices can satisfy proof, whether only a whole-policy check can, and how eagerly runtime-owning commands refresh statistical evidence.

recommendation.why: A measures work where users already expect it and safely reuses exact matching facts. It avoids both hidden work and needless repeated checks.

whyNot.reason: B forces a full budget check even when another command already produced the exact fact that proof needs.
C makes ordinary build and development commands run extra statistical work that users did not request.

recommendation.tradeoff: A needs strict rules for deciding when saved evidence still matches. Those checks are necessary to prevent stale results from passing.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps whole-policy checks, lets each command measure only work it owns, and reuses exact matching facts without treating a slice as full coverage.

harvest.aspect: Exact matching facts can avoid repeated work.
harvest.use: Keep fact-level reuse with strict context checks.

harvest.aspect: A full budget check remains the clearest whole-policy report.
harvest.use: Keep that command as the complete policy view.

harvest.aspect: Commands should measure only workloads they already own.
harvest.use: Keep this boundary but do not make every possible measurement eager.

decisions.title: Live queries: effect-tracked server functions with automatic subscription invalidation
decisions.gist: A pure Db.Read server function becomes a live query: clients subscribe, and committed transactions that touch its data push fresh results automatically.
decisions.lesson:
Convex made backends feel magic with one loop. Server queries are deterministic and their database reads are tracked. So the platform knows exactly which client results a write changed, and pushes updates. Nobody writes cache invalidation or websocket plumbing, and no UI goes stale.

Jet already owns every ingredient as ratified law. Effect rows prove a function only reads the database (D-EFF1, D-EFFTREE1). `@Pure` proves determinism (S60). `#Transact` is the write boundary (D-TXN1-4). `core.reactive` gives Signals (D-REACT1). The app graph is sema-known (D-WEBAPP1) and `core.ws` is the push channel (D-WS1=B). This ballot decides whether Jet wires them into a language-level live-query loop.
decisions.story: Frank builds a support dashboard. Ticket lists must update the moment a teammate closes one. Today he writes websocket handlers, invalidation keys, and refetch logic — and still ships a stale-list bug. In Convex this whole layer does not exist. Frank wants that in Jet, self-hosted, without a platform.

options.name: Compiler-integrated live queries
options.detail:
`app.live(query, args)` accepts only a function whose effect row is inside `Db.Read` and whose body is `@Pure` modulo those reads. Sema records the query's read footprint; the runtime binds it to the argument values. A committed `#Transact` whose write set intersects a live footprint invalidates exactly those subscriptions, re-runs them, and pushes results over `core.ws` into a client `Signal<T>`.

Passing an unqualified function is a compile error naming the offending effect. No invalidation keys exist anywhere. This runs in `jet dev` and any self-hosted server — no platform dependency.
options.code:
tickets :: app.live(open_tickets, team)

$ jet check app.jet   # query does I/O beyond Db.Read
error[E07xx]: `open_tickets` cannot be a live query
  its effect row includes `Net` (http fetch at line 14)
  a live query may only read the database — move the fetch to an action

options.name: Library subscriptions with manual invalidation keys
options.detail:
Core ships `app.subscribe(key, fetch)` and `app.invalidate(key)`. The developer names a key per query and calls invalidate in every mutation that affects it. No compiler involvement.

This is the Redis/Firebase pattern every stack already has. The failure mode is the famous one: a new mutation forgets an invalidate call and some client goes stale. The compiler knows the read and write sets and would just not be telling anyone.

options.name: Polling reactivity
options.detail: `app.live` re-runs the query on an interval and pushes when the result differs. No tracking, no invalidation, works with any function. Latency is the poll period, load grows with subscriber count times poll rate, and a write is visible only on the next tick. It is the shape teams settle for, not the one they want.
options.code:
tickets :: app.live(open_tickets, team, every: 2000ms)
// close() commits… clients see it up to 2s later

comparisons.note: Convex tracks read sets in deterministic V8 isolates and retries mutations on conflict. It proved the model but requires their cloud; Jet can prove the same facts in sema and stay self-hosted.
comparisons.code:
export const openTickets = query(async ({ db }, { team }) =>
  db.query("tickets").withIndex("team", q => q.eq("team", team)).collect());

comparisons.note: LiveView pushes server-rendered updates but invalidation is hand-wired PubSub topics — option B's failure mode with nicer plumbing.

recommendation.why: Jet already paid for the proofs — effect rows, purity, transaction boundaries, the sema-known app graph. A is the first feature that spends them on something no mainstream language has: stale-free realtime by construction, self-hosted. It is the strongest possible answer to what a language-level effect system is for.

whyNot.reason: Manual keys reintroduce the exact bug class the ingredients exist to kill, while the compiler silently holds the answer.
Polling trades correctness timing for simplicity Jet does not need, and collapses under subscriber count.

recommendation.tradeoff: The runtime carries a footprint index and re-run scheduler; queries that want liveness must actually be @Pure + Db.Read, which constrains how people write them (the constraint is the feature).

hybrid.synthesis: A can expose B's primitives underneath as the expert floor. `app.subscribe`/`app.invalidate` stay public for exotic sources the tracker cannot see. C's `every:` becomes an expert option for non-tracked queries. Beginner magic on top, manual valves below.

harvest.use: the default loop
public expert floor for sources outside the tracker
expert `every:` option for queries that opt out of tracking

decisions.title: Schedule-as-code: a declarative #Every marker on #Task functions
decisions.gist: Let code declare its own schedule next to the function, consumed by dev, services, and jetos from one declaration.
decisions.lesson:
Recurring work — prune sessions nightly, refresh a cache every five minutes — needs a schedule. Jet has runtime timers (`tasks.interval`, D-TASKRUNTIME1) and jetos has service timers, but no way for an application to declare a schedule as source.

Today the schedule lives wherever the deployment lives: a jetos timer, a cron entry, or a hand-rolled loop. The function and its cadence drift apart. Convex put the schedule next to the function and it reads like the requirement. Jet already ratified the task surface this could ride: a task is an ordinary `#Task fn` (D-JPK-TASKRUN1).
decisions.story: Susan ships a session store. The requirement says expired rows vanish nightly at 3am. She writes the delete in Jet, then leaves the repo to write a systemd timer that shells back into her own binary. Six months later someone renames the task and the timer silently runs nothing.

options.name: `#Every(…)` marker on `#Task fn`
options.detail:
One directive marker on the already-ratified task surface. `#Every(5min)` takes a duration literal (D-UNITLIT1); `#Every("03:00")` takes a daily wall-clock time; both are checked at compile time (unknown shape is an error, not a runtime surprise). Every consumer reads the same declaration. `jet dev` runs due tasks in the dev loop, the service runtime (D-SERVICE1) schedules them in production. A jetos generation projects them as real timer units.

The schedule lives in source, versioned and reviewed with the function it drives. Renaming the fn cannot orphan the schedule.
options.code:
#Task #Every("03:00")
fn prune_sessions() { db.exec("DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expired")? }

$ jet check jobs.jet
error[E13xx]: `#Every("3am")` is not a schedule
  write a daily time as "HH:MM" (e.g. "03:00") or a duration literal (5min)

options.name: Manifest field — schedules in pkg.jet
options.detail: Schedules live in the manifest: `tasks: { prune_sessions: { every: "03:00" } }`. Deployment data stays out of code, and an operator can change cadence without touching source. The cost is the drift Susan hit: the schedule names a function from far away, the rename hazard survives, and a reader of the function cannot see it runs nightly.

options.name: Runtime API only — status quo
options.detail: No declarative surface. A long-lived service loops on `tasks.interval` and calls the work itself. This already works and stays fully general. But every consumer difference is hand-built: `jet dev` cannot list or run due jobs, jetos cannot project a timer unit, and one-shot deploys need a resident process just to own a loop.

comparisons.note: Convex crons are code beside the functions they schedule — the readability this ballot transplants.
Timer units are powerful but live in a different language and directory from the code they invoke — the drift-by-distance option B inherits.

recommendation.why: The schedule is a fact about the function, so it belongs on the function — same reasoning that put effects and contracts on signatures. One declaration feeding dev, services, and jetos is exactly the one-mechanism law (I8) applied to time.

whyNot.reason: Manifest schedules keep the rename hazard and hide cadence from the function's reader; operators can still override at the jetos layer, which is where operational overrides already live.
A resident loop per app re-implements a scheduler everywhere and gives tooling nothing to read, list, or project.

recommendation.tradeoff: Complex calendars (cron expressions, timezones, jitter) are deliberately out of the v1 marker; those cases keep the runtime API or a jetos timer.

hybrid.synthesis: A is the declaration. C's runtime API stays as the expert floor for dynamic schedules. B's operational override survives where it already lives — jetos/service deployment can re-time a declared task with provenance.

harvest.aspect: schedule as a checked source fact on the task
harvest.use: the default surface
stays at the jetos/service layer with explain provenance, not in pkg.jet
tasks.interval remains for schedules computed at runtime

decisions.title: The override law: warnings never block by default; every bypass is spelled and recorded; teams add walls via policy
decisions.gist: One law for every expert escape hatch: the tool advises, the human decides, the record remembers, and only team policy builds walls.
decisions.lesson:
Jet already has expert escape hatches, each minted separately: `#Unsafe("reason")` (S58), `--try-anyway` (D-DEV1), `--allow-impure` (D-CTEFFECT1), `--allow-<root>` effect flags, `assume_deterministic { }` (D-DET1), `#[allow(lint)]` (D-DECIMAL1). They behave similarly by accident, not by law.

Your stated principle: we are not their parents. An expert may ignore warnings, effects, or determinism without being babied. Enterprises still need enforcement and audit. Memory and type safety are never in this conversation — I1 has no override and this ballot does not touch it.

The missing piece is the law that keeps the next ten gates consistent, the way D-MARKER-FAMILY1 made every sigil predictable.
decisions.story: Carl prototypes a scraper on a Saturday. The build nags about an unused fallible result and a float in a money-named field. He does not care yet; he wants to see data flow. At work on Monday, his team's CI must hard-fail those exact lints. Today the first experience depends on each lint's ad-hoc mood, and the second needs tribal knowledge.

options.name: Codify the three-point override law
options.detail:
One law, binding on every current and future gate. First: warnings and lints never fail a build by default — errors are reserved for programs Jet cannot compile safely or unambiguously. Second: every bypass is spelled at the site or on the command line, never in hidden config, and lands in the audit record (`jet inspect dossier`, effect-budget provenance, build facts). Third: walls are team policy only — the ratified `policy:` namespace (D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1) gains `lints: { deny: [...] }`, joining effect budgets and trust; host/org policy narrows, never widens (already law).

Existing gates keep their spellings; the law standardizes their behavior and every future gate's design.
options.code:
$ jet build --allow-impure          # solo expert: builds, bypass recorded
$ jet inspect dossier build | grep bypass
  bypass: comptime impure (flag --allow-impure, 2026-07-11T14:02)

$ jet build                          # same code under team policy:
error[E13xx]: lint `float_money` is denied by policy (pkg.jet:12)
  price: Float in struct Invoice — use Decimal (core.numeric)
  policy owner: pkg.jet `policy.lints`

options.name: Deny-by-default lints, per-site suppression
options.detail: Default-on lints fail the build; the expert writes `#[allow(...)]` at every site. Codebases stay loud-clean and nothing ships un-acknowledged. It is also the babying your principle rejects: the Saturday prototype fights its tools, and beginners meet walls before they meet the language. Rust's clippy-in-CI culture shows the result — suppression attributes everywhere, signal lost.
options.code:
$ jet run scraper.jet
error[L0504]: float in money-named field
  #[allow(float_money)] to proceed
// …repeat per site, per lint, before anything runs

options.name: Status quo — each gate decides alone
options.detail: No law. Every future gate re-litigates blocking behavior, spelling, and audit. The surface stays inconsistent exactly where consistency teaches trust: some bypasses are flags, some markers, some silent; some are recorded, some vanish. Carl's Saturday and Monday stay unpredictable.
options.code:
// today: six gates, six shapes
#Unsafe("reason") { … }      // marker + reason, audited
--try-anyway                  // flag, unrecorded
#[allow(float_money)]         // attribute, silent

comparisons.note: Permission flags proved explicit-bypass ergonomics, but Deno records nothing — the audit half is missing. Jet already has the audit rails.
gofmt/vet advise and never block a local build; teams enforce in CI. Twelve years of evidence that advise-by-default plus team walls keeps both audiences happy.
comparisons.code: go vet ./...   # exit code matters only where the team says so

recommendation.why: It turns your principle into enforceable law: freedom by default, walls by team choice, memory on everything. Every existing rail is already ratified — this ballot only forbids future gates from drifting.

whyNot.reason: Deny-by-default is parenting: it taxes the solo expert and the beginner to serve the enterprise, which policy already serves better.
No law means the next ten gates each invent their own bypass shape, and the audit story stays accidental.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some real bugs ship in solo projects that a blocking lint would have caught. The bet: respect plus a recorded advisory beats a wall. Teams that disagree get their wall in one line of policy.

hybrid.synthesis: A already contains B for those who want it — `policy.lints.deny` IS deny-by-default, scoped to the people who chose it. C's per-gate freedom survives as spelling variety only; behavior and audit become uniform.

harvest.use: the law
available verbatim through policy.lints.deny for teams and CI
kept — the law fixes behavior and audit, not the sigil

decisions.title: cobol.* binder — call the COBOL estate in place
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a cobol.* binder so Jet code can call existing COBOL programs directly.
decisions.lesson:
COBOL is a business programming language from 1959. It still runs core batch jobs at banks, insurers, and government agencies, and almost nobody writes new COBOL. A copybook is a COBOL include file that describes a record layout: fixed-width fields at fixed byte offsets, with money often stored as a packed decimal (called COMP-3), not a floating-point number.

GnuCOBOL is an open-source COBOL compiler that translates COBOL into C and exposes each program through the C calling convention (the C ABI).

D-FFI-UNIFY1 is Jet's ratified rule that every foreign language mounts as `<lang>.<lib>`, generates safe wrappers, and turns foreign toolchain errors into normal Jet diagnostics. @Codable is Jet's ratified struct marker for types that map to an external wire format. Decimal is Jet's exact base-10 number type from core.numeric; Float is binary and rounds, so it is wrong for money.
decisions.story: Marcus Bell maintains payroll for a county government. The gross-to-net calculation lives in a 1980s COBOL program, PR-CALC, that nobody dares rewrite: it encodes decades of tax and pension rules, and it is correct. Marcus wants a new Jet web portal to show each employee their net pay, computed by the exact same code the nightly batch uses. Today he would shell out to the batch job or reimplement the rules and risk a mismatch.
decisions.inWild:
A Jet payroll service calls the county's COBOL net-pay program with a typed copybook struct and gets an exact Decimal back, no reimplementation.

```jet
use cobol.payroll as pay

// copybook PR-EMP-REC imported as a struct; money is Decimal, not Float
rec :: pay.PrEmpRec.{
    emp_id: "004821",
    gross:  Decimal("5320.00"),
    filing: .married,
}
net :: pay.pr_calc(rec)?          // calls the real COBOL PR-CALC
print("net pay: {net.take_home}") // net pay: 4187.63
```

options.name: GnuCOBOL C-ABI binder
options.detail: `use cobol.<lib>` compiles the COBOL source with GnuCOBOL on a cache miss and calls each program through the generated C ABI, exactly like the ratified C binder (S59). Copybooks import as @Codable structs: each field carries fixed-width offset and length facts, and COMP-3 money fields become Decimal from core.numeric, never Float. Wrappers are safe by construction (I1); a GnuCOBOL compile error becomes a Jet diagnostic (I2), never raw compiler output.
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind cobol ./payroll
cobol.payroll → .jet/bindings/cobol/payroll.jet
  PR-CALC        program → fn pay.pr_calc(rec: PrEmpRec) -> PrResult
  PR-EMP-REC     copybook → struct PrEmpRec  (@Codable, #[Layout(cobol)])
    EMP-ID   PIC X(6)          → emp_id: String   @ off 0  len 6
    GROSS    PIC S9(7)V99 COMP-3 → gross: Decimal @ off 6  len 5 (packed)

// A bad field type is a Jet diagnostic, not a GnuCOBOL error:
$ jet build
error[JT0412]: money field bound to Float loses cents
  --> portal/pay.jet:9
   |
 9 |     gross: Float,
   |            ^^^^^ COMP-3 field GROSS is exact base-10
   = fix: use Decimal; COMP-3 stores packed decimal, Float rounds

options.name: No binder — hand-wrap or rewrite
options.detail: Jet ships no COBOL support. Teams keep doing what they do today: call the batch job over a file or queue, hand-write a C shim, or rewrite the program in another language. The estate stays a black box behind a batch boundary, and any migration is big-bang because there is no way to call one program at a time from Jet.

comparisons.lang: IBM watsonx Code Assistant for Z
comparisons.note: IBM's flagship COBOL story is AI-assisted rewrite to Java — a translation project that leaves two codebases to reconcile. The binder path instead calls the proven COBOL in place, so the running logic never forks.
comparisons.code:
// watsonx: COBOL --(AI translate)--> Java, then reconcile behavior.
// Jet binder: Jet --(C ABI)--> the same COBOL, no second codebase.

comparisons.note: The standard safe-migration pattern wraps a legacy system, then replaces it piece by piece behind a stable interface. The cobol.* binder is the wrapping step; D-FFI-UNIFY1 in-situ replacement is the piece-by-piece step.

recommendation.why: The binder turns an untouchable estate into a set of callable, typed programs. Marcus calls the real PR-CALC from Jet with a typed copybook struct, gets exact Decimal money, and never reimplements a tax rule. It reuses the ratified C-ABI binder wholesale, so COBOL is just another D-FFI-UNIFY1 language.
recommendation.tradeoff: GnuCOBOL becomes a provisioned runtime dependency, acquired only when a project uses cobol.*, hash-pinned and jetpack-managed like CPython for py.*. That cost buys safe, gradual, call-site-stable access to code that otherwise stays behind a batch wall.

whyNot.reason: Leaves every team hand-writing C shims and packing copybook bytes by hand under #Unsafe, where one wrong offset or a Float cent is a silently wrong paycheck. It forces big-bang rewrites because no single program can be called in isolation.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the GnuCOBOL C-ABI binder as the one COBOL surface. Option B is not a second mechanism to keep; it is the status quo the binder replaces. The binder subsumes B's only real use — reaching the estate — while removing its footguns.

harvest.aspect: Typed copybooks + Decimal money over the C ABI
harvest.use: The shipped mechanism: programs become functions, copybooks become @Codable structs with layout facts, COMP-3 money is Decimal, errors are Jet diagnostics.

harvest.aspect: The estate must stay callable in its current form
harvest.use: Kept as the binder's guarantee: call in place with no rewrite, so migration is gradual and the running COBOL logic is never forked.

decisions.title: octave.* sidecar — call MATLAB-compatible .m code from Jet
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships an octave.* root that runs existing .m scripts in a sidecar and marshals matrices to typed Jet values.
decisions.lesson:
MATLAB is a commercial numerical computing environment used heavily in engineering and academia; its programs are `.m` script files built around matrix math. GNU Octave is an open-source language that runs most MATLAB `.m` code unchanged and needs no MATLAB license.

A sidecar is a separate helper process Jet talks to over a typed message boundary, so a crash or bug in it cannot corrupt Jet's own memory. Jet already uses this model for Python (D-FFI-PY1) and R.

`Matrix<M,N>` is Jet's fixed-size numeric matrix type and `Tensor<T>` its N-dimensional array. An effect root is Jet's way of marking that calling into a subsystem carries a tracked effect, like `#(Py)` for Python. jetpack is Jet's package manager; it provisions foreign toolchains so the user never installs them by hand.
decisions.story: Diane Fletcher is a controls engineer. Her team's flight-surface filter was designed years ago in MATLAB as `designNotchFilter.m`, validated against flight data, and treated as ground truth. She is writing the new control loop in Jet. She wants to call that exact filter-design function during startup, get its coefficient matrix, and run the loop natively. Buying MATLAB seats for the whole team, or porting math she does not want to re-validate, are both off the table.

options.name: Sidecar Octave worker
options.detail: `use octave.<lib>` runs a supervised Octave worker in a sidecar, exactly like the ratified py and R roots. Matrices round-trip as typed values: an Octave matrix becomes `Matrix<M,N>` when the shape is known, or `Tensor<T>` otherwise, and Jet matrices marshal back the same way. Any `.m` script is callable. Calls carry an `#(Octave)` effect. Octave is provisioned by jetpack, acquired only when a project uses octave.*. Octave errors are laundered into Jet diagnostics (I2).
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind octave ./filters
octave.filters → .jet/bindings/octave/filters.jet
  designNotchFilter.m → fn flt.design_notch_filter(freq: F64, q: F64)
                        -> Matrix<2, 3>  #(Octave)

// A shape mismatch is a Jet diagnostic, not an Octave stack trace:
$ jet build
error[JT0431]: matrix shape mismatch at boundary
  --> loop/ctl.jet:5
   |
 5 |     coeffs: Matrix<3, 3> :: flt.design_notch_filter(freq: 60.0, q: 30.0)?
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ script returns 2x3, binding declares 3x3
   = fix: annotate Matrix<2, 3>, or Tensor<F64> for a dynamic shape

options.name: No octave root — export to C or rewrite
options.detail: Jet ships no Octave support. To reach MATLAB logic, Diane either runs it through MATLAB Coder (a proprietary tool that generates C from a licensed MATLAB install) and binds the C, or rewrites the algorithm in Jet. The open path is a full manual port; the automated path requires paid MATLAB seats, the exact cost the team is trying to avoid.

comparisons.note: rpy2 proved the sidecar bridge model: run the foreign numeric runtime in a companion process and marshal arrays across a typed boundary. Jet's octave root is the same shape as its already-shipped py and R roots, so it is a fourth instance of one mechanism, not a new one.
comparisons.code:
# rpy2: robjects.r['designNotchFilter'](60, 30) -> R matrix -> numpy
// Jet:  flt.design_notch_filter(freq: 60.0, q: 30.0) -> Matrix<2,3>

comparisons.note: MathWorks' own bridge requires a licensed MATLAB runtime on every machine that calls it. The Octave sidecar gives the same MATLAB-compatible call surface with an open runtime jetpack provisions, so there is no per-seat license gate.
comparisons.code:
// Engine API: needs MATLAB installed + licensed to run at all.
// octave.*: jetpack fetches Octave; no license, same .m surface.

recommendation.why: The sidecar lets Diane call her validated `.m` filter design straight from Jet, get a typed Matrix, and run the loop natively — no rewrite, no MATLAB seats. It slots into the existing py/R sidecar precedent, so octave.* is just another D-FFI-UNIFY1 language with crash isolation for free.
recommendation.tradeoff: Octave becomes a jetpack-provisioned runtime dependency, acquired only when a project uses octave.*. Sidecar calls cross a process boundary, so hot inner loops should marshal once and compute in Jet. That is how the worked example uses it: fetch coefficients once, run the loop natively.

whyNot.reason: Both of its paths are dead ends for this team. MATLAB Coder demands the paid seats they are avoiding. A hand rewrite means re-deriving and re-validating flight-critical math where a single sign error is a safety hazard.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the sidecar Octave worker as the one octave surface. Option B is not a second mechanism; it is the status quo the root replaces. The sidecar delivers B's goal — reaching MATLAB logic — without the license gate or the re-validation risk.

harvest.aspect: Typed matrix round-trip over a crash-isolated sidecar
harvest.use: The shipped mechanism: .m scripts become effect-carrying functions, matrices map to Matrix<M,N>/Tensor<T>, Octave provisioned by jetpack, errors laundered.

harvest.aspect: MATLAB-compatible surface without a MATLAB license
harvest.use: Kept as a design requirement the sidecar satisfies: the open Octave runtime runs the same .m code, so no seat cost and no forced rewrite.

decisions.title: Source-level importer framework — jet import <lang> <dir>
decisions.gist: The law every per-language source importer must obey when it translates foreign source code into editable Jet.
decisions.lesson:
Jet already imports foreign metadata: `jet import <ecosystem> <path>` (D-JPK-IMPORTCMD1) reads a manifest — an npm package.json, a PyPI project, a Cargo.toml — and writes canonical, editable Jet describing the project. Nothing imports the actual source code.

This ballot fixes the framework law for source importers, not any one language; each per-language importer (cobol2jet, py2jet, c2jet, and so on) ships later under this law.

Key ratified rules it must extend: editable canonical output means the importer emits normal Jet you own and edit, never a sealed artifact (D-WD5). A TODO diagnostic (D-JPK-IMPORTTODO1) is a structured error carrying what could not be translated, why, the fix, the source path, and the migration status. The omissions discipline (D-JOS-NIXIMPORT1=C) means anything the importer cannot represent is reported explicitly and audited, never silently dropped.

A binder-backed FFI stub is a generated Jet function whose body calls the original foreign code through that language's binder — a placeholder that runs correctly until a human ports the body.
decisions.story: Marcus Bell, the same county payroll maintainer, has the COBOL binder working: Jet calls PR-CALC in place. Now he wants to actually own the code — read it, diff it, unit-test it as Jet, and delete the COBOL. He runs `jet import cobol ./payroll`. The result must be Jet he can read and trust, with an honest list of exactly what did not translate — not a pile of machine-generated code he cannot follow.
decisions.inWild:
`jet import cobol ./payroll` converts programs and copybooks to editable Jet, lists every construct it could not translate as a TODO diagnostic, and drops one unresolved program to a binder-backed stub.

```shell
$ jet import cobol ./payroll
payroll/ → jet/payroll/           37 programs, 214 copybooks
  copybooks   → @Codable structs   (fixed-width via #[Layout(cobol)] facts)
  PERFORM     → fn call graph       35 / 37 programs fully translated
  goldens     → 18 Jet tests        (batch fixtures carried over)
  1 binder stub: PR-DIST calls cobol.payroll in place (body not translated)

11 TODO diagnostics (JT01xx):
  JT0102  jet/payroll/dist.jet:44  GO TO fan-in from 3 sites → verify control flow
  JT0107  jet/payroll/tax.jet:12   ALTER statement has no Jet form → hand-port

$ jet import cobol ./payroll --dry-run   # preview, write nothing
$ jet import cobol ./payroll --update    # re-run; keeps your edits, re-flags TODOs

options.name: Semantic importer framework law
options.detail:
One law all per-language source importers obey. Output is editable canonical Jet (D-WD5), never a black box. Every construct the importer cannot faithfully translate becomes an explicit TODO diagnostic (D-JPK-IMPORTTODO1) with what/why/fix/source/status. Omissions are reported, never silently dropped (D-JOS-NIXIMPORT1 discipline). Detectable tests and goldens carry over as Jet tests. 

Import is idempotent and re-runnable with D-JPK-IMPORTCMD1's update/dry-run/conflict policy. A body the importer cannot translate falls back to a binder-backed FFI stub plus a TODO — so option B's behavior is this framework's guaranteed per-construct floor, not a separate mode.

options.name: Facts-only importers
options.detail: Importers emit only a skeleton: struct and function signatures plus FFI stubs that call the old code through the binder. No bodies are ever translated; humans port every body by hand. Smaller promise, still gradual, still call-site-stable — but the estate's actual logic stays foreign forever unless someone hand-ports it, and the importer never gets to translate the easy 90%.

options.name: No source importers
options.detail: Binders are the whole migration story: call the estate in place forever, never translate source. `jet import` stays metadata-only. Teams reach foreign code but can never own it as Jet, so the foreign toolchain stays a permanent dependency and the estate is never actually retired.

comparisons.note: c2rust proved automated transpile-in works, but its output is unreadable machine Rust nobody maintains — the exact failure mode A's editable-canonical rule exists to prevent. A's TODO-and-stop discipline keeps the output honest instead of emitting opaque code to hit 100%.
comparisons.code:
// c2rust: emits compiling-but-unreadable Rust; humans avoid touching it.
// Jet A: emits readable Jet + explicit TODOs where it could not translate.

comparisons.note: py2many transpiles Python to several languages best-effort, silently degrading on constructs it cannot map. A forbids the silent-degrade: an untranslatable construct is a binder stub plus a TODO diagnostic, so the migration status is always visible and auditable.
comparisons.code:
// py2many: unsupported construct → wrong or dropped output, quietly.
// Jet A: unsupported construct → binder stub + TODO JT01xx, loudly.

recommendation.why: A gives Marcus Jet he can read, diff, and test, plus an honest list of exactly what did not translate. It translates the easy majority, drops the rest to running binder stubs with TODOs, and re-runs idempotently. It extends the ratified importer discipline instead of inventing a new one.
recommendation.tradeoff: A is a framework law, not one importer; each language's importer ships later and cites it. That is the point: fixing the law once means every future importer is honest, editable, and re-runnable by construction, with no per-language relitigation of the rules.

whyNot.reason: Facts-only refuses to translate any body, so the estate's logic stays foreign until a human ports all of it by hand. A already contains B as its per-construct fallback, and adds the automatic translation of everything the importer can prove — strictly more, never less.

Call-in-place-only means the foreign toolchain is a permanent dependency and the estate is never retired. It gives teams no path to ever own their code as Jet, which contradicts the replace half of the polyglot north star.

hybrid.synthesis: A is already the hybrid. It is the semantic framework with B folded in as its guaranteed per-construct fallback and C's binder as the transport that fallback rides on. One law: translate what you can prove, stub-and-TODO what you cannot, never seal or silently drop.

harvest.aspect: Editable canonical Jet + explicit TODO diagnostics + idempotent re-run
harvest.use: The framework law itself: readable output you own, every gap reported with what/why/fix, carried-over tests, update/dry-run/conflict policy.

harvest.aspect: Binder-backed FFI stub for untranslatable bodies
harvest.use: Absorbed as A's per-construct fallback floor: a body the importer cannot translate becomes a running binder stub plus a TODO, never a silent drop.
Kept as the transport under the stub fallback: the binder is how a not-yet-ported body still runs, so the imported project builds and passes tests from day one.

decisions.title: Binary patterns for byte parsing
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets declarative bit-level patterns for parsing raw binary formats.
decisions.lesson:
Binary format means raw bytes with fields packed at the bit level, like a network packet header.

Bit syntax is Erlang's notation for slicing those bits by declaring each field's width.

A bit-typed hole is a named slot in a pattern with a fixed width and byte order. Example: {len:U16be} reads a big-endian 16-bit number.

A refutable pattern may fail to match, so it needs a fallback arm.

Exhaustiveness means the checker proves every possible input is handled.

Non-greedy anchoring means the {rest:...} tail claims only what is left after the fixed fields, never more. Jet already uses this law for string patterns.
decisions.story:
Marcus Bell writes a game server. Clients send a 20-byte header, then a variable body.

Today he reads each field by hand, tracking a byte offset and shifting bits. One off-by-one corrupts every field after it.

He wants to name the shape once and let the compiler slice it. He also wants a bad packet to be a clean no-match, not a silent misread.
decisions.inWild: A protocol router matches an incoming frame against several packet shapes and dispatches on the opcode. The same shapes must also drive a streaming cursor that consumes bytes as they arrive.

options.name: Binary pattern literals in the one pattern engine
options.detail:
b"..." literals hold bit-typed holes. They work anywhere string patterns work: ==-tests, if-table arms, and Reader.take_pattern consume mode.

Same engine, same non-greedy anchoring law, same exhaustiveness rules as string patterns. A refutable match without a fallback is a checked error.

options.name: Cursor-only: more typed reads, no literal
options.detail:
No pattern literal. Reader grows sub-byte reads like read_bits, and parsing stays imperative.

Every field is a separate call. There is no whole-value == test and no if-table arm over bytes.

options.name: Comptime packed layout structs
options.detail:
Declare a #Layout(packed) struct and decode bytes into it. Declarative, but a second mechanism beside patterns.

Fields decode at fixed offsets. There is no mid-stream anchor, so a variable-length field before the tail cannot be expressed.

comparisons.note: Bit syntax is the feature systems programmers cite as the reason to reach for Erlang on protocol work. Jet folds it into the one pattern engine instead of a bespoke syntax.
Kaitai declares binary formats in a separate YAML file and generates a parser. That is a second schema language living outside the program. Option A keeps the shape inline and typed.
comparisons.code:
seq:
  - id: version
    type: b4
  - id: len
    type: u2be

recommendation.why:
One pattern engine handles strings and bytes, so users learn anchoring and exhaustiveness once (I8). Erlang proved bit syntax is the ergonomic win for protocol and parser work.

A refutable binary match is checked like any other pattern, so a malformed packet is a clean no-match, never a silent misread.
recommendation.tradeoff: Bit-typed holes add grammar to the pattern engine, and byte-order and width rules must be learned. The payoff is that one surface covers text and binary parsing with the same laws.

whyNot.reason: Imperative reads force a separate call per field and repeat the offset bookkeeping the owner wants cut. No whole-value match means no if-table dispatch over frames.
A packed struct is a second parsing mechanism beside patterns, against I8. Fixed offsets cannot express a variable-length field before the tail, which most real protocols need.

hybrid.synthesis: The pattern literal is the surface. It reads through the same cursor primitives option B would expose, and a destructuring bind recovers the named-field feel option C offered, with no second grammar.

harvest.aspect: Pattern literal in the one engine
harvest.use: Ship as the canonical binary parsing surface, valid in tests, arms, and consume mode.
Keep as the cursor primitives the literal lowers onto, available when a user wants manual stepping.
Recover by binding holes to names in the pattern, so no separate struct schema is needed.

decisions.title: Atomic memory transactions across shared handles
decisions.gist: Whether #Transact can commit reads and writes across several Shared handles atomically.
decisions.lesson:
Shared<T> is Jet's ratified handle for state two tasks touch at once. You read or edit it inside a short closure that holds a lock.

STM means software transactional memory. You mark a block atomic. If another task changed the same state first, the runtime discards the work and retries, so there are no locks to order by hand.

A deadlock is two tasks each holding one lock and waiting for the other's, so both stall forever. Hand-ordered locking is the classic source.

An irreversible effect is an action that cannot be undone on retry, like sending a network packet. Jet already rejects those inside #Transact with E0746.
decisions.story:
Ruth Callahan runs an inventory service. A transfer moves stock from one warehouse handle to another under heavy concurrent load.

With two separate edit closures, a second task can slip between them and read a total that is briefly wrong. If she locks both by hand, one bad ordering deadlocks production at 2am.

She wants both changes to land together or not at all, with the runtime handling the retry.
decisions.inWild: A bank-style transfer debits one account handle and credits another. Dozens of tasks run transfers concurrently, and no intermediate state may ever be observable.

options.name: #Transact gains the Shared plane
options.detail:
When a #Transact block touches Shared handles, every read and write inside becomes one atomic commit, retried on conflict. No new marker (I8).

The existing rule that rejects irreversible effects inside the block still applies, so a retry is always safe.

options.name: Multi-lock API with canonical ordering
options.detail:
A new call locks a set of handles at once, sorted into a canonical order so it cannot deadlock. It has no retry, so it blocks until every lock is free.

This is a second concurrency mechanism beside #Transact.

options.name: Status quo: nested edit closures
options.detail:
Keep only single-handle edit closures. The user nests them and owns the lock ordering entirely.

Correctness rests on discipline, and a wrong ordering deadlocks with no compiler help.

comparisons.note: STM composes atomic blocks and retries on conflict, which killed the deadlock class for good. Jet borrows the semantics but keeps the one marker it already has, rather than a new monad.
comparisons.code:
atomically $ do
  modifyTVar from (subtract 100)
  modifyTVar to   (+ 100)

comparisons.note: Refs and dosync give the same conflict-retry model with mutable identities. Jet reaches the same guarantee through Shared handles inside #Transact, so there is one boundary, not two.

recommendation.why:
One marker already means atomic in Jet. Extending #Transact to the Shared plane makes the transfer safe by construction, with the runtime retrying on conflict and no lock order to get wrong.

E0746 already blocks irreversible effects inside, so every retry is provably safe.
recommendation.tradeoff: Atomic memory blocks can retry, so the code inside must be free of irreversible effects, which the checker enforces. The gain is that the deadlock class disappears entirely.

whyNot.reason: A separate multi-lock call is a second concurrency mechanism against I8. It blocks rather than retries, so a slow edit stalls every other transfer touching the same handles.
Hand-ordered nested locks put correctness on the user and offer no diagnostic when an ordering deadlocks. This is the exact footgun STM was invented to remove.

hybrid.synthesis: #Transact is the single atomic boundary for both locals and shared state. It gives option B's deadlock-freedom and more, because it retries instead of blocking, and it retires option C's manual ordering.

harvest.use: Ship as the canonical way to change several shared handles together.
Keep as an internal acquisition strategy for the transaction runtime, not a user-facing second API.
Remains the primitive for one-handle changes, unchanged, under the transaction layer.

decisions.title: core.auth batteries for web apps
decisions.gist: How much of authentication ships in the standard library versus staying the user's problem.
decisions.lesson:
A session is how a server remembers a logged-in user between requests, usually via a signed cookie.

argon2id is a slow, memory-hard hash for passwords, so a stolen database is expensive to crack. It is the current best-practice default.

OAuth and OIDC are the standards behind Sign in with Google or GitHub. JWT and PASETO are signed tokens an API checks without a database lookup.

A magic link is a one-time sign-in URL emailed to the user, so there is no password at all.

httponly, secure, and samesite are cookie flags that block common theft and cross-site attacks. Constant-time compare checks a secret without leaking its length through timing.

A .Credential taint marks a value as a secret the compiler tracks, so it cannot be logged or leaked by accident.
decisions.story:
Dale Whitmore is a solo founder shipping a SaaS. He needs email-and-password login, Sign in with Google, and secure sessions.

In most stacks this is a week of wiring cookie flags, hashing, and OAuth callbacks, with a real chance of a subtle leak. Firebase and Clerk made it an afternoon and won his kind of user.

He wants the magic default now and the knobs later when an enterprise buyer asks.
decisions.inWild: A new app needs a login page, a protected dashboard, Sign in with Google, and an API that accepts a bearer token. Later a customer demands two-factor for admins.

options.name: Full batteries suite
options.detail:
core.auth ships sessions, password login, OAuth and OIDC, email magic links, and JWT or PASETO verification. app.auth gives a magic default with safe cookie flags.

Every knob is expert-overridable. Credentials carry the .Credential taint, and policy can require stronger factors.

options.name: Primitives only
options.detail:
core.crypto grows password hashing and token signing. The actual login flows, sessions, and OAuth callbacks stay in userland or community packages.

Experts get clean building blocks. Beginners still assemble the dangerous parts themselves.

options.name: Sessions and password only
options.detail:
Ship sessions and password login now. Defer OAuth, OIDC, and magic links to a later card.

Covers the simplest app. A user who needs Sign in with Google reaches for a third-party package and leaves the safe defaults.

comparisons.note: These platforms made auth a magic default and won beginners, at the cost of a cloud dependency. Jet delivers the same one-line feel with a local-first library and no vendor lock-in.
comparisons.code:
// Clerk
<SignIn />   // hosted, magic, but tied to their cloud

comparisons.note: has_secure_password is a pleasant primitive, but real apps still reach for Devise, a large gem that many teams misconfigure. A safe batteries default avoids that sprawl.

recommendation.why:
Auth is where beginners get hurt most, so the safe path must be the default one. A batteries suite with httponly, secure, samesite, argon2id, and constant-time compares removes the whole footgun class.

One mechanism serves both facets: the same app.auth a beginner calls exposes every knob an expert needs.
recommendation.tradeoff: A broad auth surface is a large ongoing security commitment for the standard library. The alternative is every app reinventing it and shipping the same leaks, which safety cannot accept.

whyNot.reason: Primitives leave beginners assembling cookie flags and OAuth callbacks, which is exactly where the dangerous mistakes live. Safety ranks above minimalism here.
Dropping OAuth and magic links pushes the most common real need onto third-party packages, so users leave the safe defaults for the feature they most wanted.

hybrid.synthesis: app.auth is the one entrypoint. Its internals are exactly option B's crypto primitives, and option C's sessions-and-password path is simply the default before providers are added.

harvest.use: Ship as core.auth, the single auth surface for both beginners and experts.
Provide as the audited building blocks core.auth is built on and experts can drop to.
Treat as the zero-config starting state of the same suite, with providers added by one call.

decisions.title: CRDT sync value types
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships conflict-free collaborative value types or stays server-authoritative.
decisions.lesson:
A CRDT is a conflict-free replicated data type. Two people can edit their own copy offline, and the copies merge to the same result with no coordination and no lost work.

Offline-first means the app keeps working with no network and syncs when it reconnects.

Last-write-wins means a later edit silently overwrites an earlier one, which loses data when two people edit at once.

A vector clock is the small bit of bookkeeping a CRDT uses to know which edits each copy has already seen.

Live queries are Jet's ratified server-push channel: when data a client watches changes, the server pushes the new result.
decisions.story:
Nora Fitzgerald builds a flight-planning app. Two dispatchers open the same route note, and one is on a plane with spotty wifi.

Both add a line at the same time. She wants the Figma feel: both edits survive, merged cleanly, with no dialog asking who wins.

Today she would hand-roll a CRDT or buy one, then wire it to her push channel by hand.
decisions.inWild: A shared document has a title, a body of text, a list of waypoints, and a like counter. Several users edit all of it at once, some offline, and everyone must converge.

options.name: core.sync CRDT value types
options.detail:
SyncText, SyncMap, SyncList, and SyncCounter are @Codable and merge deterministically. app.sync carries them over the live-query channel.

Offline edits merge conflict-free on reconnect. Experts can reach the merge metadata and vector clocks.
options.code:
doc :: SyncText.new()
doc.edit(at: 120, insert: "flap angle")   // offline OK
app.sync(doc, over: session)               // merges on reconnect

likes :: SyncCounter.new()
likes.inc()                                // two clients, no lost count

// expert view of the merge bookkeeping:
clock :: doc.metadata().vector_clock()

options.name: Server-authoritative only
options.detail:
No CRDTs. Live queries push server state, and fields use last-write-wins. Offline edits queue and replay as mutations on reconnect.

When two offline edits collide, the conflict surfaces as an error the app must handle.

comparisons.note: These libraries made CRDTs practical, but every team wires them to a transport and a store by hand. Jet ships the value types already riding its own push channel.
Linear's sync engine is a headline feature that took years to build. Providing the same conflict-free feel as a library is how Jet makes that class of app easy by default.
comparisons.code: // Linear: local mutation applies instantly, syncs and merges in the background

recommendation.why:
Collaborative and offline-first apps are table stakes, and the safe path is a merge that never loses a user's work. CRDT value types on the existing live-query channel deliver that with no plumbing.

The beginner writes one edit call and one sync call. The expert can still inspect the merge metadata.
recommendation.tradeoff: CRDT types carry merge metadata, so they use more memory and cannot express arbitrary custom conflict rules. The gain is convergence with no lost edits and no conflict dialogs.

whyNot.reason: Last-write-wins silently drops a user's edit, which safety ranks below convergence. Surfacing every offline collision as an error pushes the hardest merge work back onto app authors.

hybrid.synthesis: core.sync rides the same live-query push channel option B already provides, so there is one transport. The server-authoritative path stays for plain non-collaborative data that needs no merge.

harvest.use: Ship as core.sync for collaborative and offline-first data, over the live-query channel.
Keep as the default for ordinary data where a single source of truth is correct and simpler.

decisions.title: Validation lives in the struct definition: a validate block on fields, with a use-site chain only for what the definition cannot know
decisions.gist: Rules are declared inside the struct body as chains on the field names; a use-site escape exists only for context the definition cannot see.
decisions.lesson:
Your direction: the validator belongs in the struct definition, not at use sites. Use-site chaining survives only as the escape for rules the definition cannot express — rules needing outside context like a database or config.

The struct body already hosts more than fields: computed fields read siblings by bare name (D-FIELDPOL1), `state` blocks declare typestates (D-STATE1), and in-body sections are ratified grammar (S82). A validation section fits that family.

Layer zero stays free: constraints that fit the type system — `distinct Int(13..120)` (D-RANGETYPE1), `#Invariant` refinements (D-REFINE1) — are compile-checked and need no rule at all.
decisions.story: Wanda declares Signup once. She wants the email, age, and password rules readable in the same place the fields are declared — the struct IS the schema, rules included. Her one context-dependent rule — username not already taken — cannot live there, because the definition has no database. That rule, and only that rule, belongs at the use site.

options.name: validate block in the struct body; Validate.over stays as the context escape
options.detail:
A `validate { … }` section inside the struct body — the declaration plane, beside fields, like `state` blocks. Rules are dot-chains on bare field names (the D-FIELDPOL1 sibling-access rule, reused); cross-field rules use `check(cond, at: field, "msg")` in the same block. All rules ACCUMULATE into `[FieldError]` (the DecodeError path shape).

`decode<T>()` runs the block automatically — one call, shape errors and rule errors in one list. `Signup.validate(value)` runs it standalone. `Validate.over(s)` remains, same rule vocabulary, one engine (I8), only for rules needing context the definition cannot see.

options.name: Rules chained inline on each field's type
options.detail: Rules attach on the field line itself: `email: String .email().max_len(254)`. Maximally local — the rule is ON the field. Costs: wide structs turn into long lines, cross-field rules still need a block somewhere anyway, and the field line now mixes type grammar with rule grammar.

options.name: Field markers — #[Check(…)] per field
options.detail: Rules as `#`-plane field markers, like the serde wire markers: `#[Check(email, max_len(254))]`. Consistent with an existing family, but it is exactly the marker soup you called clunky, and cross-field rules do not fit a per-field marker at all.

comparisons.note: Pydantic v2 declares rules in the class body (Field constraints + model_validator) — the in-definition shape; its success is why forms code reads well in Python.
Ecto keeps rules in a changeset function beside the schema — in the module, not at call sites; call sites just pipe data through.
comparisons.code:
def changeset(user, params) do
  cast(user, params, [:email])
  |> validate_length(:password, min: 12)
end

recommendation.why: It is your stated shape with the chain ergonomics kept: rules live where the fields live, decode runs them with zero call-site ceremony, and the use-site escape is scoped to exactly the rules a definition cannot know. One rule vocabulary, one engine, two homes with a bright line between them.

whyNot.reason: Inline chains bloat field lines and still need a block for cross-field rules — so the block exists anyway and the inline form becomes a second spelling.
Per-field markers are the clunky shape you rejected, and cross-field rules have no home in them.

recommendation.tradeoff: The struct body gains a section kind; the validate block's rule vocabulary is a Core API surface that grows under the stdlib rubric.

hybrid.synthesis: A already carries B's locality (rules name their field on their own line inside the block) and C's family consistency (an in-body section is ratified S82 grammar). The use-site chain survives only as the context escape, with the same vocabulary — no second engine.

harvest.aspect: validate block in the definition + scoped use-site escape
harvest.use: adopted
kept — one line per field inside the block, bare-name access

harvest.aspect: family consistency with existing in-body grammar
harvest.use: kept via the S82 section shape instead of per-field markers

decisions.title: Typed row-level access policies
decisions.gist: Whether the database enforces per-row access below app code or leaves it to convention.
decisions.lesson:
RLS means row-level security. The data layer, not the app, decides which rows a given user may see or change, so a forgotten filter cannot leak data.

Multi-tenant means one deployment serves many customers whose data must never cross. One missing WHERE clause is the classic leak.

An effect is a tracked capability in Jet, like reading the database. The compiler already reasons about which code touches which effect.

A runtime filter is a condition the system adds to every query automatically, so rows outside the policy never come back even if app code forgot to ask.

Live queries are the ratified server-push path. A policy must cover those too, not only direct reads.
decisions.story:
Edith Hollis runs a multi-tenant support tool. Every ticket belongs to a team, and no team may ever see another's tickets.

Her safety rests on remembering a WHERE team clause on every query and every live subscription. One forgotten clause on one endpoint is a cross-tenant leak and a breach report.

She wants the rule declared once, enforced below her handlers, and impossible to forget.
decisions.inWild: A Ticket table is read by list endpoints, a search box, and a live query, and written by an update handler. Every one of those paths must be confined to the caller's own team.

options.name: Typed row policies enforced below app code
options.detail:
db.policy declares a per-row rule. Every query and mutation path, including live queries, either provably satisfies it or gets the generated runtime filter.

A path that could violate the policy is a compile-time effect error where provable, and the filter covers the rest. Audit lists active policies.

options.name: Library filter by convention
options.detail:
A .scoped(user) helper adds the team filter when the author remembers to call it. Nothing is enforced.

It reads clean on the paths that use it, and leaks on the one path that forgets.

comparisons.note: Postgres enforces row policies in the database, which is why Supabase can expose tables to the client safely. Jet lifts the same guarantee into the type system so violations surface at compile time where provable.
comparisons.code:
CREATE POLICY team_isolation ON tickets
  USING (team = current_setting('app.team')::uuid);

comparisons.note: default_scope adds an implicit filter, but unscoped bypasses it and it applies unevenly, so teams still leak rows. A checked policy cannot be silently skipped.

recommendation.why:
Cross-tenant leaks are among the worst failures a web app ships, and today they hinge on remembering a clause on every path. A checked policy makes the rule declared once and enforced everywhere.

Where the compiler can prove a path lacks caller identity it errors. Otherwise the generated filter guarantees the confinement.
recommendation.tradeoff: Policies require the caller identity to be in scope on data paths, so some helpers must thread a user they did not before. That is the cost of making a leak structurally impossible.

whyNot.reason: A convention that must be remembered on every query will eventually be forgotten on one, and that one is the breach. Safety cannot rest on discipline where enforcement is available.

hybrid.synthesis: The checked policy is the mechanism, and option B's .scoped helper becomes the readable way to spell an explicit exception, such as an audited admin export marked #Unsafe. Convenience without giving up enforcement.

harvest.use: Ship as db.policy, enforced across queries, mutations, and live queries.
Keep as the sanctioned way to name an audited exception to a policy, never as the only line of defense.

decisions.title: Shell auto-activation for jet env
decisions.gist: Whether entering a project directory activates its env automatically or stays explicit.
decisions.lesson:
An env in Jet is a per-project dev shell, declared in env.jet, that sets tools and variables for that project.

A shell hook is a small snippet the shell runs on every directory change, so a tool can react to where you are.

direnv is the popular tool that pioneered this: cd into a project and its environment loads, leave and it unloads.

A trust prompt is Jet's ratified rule that the first time an untrusted directory would run code, the tool asks the user to approve it.

Opt-in means nothing happens until the user installs the hook themselves with one line.
decisions.story:
Warren Boyd hops between six repos a day. Each needs its own toolchain and variables.

With explicit activation he types jet env enter in every one, and forgets it often enough to debug with the wrong tool version. His direnv habit trained him to expect the shell to just follow the project.

He wants cd into a repo to load its env, and cd out to drop it, safely.
decisions.inWild: A developer clones a repo containing env.jet and changes into it. They expect the right compiler and environment variables to be active with no manual command, but only after approving an unfamiliar project once.

options.name: Opt-in cd-activation hook
options.detail:
jet env hook <shell> prints a hook the user adds to their shell config once. After that, entering a directory with env.jet activates it, and leaving deactivates.

The first activation of an untrusted env uses the same trust prompt as the rest of Jet. JET_ENV_DISABLE turns it off anywhere.
options.code:
# install once:
$ jet env hook fish | source   # or add to config.fish

$ cd ~/work/router
jet: env.jet in this directory is not yet trusted. Activate it? [y/N] y
jet env: activated (jet 0.9, PGHOST=localhost)

$ cd ..
jet env: deactivated

$ JET_ENV_DISABLE=1 cd ~/work/router   # no activation this session

options.name: Status quo: explicit enter only
options.detail:
Keep activation manual. The user runs jet env or jetpack enter in each project.

Nothing runs on cd, so there is no hook to install, but the developer must remember every time.
options.code:
$ cd ~/work/router
$ jet env enter        // must remember, every directory, every session
jet env: activated

# forget it and you build with the wrong toolchain, no warning

comparisons.note: direnv made cd-activation the habit a generation of developers now expect, guarded by an explicit allow per directory. Jet mirrors the model and reuses its own trust prompt for the approval step.
comparisons.code:
$ cd myproject
direnv: error .envrc is blocked. Run `direnv allow` to approve.

comparisons.note: mise activate installs a shell hook that swaps toolchains per directory. It proved the one-line opt-in install is the right ergonomic. Jet follows the same shape with jet env hook.
comparisons.code: eval "$(mise activate zsh)"   # one line in your shell config

recommendation.why:
Auto-activation is the ergonomic developers already expect from direnv and mise, and forgetting to activate is a real source of wrong-toolchain bugs. The hook removes that whole failure mode.

It stays safe because the first activation of an unfamiliar project goes through Jet's existing trust prompt.
recommendation.tradeoff: A shell hook runs on every directory change, so it must stay fast and is opt-in rather than on by default. The payoff is that the environment always matches the project you are in.

whyNot.reason: Explicit enter is easy to forget, which silently builds with the wrong toolchain and gives no warning. It leaves a papercut every other tool in this space has already removed.

hybrid.synthesis: The opt-in hook is the feature, and the explicit enter of option B stays available for one-off shells and for anyone who declines to install the hook. Auto by choice, manual always possible.

harvest.use: Ship as jet env hook, opt-in, reusing the ratified trust and disable controls.
Keep as the manual path for scripts, one-off shells, and users who prefer no hook.

decisions.title: Live runtime inspector
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a live view of a running program or relies on post-mortem traces.
decisions.lesson:
A task is Jet's unit of concurrent work, and tasks form a tree as one spawns another.

A channel is a typed pipe between tasks. Its depth is how many messages are waiting, and a full channel means a producer is blocked.

A deadline is a time budget on a task, from the ratified #Context machinery.

An arena is a region of memory freed all at once. Its stats show how much the program is holding.

Post-mortem means you inspect a recording after the run. Live means you attach to a process and watch it right now. .jtrace and jet perf are Jet's existing recording and profiling rails.
decisions.story:
Clara Dawson's data pipeline hangs in staging. Nothing crashes; it just stops making progress.

A post-mortem trace tells her what happened after she kills it, but not what is stuck while it hangs. She needs to see, right now, which channel is full and which task is blocked on it.

In Erlang she would open observer and watch the process live. Jet's runtime is opaque while it runs.
decisions.inWild: A running pipeline stalls with no error. The developer wants a live picture of the task tree, each channel's depth, pending deadlines, and current effect activity, without stopping the process.

options.name: jet inspect live
options.detail:
jet inspect live shows a live task tree, channel depths, deadlines, effect activity, and arena stats. It attaches to a jet dev session or any process started with observe enabled.

It is a viewer over the existing observability rails, not a new fact producer. The same facts feed Canvas's proof rail.
options.code:
$ jet inspect live --attach 48213
task tree                         chan depth    deadline
main                                            -
 ingest         running          in:0          -
   transform    BLOCKED          out:1024/1024 480ms
     write      idle             -             -
effects: Db.Read x3   Net.Send x0
# transform is blocked pushing to a full channel; write task is idle

options.name: Post-mortem only
options.detail:
No live attach. Richer .jtrace recording plus the jet perf viewer cover analysis after the run.

Good for a run that finishes or crashes. Useless for a hang you must observe while it is happening.
options.code:
$ jet run --trace pipeline.jet     // records a .jtrace
$ jet perf view pipeline.jtrace    // inspect afterward

// but a live hang never ends, so there is no finished trace:
$ jet perf view pipeline.jtrace
error: trace is incomplete; process still running

comparisons.note: observer shows every process, mailbox, and memory cell of a live node, and is the tool Erlang developers reach for on a stuck system. jet inspect live brings that live picture to Jet's tasks and channels.
comparisons.code: 1> observer:start().   %% live process and mailbox view

comparisons.note: Go has pprof for profiling and a goroutine dump on demand, but no continuous live view of a running scheduler. A dedicated live inspector fills that exact gap.
comparisons.code: curl localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2   # a one-shot dump, not live

recommendation.why:
A hang has no post-mortem, because the run never ends, so only a live view can show which channel is full and which task is blocked. That is the case where developers are most stuck.

It adds no new fact producer. It views the observability rails that already exist and feeds the same facts to Canvas.
recommendation.tradeoff: Live attach means a process must expose an inspection endpoint, on by default in jet dev and opt-in elsewhere. The benefit is diagnosing a stall while it is happening rather than guessing after.

whyNot.reason: Post-mortem traces cannot help with a hang that never terminates, which is the motivating failure. Profiling a finished run is a different job the perf viewer already covers.

hybrid.synthesis: The live inspector and the post-mortem tools are complementary views over the same observability facts. jet inspect live handles the running system, and .jtrace and jet perf handle the finished one.

harvest.use: Ship as jet inspect live for stalls and running-system diagnosis, feeding Canvas's proof rail.
Keep .jtrace and jet perf as the post-mortem path for completed or crashed runs.

decisions.title: Windows COM automation binder (the Office / VBA estate)
decisions.gist: How Jet reaches the Windows COM estate — Excel, Word, and Outlook automation plus VBA-macro migration.
decisions.lesson:
COM is the Windows component ABI. It is a binary contract that lets one program drive another. Office exposes all of its features through COM.

IDispatch is COM's dynamic call interface. A caller invokes methods by name at runtime instead of through a fixed table.

A type library is a machine-readable description of a component's API. It names the methods, arguments, and types.

VBA is the macro language that scripts Office through COM. Millions of business workbooks carry VBA logic that nobody wants to lose.
decisions.story:
Ruth Callahan runs the quarterly close for a finance team. Their reporting lives in twenty Excel workbooks driven by VBA macros.

The macros are fragile and the person who wrote them left years ago. Ruth wants to automate the close from a Jet service today.

She also wants to migrate the macros into Jet gradually, without a big-bang rewrite that could change a number.
decisions.inWild:
use com.excel as xl

wb :: xl.workbooks.open("q3.xlsx")?
wb.sheet("Summary").cell("B4").set(total)
wb.save()?

options.name: com.* root, Windows-gated, typed stubs from the type library
options.detail: Mount COM as `com.*`, Windows-only with an honest gated error elsewhere (the ratified swift precedent). `use com.excel as xl` binds from the installed type library. `jet inspect bind com` generates committable typed stubs, the way the js binder emits `.d.ts` stubs. Libraries with no type library get a dynamic IDispatch fallback behind `#Unsafe`. The same surface serves both live automation and VBA-estate migration, since the D-MIGRATE-SRC1 importer emits Jet calling `com.*`.
options.code:
use com.excel as xl                       // binds from the installed type library

fn write_summary(total: Money) -> Unit ? ComError {
    wb :: xl.workbooks.open("q3.xlsx")?
    wb.sheet("Summary").cell("B4").set(total)
    wb.save()?
}

// On a non-Windows host the gated error is honest, like swift off macOS:
$ jet build --target linux
error[E3260]: `com.*` needs a Windows host
  ── close.jet:1:5
  use com.excel as xl
      ^^^^^^^^^ COM automation runs only on Windows
  = help: build with --target windows, or run this module on a Windows host

options.name: No COM root — pwsh sidecar or hand C FFI
options.detail: Ship no `com.*` root. Office automation goes through a pwsh sidecar or a hand-written C FFI layer over raw IDispatch. Both work, both are miserable, and both concede the estate. Values cross as interpolated text with no type checks, and there is no migration path.

comparisons.note: pywin32 drives Office through late-bound IDispatch. Calls are dynamic, so a misspelled property or a wrong type fails at runtime, not before. Jet's typed stubs from the type library move those failures to build time.
The old estate glue is VBScript over COM, now deprecated on modern Windows. It has no types and no package story. A typed com.* surface replaces it without a rewrite of the underlying components.

recommendation.why: Option A is the only path that both automates the estate and migrates it. The type library gives a typed, checked surface with no string scraping. The gated error follows the ratified swift precedent, so non-Windows builds fail clearly. The IDispatch fallback still reaches old components that ship no type library.
recommendation.tradeoff: The `com.*` surface runs only on Windows. That is inherent to COM, not a Jet limit. A cross-platform caller wraps the module behind a service boundary and calls it from a Windows host.

whyNot.reason: Option B leaves Office behind a stringly-typed pwsh script or a hand-marshaled C shim. Values cross as interpolated text, so a wrong cell type fails at runtime instead of at build. It also gives no migration path, so the VBA estate stays trapped.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The typed type-library surface is the default. IDispatch behind `#Unsafe` is the escape hatch for components with no type library. The pwsh path from B stays available for one-off glue, never as the Office story.

harvest.use: the shipped com.* surface with committable stubs
pwsh sidecar remains for throwaway automation outside the estate

decisions.title: PowerShell binder and object pipeline
decisions.gist: How Jet calls PowerShell and carries its object pipeline across the boundary.
decisions.lesson:
PowerShell is Microsoft's automation shell and scripting language. PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

A cmdlet is a built-in command that returns objects, not text. PowerShell pipelines pass whole objects between commands rather than strings.

DataTree is Jet's ratified dynamic value. It is a self-describing tree of typed fields, and it is how loosely shaped foreign data crosses into Jet.
decisions.story:
