whyNot.reason: Per-variant records repeat the same operation/resource/cause law and force generic tooling to normalize several shapes. Future shared audit facts would touch every constructor.
It contradicts the already-ratified structured contract: cancellation, timeout, invalid input, and closed lifecycle become unmatchable strings after nominal conversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: A exposes a small IOContext value even for simple path errors. That value is the canonical place for cross-adapter facts and avoids a second native-error channel.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the single public tree. Harvest B's concise matching through enum-pattern ergonomics and keep C's short Display text, without flattening stored facts.

harvest.use: Canonical storage and adapter mapping.
Pattern examples bind only fields callers need.
Display remains short while typed context stays available.

decisions.title: platform.<os>: sugar for OS-conditional lists
decisions.gist: How a dev shell adds Linux-only packages: a platform.linux sugar block, or always the explicit comptime if target.os guard.
decisions.lesson: Platform-conditional lists get an ergonomic sugar that desugars to the ratified comptime if. The expert can still write the if directly, so one mechanism serves both.
decisions.story: The flake used lib.optionals stdenv.isLinux to add chromium, gtk4, and bubblewrap only on Linux. Nate wants that common case short, without hand-writing a comptime guard around every OS-specific list.

options.name: platform.<os> sugar
options.detail: platform.linux (and .macos, .windows) is a sugar block that desugars to the ratified comptime if target.os guard. The common OS-list case reads in one line, and an expert who needs a richer condition writes the if directly.

options.name: Always the explicit comptime if
options.detail: No sugar; every OS-specific list is wrapped in a comptime if by hand. The most common conditional in a dev shell, an OS package list, pays full ceremony every time it appears.

comparisons.note: lib.optionals stdenv.isLinux is the flake's idiom for the same job. platform.linux is the one-line Jet sugar over the ratified comptime guard.
comparisons.code: packages = base ++ lib.optionals stdenv.isLinux [ chromium gtk4 bubblewrap ];

recommendation.why: platform.<os> gives the most common conditional, an OS package list, a one-line spelling while desugaring to the ratified comptime if the expert can still write directly.
recommendation.tradeoff: Sugar adds a second way to write an OS guard. It desugars to the exact if, so there is one semantics and the formatter can show either form.

whyNot.reason: Forcing an explicit comptime if on every OS list charges full ceremony for the single most common dev-shell conditional.

hybrid.synthesis: The sugar and the comptime if are one mechanism: platform.linux desugars to the if. Beginners get the short form, experts the explicit guard, with identical behavior.

harvest.use: The default sugar for the common conditional.
Kept as the desugaring target and the expert form for richer conditions.

decisions.title: runtime: package field for runtime PATH deps
decisions.gist: How a package declares the tools it shells out to at runtime, distinct from build-time deps, and referencable by other tiers.
decisions.lesson: Runtime PATH deps are a distinct kind from build deps. Naming them their own field lets wrap and dev tools reference packages.<n>.runtime instead of restating the list.
decisions.story: jet build and jet run shell out to rustc, cc, lld, ruby, php, and R at runtime. The flake called this jetRuntimePath. Nate wants one named list the binary wrapper and the dev shell both point at.

options.name: Distinct runtime field
options.detail: runtime is its own package field for tools needed on PATH at run time, separate from build deps. It is referencable as packages.jet.runtime, so wrap and the dev-shell tools point at one list instead of copying it.

options.name: Fold runtime into a generic deps list
options.detail: There is one deps list mixing build-time and runtime tools. Nothing distinguishes what must be on PATH at run time, so wrap cannot select just the runtime set and the two intents blur into one bag.
options.code:
deps: [ rustc, stdenv.cc, lld, ruby, php, R ]  // build-time? runtime? both?
wrap: Wrap.{ path_prefix: deps }  // over-wraps: build-only tools leak onto PATH

comparisons.note: jetRuntimePath is a named list the flake reuses for the wrapper prefix and the dev shell. runtime is the direct field for that intent.
comparisons.code: jetRuntimePath = [ rustc stdenv.cc lld ruby php R ]; # reused in wrapProgram and devShell

recommendation.why: A distinct runtime field names exactly the tools needed on PATH at run time and is referencable, so wrap and the dev shell share one list instead of copying it.
recommendation.tradeoff: Packages now distinguish runtime from build deps, one more field to think about. That distinction is what lets wrap select the right set and avoid leaking build-only tools.

whyNot.reason: A single deps bag cannot say what belongs on the runtime PATH, so wrap over-wraps and build-only tools leak into the shipped binary.

hybrid.synthesis: runtime is the named, referencable list; build deps stay separate in the build recipe. One intent per field, and cross-tier refs replace copying.

harvest.use: The referencable source wrap and dev tools both point at.
Kept only for build deps inside the recipe, not for runtime PATH.

decisions.title: formatter: passthrough for non-.jet files
decisions.gist: Whether jet fmt can format non-.jet files by delegating to an external formatter named in the manifest, or only formats .jet.
decisions.lesson: jet fmt is native for .jet. A formatter passthrough lets one command also format the project's non-Jet files, so contributors run one tool, not several.
decisions.story: The flake set formatter to nixfmt so nix fmt formatted the .nix files. Jet has native jet fmt for .jet. Nate wants jet fmt to also format the remaining .nix files without a second tool.

options.name: formatter passthrough
options.detail: formatter names an external formatter for non-Jet files. jet fmt formats .jet natively and delegates other languages to the named tool, so one command formats the whole tree, matching the flake's formatter attribute.
options.code:
formatter: pkgs.nixfmt

$ jet fmt --lang nix
  formatted flake.nix, shell.nix via nixfmt
$ jet fmt              # .jet files handled natively, no external tool

options.name: jet fmt formats .jet only
options.detail: jet fmt never touches non-Jet files. A project with .nix or other files invokes each external formatter separately, so contributors must know and run several tools, and CI wires each one by hand.
options.code:
$ jet fmt          # .jet only
$ nixfmt flake.nix # separate tool, separate CI step, separate to remember

comparisons.note: A flake's formatter attribute is what nix fmt runs. The passthrough gives jet fmt the same single-command reach over mixed-language repos.

recommendation.why: A passthrough lets jet fmt format the whole tree in one command, delegating non-Jet files to a named tool exactly as the flake's formatter attribute does.
recommendation.tradeoff: jet fmt gains a delegation path to external binaries. Native .jet formatting is unaffected, and the external tool runs only when its language is requested.

whyNot.reason: Limiting jet fmt to .jet forces contributors to run and remember a separate formatter per non-Jet language, splitting a single job across tools.

hybrid.synthesis: jet fmt stays native and authoritative for .jet; the passthrough adds delegation for other languages under the same command. One entrypoint, native core, delegated edges.

harvest.use: The default: native .jet plus delegated non-Jet files.
Kept for .jet, which jet fmt always formats itself, never delegating.

decisions.title: jet split/fold law (Fold-only)
decisions.gist: If D-ECO1 selects Fold: the exact law for jet split and jet fold — what moves, what round-trips, and when split refuses.
decisions.lesson: This ballot applies only if D-ECO1 is Fold; otherwise it does not ship. Split moves whole modules byte-identically and refuses when top-level bindings are shared across a boundary.
decisions.story: Under Fold, Nate runs jet split env to lift module env.dev into env.jet, then jet fold env to reverse it. He needs a guarantee the round-trip is byte-identical and a clear error when it cannot be.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet split env      # module env.dev (with leading comments) -> env.jet, byte-identical
$ jet fold env       # reverses; STABILITY test pins split -> fold -> original

$ jet split system
E13xx: cannot split -- top-level `let toolset` is used by system.build-box and env.dev
  fix: route the value through its namespace field (packages.jet.runtime), or inline it

options.name: Adopt the law as written
options.detail: Split moves whole modules plus attached comments into the conventional file, computed fields verbatim. A STABILITY test pins byte-identical round-trip. If a top-level binding is shared across the split boundary, split refuses with E13xx naming both referents and the fix. Reversibility is guaranteed for whole modules.

options.name: Require unconditional reversibility
options.detail: Split must always succeed, auto-rewriting shared top-level bindings to make the move fit. But byte-identical round-trip cannot survive an automatic rewrite, so this either corrupts manifests or silently restructures the user's code. It removes the honest refusal and, with it, Fold as designed.
options.code:
$ jet split system   # never refuses; silently rewrites `let toolset` into two copies
// round-trip is no longer byte-identical -> the STABILITY guarantee is gone

options.name: Reject split tooling
options.detail: No jet split or jet fold exists. Files never move under tooling, which means Fold has no mechanism. Choosing this is equivalent to selecting Roles in D-ECO1, where files are fixed and reserved.
options.code:
// no `jet split` / `jet fold`; layout is fixed at authoring time
// -> this is just Roles; pick Roles in D-ECO1 instead

comparisons.note: jet fmt silently corrupted serde markers for months when its round-trip was not pinned. Split is the same class of tool and needs the same STABILITY pin.
comparisons.code: // STABILITY test: split(x) then fold gives back byte-identical x, comments included

recommendation.why: The written law makes whole-module moves byte-identical and pinned, and turns the one unsafe case, shared top-level bindings, into an honest error with a fix rather than a silent rewrite.
recommendation.tradeoff: Reversibility is conditional: a file whose modules share a top-level binding must be restructured before it splits. The ported repo already avoids this by routing values through namespace refs.

whyNot.reason: Auto-rewriting shared bindings destroys the byte-identical round-trip and silently restructures user code, the exact corruption the STABILITY pin exists to prevent.
Removing split leaves Fold with no mechanism; it is Roles under another name and should be chosen as Roles in D-ECO1.

hybrid.synthesis: The law keeps split total for the safe case (whole modules) and honest for the unsafe case (shared bindings refuse with a fix). Neither corruption nor a hard block on the common path.

harvest.use: The shipping law: byte-identical round-trip plus E13xx refusal.
Rejected as a rewrite, but its goal is met for whole modules, which always round-trip.
Available as choosing Roles in D-ECO1, not as a Fold variant.

decisions.title: Reaffirm U7: a lone script needs no project file
decisions.gist: Whether to reaffirm that a lone script never needs a project file, in every file model.
decisions.lesson: U7 stands: jet run script.jet works with zero manifest. Every framework in this wave preserves the zero-ceremony path; this ballot just pins it against erosion.
decisions.story: A beginner writes hello.jet and runs it with no pkg.jet, project.jet, or anything else. Nate wants that guarantee reaffirmed so no framework in this wave quietly makes a manifest mandatory.
decisions.inWild:
$ cat hello.jet
fn main() { print("hello") }

$ jet run hello.jet     # no pkg.jet, no project.jet, nothing else on disk
hello

options.name: Reaffirm U7
options.detail: A single script runs with no manifest of any kind, under Deck, Roles, or Fold alike. A project file appears only when the user wants a name, dependencies, or an env. The zero-ceremony beginner path is guaranteed.

options.name: Revisit U7 (require a minimal manifest)
options.detail: Running any script requires at least a minimal project file. This adds ceremony to the very first thing a beginner does and breaks the magic-out-of-the-box path. Listed for completeness; not recommended.

comparisons.note: cargo run needs a Cargo.toml and a package layout; there is no zero-file path. U7 is deliberately the opposite for beginners.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo run
error: could not find `Cargo.toml`

recommendation.why: Reaffirming U7 keeps the zero-ceremony first run intact across all three file models, protecting the magic-out-of-the-box path this wave must not erode.
recommendation.tradeoff: None of substance: the manifest stays optional and appears the moment a real project needs a name, deps, or an env.

whyNot.reason: Requiring a manifest for a lone script adds ceremony to the first thing a beginner does and breaks the zero-file path.

hybrid.synthesis: The zero-file run and the optional manifest are one continuum: nothing for a script, a project file when the project earns one. U7 is that continuum, reaffirmed.

harvest.use: The guaranteed beginner path, reaffirmed in every framework.
Kept as an opt-in the moment a project wants a name, deps, or an env.

decisions.title: module fleet.<name> spelling (un-freezes fleet surface)
decisions.gist: Whether to define module fleet.<name> now, with hosts, rollout, health, and proof, which un-freezes fleet surface that D-JETOS-FREEZE1 froze.
decisions.lesson: Giving fleet equal depth in this wave re-opens surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 froze. This is a real ballot, not a silent inclusion. Fleet has no flake anchor, so its fixture is the owner's halcyon host.
decisions.story: Nate deploys build-box and halcyon together with a rolling policy and a health gate before each batch. No flake construct describes a fleet. He must decide whether to spell fleet now or leave it frozen.

options.name: Adopt module fleet.<name> now
options.detail: Fleet gets its spelling at equal depth in this wave: hosts, rollout, health, and proof. This un-freezes the fleet surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 deferred, per the owner's equal-depth scope ruling. The acceptance fixture is the halcyon host.
options.code:
$ jet fleet prod --plan
  batch 1/2: build-box  -> health `curl -sf .../health` must pass before batch 2
  proof: .Vm required before rollout (D-WD8)
// spelling lands now; realization follows the risk-class proof law

options.name: Keep frozen, drop fleet from this wave
options.detail: Fleet stays deferred under D-JETOS-FREEZE1 until its planned epoch. This wave ships with no fleet spelling, so multi-host rollout has no manifest surface yet and the halcyon fixture waits.
options.code:
// no module fleet.<name> in this wave
// multi-host rollout remains a frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1)

comparisons.note: A flake has no fleet primitive; multi-host rollout is bolted on with deploy-rs or colmena. Fleet would make host sets and rollout first-class.

recommendation.why: The owner's equal-depth scope ruling puts fleet alongside the other tiers in this wave, and the halcyon host gives it a concrete acceptance fixture despite no flake anchor.
recommendation.tradeoff: Adopting fleet re-opens surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 froze; this ballot exists so that un-freeze is an explicit owner decision, not a silent inclusion.

whyNot.reason: Keeping fleet frozen leaves multi-host rollout with no manifest surface in a wave that gives every other tier equal depth.

hybrid.synthesis: Fleet is a role module like env and system: one mechanism, placed by the chosen file model. Adopting it now keeps the tier set complete under the equal-depth ruling.

harvest.use: The adopted spelling: hosts, rollout, health, proof.
Honored by making this un-freeze an explicit ballot rather than a quiet add.

decisions.title: module system.<name> at equal depth (un-freezes system surface)
decisions.gist: Whether to spell module system.<name> at equal depth in this wave, which un-freezes system surface frozen by D-JETOS-FREEZE1.
decisions.lesson: System is the jetos host tier. Placing it at equal depth now re-opens surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 froze; this ballot names that trade rather than smuggling it in.
decisions.story: Nate's build-box is a jetos host with a target, packages, services, and ordered options. The ported flake and the owner's ~/nixos both define such hosts. He must decide whether system gets a spelling now or stays frozen.

options.name: Adopt module system.<name> now
options.detail: System gets its spelling at equal depth with the other tiers: target, packages, services, and the ordered options list. This un-freezes the system surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 deferred, per the owner's equal-depth scope ruling, with ~/nixos halcyon as the fixture.

options.name: Keep frozen, drop system from this wave
options.detail: System stays deferred under D-JETOS-FREEZE1. This wave ships with no host spelling, so jetos hosts have no manifest surface yet and the ~/nixos parity fixture waits for a later epoch.
options.code:
// no module system.<name> in this wave
// jetos hosts remain a frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1)

comparisons.note: A NixOS host is nixosConfigurations.<name> with options set across modules. system.<name> is the direct Jet spelling, with an ordered options list.

recommendation.why: The equal-depth ruling puts system alongside env, image, and fleet in this wave, and ~/nixos gives it a concrete parity fixture the other tiers reference.
recommendation.tradeoff: Adopting system re-opens surface D-JETOS-FREEZE1 froze; this ballot makes that un-freeze an explicit owner decision instead of a quiet inclusion.

whyNot.reason: Keeping system frozen leaves jetos hosts with no manifest surface while every other tier in the wave gets equal depth.

hybrid.synthesis: System is a role module like env and fleet: one mechanism, placed by the chosen file model. Adopting it now completes the tier set under the equal-depth ruling.

harvest.use: The adopted spelling: target, packages, services, options.
Honored by making this un-freeze an explicit ballot, not a silent add.

decisions.title: check: true package field (doCheck parity)
decisions.gist: Whether a package's test targets run during realize via a check field, matching Nix doCheck, or only through a separate jet test.
decisions.lesson: check: true runs the package's declared test targets during realize, mapping doCheck. Standalone jet test needs no field; this ballot covers the build-time gate.
decisions.story: The flake set doCheck so tests ran as part of building jet. Nate wants building the package to fail if its tests fail, without separate CI wiring, while jet test still works on its own.

options.name: check: true field
options.detail: check: true makes the package's declared test targets run during realize, so a failing test fails the build. It maps doCheck exactly. A standalone jet test still runs tests on demand and needs no field.
options.code:
check: true

$ jet build jet
  built target/release/jet
  check: ran 3 test targets ... FAILED tir::codegen
  build failed: check tests did not pass

options.name: No field, standalone jet test only
options.detail: Building never runs tests; tests run only when someone invokes jet test. A package with failing tests can build and publish clean unless CI separately remembers to run jet test, losing the flake's doCheck gate.
options.code:
$ jet build jet     # succeeds even if tests would fail; no realize-time gate
$ jet test          # separate step someone must wire and remember

comparisons.note: doCheck = true runs the check phase inside the build, so a failing test fails the derivation. check: true is the direct parity.
comparisons.code: buildRustPackage { doCheck = true; }; # tests gate the build

recommendation.why: check: true reproduces doCheck exactly, gating realize on the package's own tests so a broken build cannot be published, while jet test stays available standalone.
recommendation.tradeoff: Realize now runs the package's test targets when check is set, adding that step to a build. It is opt-in per package and off by default.

whyNot.reason: Without the field, building never runs tests, so a failing package can publish clean unless CI separately remembers jet test, dropping doCheck parity.

hybrid.synthesis: check: true is the build-time gate; jet test is the on-demand run. One test surface, two triggers, so realize can gate without removing the standalone command.

harvest.use: The adopted field that fails a build on failing tests.
Kept as jet test, which needs no field and runs anytime.

decisions.title: git.root comptime builtin
decisions.gist: How a manifest gets the git top-level path: a git.root comptime builtin, or a hand-wired env var and path.
decisions.lesson: git.root is a comptime builtin resolving the git top level, replacing the flake's git rev-parse dance. JET_ROOT still overrides it at runtime for the expert.
decisions.story: The flake ran git rev-parse in its shellHook to set JET_ROOT and locate the debug binary. Nate wants that path as a comptime value, not a shell subprocess embedded in every manifest.

options.name: git.root comptime builtin
options.detail: git.root is a comptime builtin that resolves the git top-level directory during evaluation. It replaces the shellHook git rev-parse, reads as a plain value, and the JET_ROOT env var still overrides it at runtime for anyone who needs to.

options.name: Hand-wired path or env var
options.detail: No builtin; the manifest names an explicit path or reads an env var the user sets. Every project re-derives the git-root logic, and a wrong or unset value produces a broken root with no comptime check.
options.code:
env_vars: [ "JET_ROOT": env("JET_ROOT") ?? "../.." ]  // guess the depth
// each project re-invents root-finding; unset -> wrong path, no error

comparisons.note: The flake shells out with git rev-parse --show-toplevel in a hook. git.root makes that a comptime value with a clean runtime override.

recommendation.why: git.root turns the flake's git rev-parse subprocess into a plain comptime value, while the JET_ROOT env override preserves the expert's runtime control.
recommendation.tradeoff: git.root assumes a git checkout at comptime; outside a repo it is unset and the manifest must handle that. The runtime override covers relocated checkouts.

whyNot.reason: Hand-wiring the path makes every project re-derive root-finding, and a wrong or unset value yields a broken root with no comptime check.

hybrid.synthesis: git.root is the comptime default; the JET_ROOT env var is the runtime override. One value, resolved automatically, still overridable, so beginners write nothing and experts keep control.

harvest.use: The default: git top level with no subprocess.
Kept as the JET_ROOT env var, not a hand-wired guess in every manifest.

decisions.title: Typed package output accessors (pkgs.tzdata.zoneinfo)
decisions.gist: How a manifest references a sub-output of a package, like tzdata's zoneinfo directory: a typed accessor, or raw string path interpolation.
decisions.lesson: A typed output accessor names a package's sub-output, replacing string path interpolation. A wrong output name is a build error, not a dangling path discovered at runtime.
decisions.story: The flake set TZDIR to tzdata's share/zoneinfo via string interpolation. Nate wants to name that output directly, so a typo fails the build instead of producing a broken path inside the wrapped binary.
decisions.inWild:
wrap: Wrap.{ env: [ "TZDIR": pkgs.tzdata.zoneinfo ] }   // (new -- D-ECO19)
// accessor names the zoneinfo output; wrong name -> build error, not a dead path

options.name: Typed output accessors
options.detail: A package exposes named outputs as accessors, so pkgs.tzdata.zoneinfo resolves the zoneinfo output. A misnamed output fails at build with a suggestion, and the resolved path is never a hand-spliced string.
options.code:
"TZDIR": pkgs.tzdata.zoneinfoo    // typo

$ jet build jet
E05xx: package `tzdata` has no output `zoneinfoo`
  fix: available outputs are `zoneinfo`, `bin`; did you mean `zoneinfo`?

options.name: Raw string path interpolation
options.detail: The manifest splices a path by hand, like tzdata plus /share/zoneinfo. Nothing checks the sub-path exists, so a typo or a layout change produces a dangling path that only surfaces when the wrapped binary runs.
options.code:
"TZDIR": "${pkgs.tzdata}/share/zoneinfoo"   // typo builds clean
// -> TZDIR points nowhere; only fails when jet runs and can't read zoneinfo

comparisons.note: Nix interpolates ${pkgs.tzdata}/share/zoneinfo as an unchecked string. Typed accessors turn the sub-output into a checked name.

recommendation.why: Typed accessors name a package's outputs, so a wrong output fails at build with a suggestion instead of producing a dangling path that only breaks when the binary runs.
recommendation.tradeoff: Packages must declare their named outputs for accessors to resolve. That declaration is what turns a runtime path failure into a build-time error.

whyNot.reason: String interpolation checks nothing, so a typo or a layout change yields a dangling path that surfaces only at runtime.

hybrid.synthesis: Accessors are the checked default for known outputs; a raw string stays possible for a truly ad-hoc path, but never for outputs a package already names. Checked where it can be, escapable where it must be.

harvest.use: The default accessor for any declared package output.
Allowed only for genuinely undeclared paths, not named outputs.

decisions.title: Should packages and JetOS live in one project?
decisions.gist: Choose whether one project connects source code all the way to a running machine.
decisions.lesson:
A project can be pictured as a map. It shows what you build, what it needs, how you test it, and where it runs.

With one map, Jet can explain why a service runs on a server. The answer leads back through the package, compiler, and downloaded input.

This vote chooses the size of that map. Other ballots choose how it is written, split, combined, and saved.
decisions.story: Rin starts with a command-line app. It grows into an API, a development setup, a container image, and two home servers. Rin wants one place to understand the whole thing.

options.name: One typed Jet project
options.detail: Packages, development setups, checks, services, images, and machines are parts of one Jet value. A machine can point directly to the package it runs.
options.technical: Jet checks every link before building. The same project map powers run, test, build, explain, image, and operating-system commands.

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Guix puts packages and complete operating systems in one programmable language. People love its live interactive prompt, macros, and ability to reuse normal Scheme code.
options.technical: Jet would adopt Guix records, services, build descriptions, profiles, and system generations as Scheme concepts.
options.code:
;; Guile Scheme
(operating-system
  (packages (list api))
  (services (list api-service)))

$ guix system reconfigure system.scm

options.name: Bazel directly
options.detail: Host language: Starlark. Bazel puts builds in a precise target map. People love its dependable queries and control in enormous repositories.
options.technical: Packages, images, and machines would all become labeled Bazel-style targets and rules.
options.code:
jet_binary(name = "api", ...)
jetos_system(name = "halcyon", services = [":api_service"])

$ bazel query 'deps(//systems:halcyon)'

options.name: Separate package and machine projects
options.detail: The package manager and JetOS each keep a smaller map. They connect through built artifacts, but users maintain two roots, two explanations, and two histories.
options.technical: The JetOS side imports package outputs by an exact digest instead of sharing the package map.

comparisons.note: The best complete system in another language. Guix already joins packages, services, images, generations, and operating systems.
The best very-large build map. Starlark is liked because it feels familiar while staying predictable.

recommendation.why: A gives Jet Guix’s whole-system unity with Jet types, Jet errors, and no second configuration language. Beginners see one project; experts can trace every link.

whyNot.reason: Guix proves the idea, but Scheme-shaped data and errors would make Jet projects feel like another language.
Bazel gives excellent control, but labels, BUILD files, and rules add the ceremony Jet is trying to remove.
Separate projects create two sources of truth exactly where packages and machines need to agree.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Project type must cover everything from a small package to a machine. That broad type is useful because it gives every Jet tool the same truth.

decisions.comment: But open a ballot for project, that doesn’t sound right for jetos config, if this is going to fit both jetos and regular jet/jetpack it needs to be a fitting word in both cases

decisions.title: First-class cargo build field: Recipe.cargo(lock:)
decisions.gist: How a package declares its build, and whether cargo builds get a typed first-class field or only an imperative recipe function.
decisions.lesson: Common build systems deserve a typed one-liner. The escape to imperative build code stays available, but a plain cargo build should not require ceremony.
decisions.story: A contributor builds jet from Cargo.lock. The flake used buildRustPackage with cargoLock.lockFile and a check pass. She wants the same in one legible line, not a hand-written build script.

options.name: Typed Recipe.cargo field
options.detail: build takes a typed recipe. Recipe.cargo(lock:) maps buildRustPackage and cargoLock.lockFile in one line. Recipe stays open for other build systems, and an imperative fn build stays available when a recipe cannot express a build.
options.code:
build: Recipe.cargo(lock: "Cargo.lock")

// realize:
$ jet build jet
  resolved lock Cargo.lock -> 214 crates
  built target/release/jet   (check: true -> test targets ran)

options.name: Imperative build fn only
options.detail: No typed sugar; every package writes a build function that invokes cargo by hand. This repeats the same lockfile-and-invoke boilerplate in every Rust package and hides the common case behind a function body.

comparisons.note: buildRustPackage with cargoLock.lockFile is the flake's typed helper. Recipe.cargo is the direct one-line equivalent, keeping the imperative path for the rare build.

recommendation.why: Recipe.cargo gives the common cargo build a legible one-line spelling with the lockfile pinned, matching the flake exactly while leaving imperative builds reachable.
recommendation.tradeoff: Recipe is a named surface that must grow one variant per supported build system. The imperative fn build remains for anything a recipe cannot yet express.

whyNot.reason: Forcing every build through a function repeats lockfile-and-invoke boilerplate and hides the common case, against the anti-repetition principle.

hybrid.synthesis: One build field accepts both: a typed Recipe for common systems and an imperative fn for the rest. Recipe.cargo is the ergonomic default, fn build the expert escape.

harvest.use: The default spelling for the common Rust package.
Kept as the escape hatch under the same build field.

decisions.title: wrap: Wrap.{ path_prefix, env } binary wrapping
decisions.gist: How a built binary gets a runtime PATH prefix and default env vars baked in, replacing Nix wrapProgram.
decisions.lesson: Wrapping a binary with runtime PATH and default env is a declarative fact about the package, not a post-build shell step to hand-write.
decisions.story: jet shells out to rustc, cc, and lld at runtime. The flake wrapped the binary with a PATH prefix and a default TZDIR. Nate wants those baked in without writing wrapProgram.

options.name: Typed Wrap record
options.detail: wrap takes a Wrap value with path_prefix and env. It maps wrapProgram's --prefix PATH and --set-default in one place, distinguishing a PATH prefix from a defaulted env var, both as typed data.
options.code:
wrap: Wrap.{ path_prefix: self.runtime,
             env: ["TZDIR": pkgs.tzdata.zoneinfo] }

$ jet build jet
  wrapped target/release/jet: PATH+= rustc,cc,lld  TZDIR?=/nix/store/.../zoneinfo

options.name: Implicit auto-wrap from runtime
options.detail: No explicit Wrap; the compiler auto-prefixes PATH from the runtime list. This is hidden magic with no place to express a defaulted env var like TZDIR, and no way to distinguish a hard prefix from a default.

comparisons.note: wrapProgram --prefix PATH --set-default TZDIR is two distinct operations. Wrap keeps that distinction as two typed fields instead of positional shell flags.

recommendation.why: A typed Wrap keeps the flake's two distinct operations, a PATH prefix and a defaulted env var, as legible data the compiler and audit tools can read.
recommendation.tradeoff: Wrap is one more named record in the package surface. It earns its place by covering both wrapProgram operations that an implicit rule cannot express.

whyNot.reason: Implicit auto-wrap is hidden magic with no surface for default env vars, leaving --set-default TZDIR unmappable and losing parity.

hybrid.synthesis: Wrap's path_prefix defaults to the package runtime list, so the common case is nearly free while the env field still expresses defaults the implicit rule could not.

harvest.use: The declarative spelling that covers both wrapProgram operations.
Adopted as Wrap's default for path_prefix so the common case stays short.

decisions.title: alias(package, bin:) second entrypoint
decisions.gist: How a second command name is exposed from one built binary, replacing a Nix apps.* second entry.
decisions.lesson: A second entrypoint on the same binary is one line of alias, never a duplicated package. Repetition is the thing to cut.
decisions.story: The flake exposed apps.default as jet and apps.jetpack on the same binary. Nate wants a jetpack command without declaring a whole second package that repeats the build.

options.name: alias(package, bin:)
options.detail: A one-line alias names a second command on the same built binary. It maps apps.jetpack directly, shares one build, and reads as exactly what it is: a second name, not a second program.
options.code:
jetpack: alias(packages.jet, bin: "jetpack")

$ jetpack help    # dispatches into the jet binary under the jetpack name

options.name: Declare a full second package
options.detail: The second command is its own package with its own build block, duplicating build, wrap, and meta. The two blocks drift out of sync, and the user restates a build they already wrote.

comparisons.note: apps.jetpack points a second app at the same derivation. alias is the direct Jet spelling for one binary under two names.

recommendation.why: alias states one binary under a second name in a single line, matching apps.jetpack and cutting the duplicated build a second package would force.
recommendation.tradeoff: alias adds one keyword to the package surface. It exists precisely to avoid restating a build, which is the higher cost.

whyNot.reason: A full second package duplicates build, wrap, and meta, which drift apart and make the user repeat work already done.

hybrid.synthesis: alias is the single canonical way to give one binary a second name; a genuinely different second binary still declares its own package. Two jobs, two spellings, no overlap.

harvest.use: The spelling for a second command on the same binary.
Kept for a genuinely distinct second binary, not an alias.

decisions.title: meta: Meta.{…} typed package metadata
decisions.gist: How package metadata like description, homepage, main program, and platforms is declared: a typed record or a freeform map.
decisions.lesson: Metadata that tools read, like the main program and supported platforms, should be typed so a typo is an error, not a silent registry entry.
decisions.story: The flake set meta.description, homepage, mainProgram, and platforms. Nate wants the CLI and registry to trust those fields, and a typo in platforms to fail the build rather than ship.
decisions.inWild:
meta: Meta.{ description:  "Compiler for the Jet programming language",
             homepage:     "https://github.com/jet-language/jet",
             main_program: "jet",       // must name a real declared bin
             platforms:    .Unix }       // enum, not a free string

options.name: Typed Meta record
options.detail: meta takes a Meta value. main_program is checked against the package's declared binaries and platforms is an enum, so a wrong name or misspelled platform fails at build, not in the published registry entry.
options.code:
meta: Meta.{ main_program: "jett", platforms: .Unix }

$ jet build jet
E05xx: meta.main_program "jett" names no binary in this package
  fix: declared bins are `jet`; did you mean "jet"?

options.name: Freeform metadata map
options.detail: meta is an untyped map of strings. Nothing checks that main_program names a real binary or that platforms is a known value; mistakes surface only after publish, if ever.
options.code:
meta: { main_program: "jett", platforms: "unix-ish" }
// builds clean; ships a broken main_program and a nonsense platform

comparisons.note: flake meta is a free attrset; mainProgram and platforms are unchecked strings. A typed Meta catches what Nix leaves silent.
comparisons.code: meta = { description = "..."; homepage = "..."; mainProgram = "jet"; platforms = platforms.unix; };

recommendation.why: A typed Meta validates main_program against real binaries and platforms against an enum, turning a class of silent registry mistakes into build errors.
recommendation.tradeoff: Meta fixes the set of known metadata keys; a novel key needs a Meta extension rather than an ad-hoc string. That constraint is what makes the checks possible.

whyNot.reason: A freeform map validates nothing, so a wrong main_program or bogus platform ships to the registry unnoticed.

hybrid.synthesis: Meta covers the known metadata keys with types and checks, while an explicit extra map can carry rare custom keys without weakening the checked core.

harvest.use: The typed core: main_program and platforms are validated.
Allowed only in an explicit extras map, never for the checked fields.

decisions.title: Typed dev-shell fields: env_vars, library_path, git_hooks_path, banner
decisions.gist: How a dev shell sets env vars, library path, git-hooks path, and its banner: typed fields with a stderr guarantee, or one freeform shell hook.
decisions.lesson: The common dev-shell knobs deserve typed fields. The banner must render to stderr so stdout stays grep-clean, a promise a raw echo in a shell hook cannot make.
decisions.story: The flake shellHook exported JET_ROOT and TZDIR, set a library path for raylib, pointed git at scripts/githooks, and printed a ten-line banner. A raw banner leaks into piped stdout and breaks scripts.

options.name: Typed fields with stderr banner
options.detail: Each knob is its own typed field. Banner.lines carries a guarantee that it renders to stderr, so a piped command sees clean stdout. env_vars, library_path, and git_hooks_path map the shellHook exports directly.

options.name: One freeform shell hook
options.detail: All four knobs live inside a single hook body of shell-style statements. The banner is a raw print with no stderr guarantee, so it pollutes piped stdout, and every project reinvents the same exports by hand.

comparisons.note: A flake shellHook is one shell blob; its echo banner routinely leaks into stdout. Typed fields give each export a name and the banner an stderr guarantee.
comparisons.code: shellHook = ''export JET_ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel); echo "Jet dev shell"'';

recommendation.why: Typed fields name each dev-shell knob and give the banner an enforced stderr rendering, so a piped jet env never returns banner text as data.
recommendation.tradeoff: The set of typed fields is fixed; anything outside them needs the D-ECO7 hook. That boundary is deliberate and keeps the common knobs guaranteed.

whyNot.reason: A freeform hook makes the banner a raw print that pollutes stdout and forces every project to re-derive the same exports.

hybrid.synthesis: Typed fields cover the named knobs with guarantees; the trust-gated D-ECO7 hook remains the single escape for anything they cannot express. One mechanism, common case typed.

harvest.use: The default surface for env, library path, hooks path, and banner.
Preserved only as the D-ECO7 trust-gated hook, not the default.

decisions.title: Expert trust-gated dev-shell hook: fn(sh: Shell)
decisions.gist: Whether the dev shell has an expert escape for arbitrary Jet code at activation, and whether that code is trust-gated.
decisions.lesson: Typed fields cover the common case; a trust-gated hook is the one escape for what they cannot say. Arbitrary activation code without a trust gate is a supply-chain hole.
decisions.story: The flake ran clean-nix-tmp.sh once per shell so /tmp did not fill. No typed field says run-this-script-once. Nate needs an escape, but not one that lets any cloned repo run code silently on entry.

options.name: Trust-gated hook
options.detail: The hook is Jet code that runs at activation, but only after the repo's grant is approved under the trust law. A first entry prompts; a denied or unseen grant means the hook does not run. The escape exists without opening the supply-chain hole.

options.name: Typed fields only, no hook
options.detail: There is no escape hatch; only the typed D-ECO6 fields exist. The clean-nix-tmp guard cannot be expressed, so users drop back to a shell wrapper outside Jet, losing the trust boundary entirely for that step.
options.code:
// no way to say "run this once on entry"
// users re-add a raw shell wrapper around `jet env`, outside any trust gate

comparisons.note: A flake shellHook runs unconditionally on entry with no consent. The Jet hook keeps the capability but gates it behind an approved grant.
comparisons.code: shellHook = ''bash scripts/agent/clean-nix-tmp.sh''; # runs on every entry, no prompt

recommendation.why: A trust-gated hook keeps the one genuine escape the typed fields cannot cover, while the grant law ensures no cloned repo runs activation code without consent.
recommendation.tradeoff: Users meet a grant prompt the first time a repo defines a hook. That one prompt is the price of not shipping silent on-entry code execution.

whyNot.reason: Removing the escape pushes the clean-nix-tmp guard back into an ungated shell wrapper, losing the trust boundary the hook provides.

hybrid.synthesis: The typed D-ECO6 fields handle the common knobs; the trust-gated hook is the single, consent-checked escape beneath them. One escape, gated, no second unsafe path.

harvest.use: The one escape hatch, allowed only after an approved grant.
Kept as the default when a repo defines no hook: nothing runs on entry.

decisions.title: .with([…]) package customization combinator
decisions.gist: How a package is customized, such as R with an extra CRAN package: one .with combinator used inline or in an overlay, or two different override syntaxes.
decisions.lesson: There is one way to customize a package, the .with combinator. Inline and overlay are placements of the same spelling, not two mechanisms.
decisions.story: The flake used rWrapper.override with a jsonlite package. The current env.jet stopgap lists R and jsonlite as two loose entries, which never wires jsonlite into R. Nate wants a spelling that actually composes.

options.name: One .with combinator, two placements
options.detail: package.with([...]) is the single customization spelling. Inline handles a one-off; the workspace overlay uses the identical combinator via package("...").with for a reviewed, reusable override. Same mechanism, different home.

options.name: Separate inline vs overlay syntaxes
options.detail: Inline customization and overlay customization get different spellings. Users learn two ways to do one job, and moving an override from inline to a reviewed overlay means rewriting it, not relocating it.

comparisons.note: rWrapper.override is a per-package function with bespoke argument shapes. .with is one combinator that reads the same inline or in an overlay.

recommendation.why: One .with combinator means a customization reads identically inline and in an overlay, so promoting a one-off to a reviewed override is a move, not a rewrite.
recommendation.tradeoff: Every customization must fit the .with shape; a package needing something .with cannot express extends the combinator rather than inventing a new syntax. That constraint is the point.

whyNot.reason: Two override syntaxes for one job violates one-way-to-mean-it and forces a rewrite when moving inline to a reviewed overlay.

hybrid.synthesis: The overlay is not a competing mechanism; it is where .with lives when an override should be reviewed and reused. Inline and overlay are the beginner and expert surfaces of one combinator.

harvest.use: The one customization spelling, inline or in overlay.
Satisfied by the overlay home of the same .with, not a separate syntax.

decisions.title: Tool.wrap dev-loop wrappers with typed root and missing-error
decisions.gist: How the dev-loop wrappers pointing at target/debug carry their root-walk fallback and missing-binary error: typed data or a raw shell script.
decisions.lesson: A dev wrapper's root fallback and missing-binary message are typed data, so the error stays consistent and the formatter can round-trip it, unlike a hand-written shell script.
decisions.story: The flake mkJetDevBin wrapped target/debug/jet, walked up to the git root, honored JET_ROOT, and printed a fixed error when the binary was absent. Nate wants that behavior as data, not a shell heredoc.

options.name: Typed Tool.wrap
options.detail: Tool.wrap takes bin, path_prefix, root, and missing as typed fields. root carries the git-root fallback (JET_ROOT overrides it), and missing carries the fix line printed when the binary is absent, as data the tooling renders identically.
options.code:
$ jet run hello.jet
jet: no debug binary at target/debug/jet
  fix: cargo build
// error text comes from the `missing:` field, identical for jet and jetpack

options.name: Raw shell script string
options.detail: Each wrapper is a shell script literal, like writeShellScriptBin. The missing-binary error is hand-written per wrapper and drifts, the formatter cannot round-trip the embedded shell, and the root-walk is re-implemented each time.
options.code:
jet: script(''
  root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
  [ -x "$root/target/debug/jet" ] || { echo "jet: no debug binary"; exit 1; }
'')  // per-wrapper drift, no formatter round-trip

comparisons.note: mkJetDevBin and writeShellScriptBin embed shell text per wrapper. Tool.wrap lifts the root fallback and error into typed fields shared by both wrappers.

recommendation.why: Typed fields make the root fallback and missing-binary error shared data, so both wrappers print the same message and the formatter round-trips the manifest.
recommendation.tradeoff: Tool.wrap fixes the wrapper's shape to bin, path_prefix, root, and missing. A wrapper needing more extends Tool.wrap rather than dropping to shell.

whyNot.reason: Shell-string wrappers hand-write the error per wrapper, drift apart, and cannot be round-tripped by the formatter.

hybrid.synthesis: Tool.wrap turns the flake's shell wrapper into typed fields; the JET_ROOT env override still works at runtime, so the expert keeps the override without hand-writing shell.

harvest.use: The default spelling: shared root and missing-error data.
Kept as the JET_ROOT env override, not a shell reimplementation.

decisions.title: Token verification contract: audience and PASETO mode
decisions.gist: Which JWT and PASETO formats core.auth verifies, and how callers state the audience a token must target.
decisions.lesson:
A signed token is a claim packet from another system. Verification must answer two different questions. First: did the expected key sign these exact bytes? Second: was this token meant for this service, at this time? The audience claim answers the second question. Signature-only verification can accept a valid token minted for a different service.

JWT is a container whose header chooses an algorithm. That choice can create algorithm-confusion bugs unless Jet accepts a closed algorithm set. PASETO avoids algorithm choice inside the token. Its v4.public form is a signed public token; v4.local is encrypted with a shared secret and is opened, not merely verified.

A safe API therefore needs an expected audience, fixed supported formats, expiry rules, and typed failures. The current D-AUTH2 ballot chose core.auth and standalone functions, but its two-argument example manually checks audience while its prose says audience is already checked. It also names PASETO without choosing v4.public or v4.local. This decision closes those security semantics before implementation.
decisions.story: Priya's gateway accepts partner tokens. The partner also issues tokens for its billing service. Both use the same signing key. A billing token has a valid signature and expiry, but audience billing. Priya needs core.auth to reject it before handler code sees trusted claims.
decisions.inWild:
use core.auth

claims := auth.verify_jwt(req.bearer(), key: partner_key, audience: "gateway")?
print(claims.subject)

# billing token result:
# AuthError.WrongAudience { expected: "gateway", actual: "billing" }

options.name: Closed verify formats with required audience
options.detail: Keep D-AUTH2's direct core.auth functions, but require a named audience. JWT verification accepts HS256 only. PASETO verification accepts v4.public only. Both reject missing or wrong audience and expired tokens before returning Claims. Optional named issuer and clock_skew fields give expert control without changing the mechanism.
options.technical: verify_jwt signs header.payload with HMAC-SHA-256, requires alg=HS256, performs constant-time comparison, requires exp and aud, and optionally requires iss. verify_paseto implements PASETO v4.public pre-authentication encoding, Ed25519 strict verification, footer and implicit-assertion inputs, then applies the same claims policy. v4.local belongs to a future open/decrypt API, not verify. Unknown JWT algorithms and PASETO versions fail closed.
options.code:
# beginner-safe path
claims := auth.verify_jwt(token, key: shared_key, audience: "gateway")?

# expert controls, same function
claims := auth.verify_paseto(token, key: public_key, audience: "gateway",
    issuer: "partner", clock_skew: 30s, footer: [], implicit: [])?

# wrong audience -> AuthError.WrongAudience

options.name: Policy object with format agility
options.detail: Pass a TokenPolicy object that selects JWT algorithms and either PASETO public or local purpose. This exposes more formats immediately, but every call must construct policy and the token parser accepts a wider negotiation surface.
options.technical: The policy lists accepted JWT algorithms, expected audience and issuer, clock skew, and PASETO purpose/version. v4.local returns decrypted claims and therefore combines verify and open semantics in one function family.
options.code:
policy := auth.TokenPolicy.{ audience: "gateway", jwt: [.HS256, .EdDSA], paseto: [.V4Public, .V4Local] }
claims := auth.verify_jwt(token, key, policy: policy)?

options.name: Keep two arguments and manual audience checks
options.detail: Preserve the current two-argument spelling. The function verifies signature and expiry, returns audience as data, and every caller must compare it manually. PASETO remains v4.public by convention rather than a checked API contract.
options.technical: This matches the current D-AUTH2 code example but contradicts its statement that audience is already checked. Missing manual checks remain valid Jet programs.
options.code:
claims := auth.verify_jwt(token, key: partner_key)?
if claims.audience != "gateway" { return Response.forbidden("wrong audience") }

comparisons.note: Validation carries an expected audience and an allowed algorithm set; decode checks both with the signature.
v4.public is signed and verified with Ed25519. v4.local is encrypted and opened with a shared key, so they are different operations.

recommendation.why: A makes the safe requirement impossible to forget: a caller must name its audience, and Jet accepts one fixed algorithm per token family. Direct functions preserve D-AUTH2's beginner path while named controls cover expert verification context.

whyNot.reason: B makes algorithm and purpose negotiation part of every call and combines signed-token verification with encrypted-token opening. That widens one mechanism into two security jobs.
C allows a valid token for another service to become trusted whenever one handler forgets its manual audience comparison. It also leaves PASETO semantics undocumented.

recommendation.tradeoff: A initially supports only JWT HS256 and PASETO v4.public. New formats require an explicit future contract instead of a runtime algorithm string; that closed growth is accepted to prevent confusion attacks.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's closed direct functions. Harvest B's expert policy fields as optional named arguments on those same functions, not a second object mechanism. Preserve C's readable Claims audience field for logging and routing, while verification still enforces the required expected audience.

harvest.aspect: Required audience and fixed safe formats
harvest.use: Adopt as the core verification law.

harvest.aspect: Explicit issuer, clock, footer, and implicit-assertion control
harvest.use: Expose as optional named arguments on the same direct functions.

harvest.aspect: Audience remains visible in typed Claims
harvest.use: Keep it for application routing and audit output, but never rely on a manual check for acceptance.

decisions.title: How does a package expose what it can produce or run?
decisions.gist: Choose one model for libraries, commands, services, checks, and environments.
decisions.lesson:
A package output is something the package can produce or activate. Examples include a library, command, web service, test, documentation site, or development environment.

Many tools create separate namespaces for packages, apps, checks, and shells. The same build then appears several times with different wrappers. Jet can instead keep one typed output collection. Commands such as run, test, and dev select outputs by capability.

This vote chooses the representation. It does not choose output names, aliases, or default selection. Those remain separate decisions.
decisions.story: A todo project has a reusable library, a command, a web page, tests, and a development environment. Students should learn one output model rather than five special blocks.
decisions.inWild:
jet build todo.core
jet run todo.cli
jet run todo.web
jet test todo.tests
jet dev todo.dev

options.name: Typed output collection
options.detail: Every output is a value in one collection. Its type states what it can do. Commands select outputs supporting Build, Run, Check, Publish, or Enter.
options.technical: Outputs is a keyed heterogeneous collection bounded by Output. Capabilities are named traits. One output may support several capabilities without wrapper duplication.
options.code:
outputs: [
  core: Library.{ source: ./libs/core },
  cli: Executable.{ main: ./apps/cli },
  web: Service.{ main: ./apps/web },
  tests: Check.{ run: test_all },
  dev: Environment.{ tools: [Jet, Git] },
]

options.name: Separate role collections
options.detail: Libraries, commands, services, checks, and environments each have their own collection. Every item has a simple expected shape, but shared build data may repeat across roles.
options.technical: Package has closed fields libraries, executables, services, checks, and environments. Cross-role references are explicit output addresses.
options.code:
libraries: [core]
executables: [cli]
services: [web]
checks: [tests]
environments: [dev]

options.name: One product, many projections
options.detail: The package defines a smaller set of Product values. Build, run, test, publish, and dev are typed projections over each product's graph. One product may expose several named entrypoints.
options.technical: Product owns sources and build actions. Projections are pure capability views with distinct identities and policy. No projection may rebuild hidden duplicate actions.

comparisons.note: Flakes separate packages, apps, checks, and devShells. Discoverability is strong, but one executable often appears as both package and app.
Bazel uses typed rules such as libraries, binaries, and tests. Targets compose well, while BUILD ceremony and rule vocabulary can be heavy.
Cargo infers libraries, binaries, examples, benches, and tests from conventions. Beginners benefit, but custom outputs and dev environments fall outside one model.

recommendation.why: A gives every result one address and one typed value. Beginners use familiar commands; experts inspect capabilities, actions, policy, and provenance without wrapper duplication.

whyNot.reason: B is familiar, but closed role fields multiply concepts and repeat shared data as new output kinds appear.
C removes duplication aggressively, but the projection vocabulary makes a small teaching project harder to read than direct output values.

recommendation.tradeoff: A uses a heterogeneous typed collection. Tooling must present each output's capabilities plainly and reject ambiguous default selection.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps B's familiar concrete output types and C's shared action graph. Several typed outputs may point to the same underlying actions without duplicating them.

harvest.aspect: Every output has one stable address and type.
harvest.use: Keep one keyed Outputs collection.

harvest.aspect: Users recognize library, executable, service, check, and environment.
harvest.use: Provide those as standard output types, not grammar keywords.

harvest.aspect: Several user views should reuse one build graph.
harvest.use: Deduplicate actions by semantic identity beneath output values.

decisions.title: What should changing a JetOS machine feel like?
decisions.gist: Choose the everyday path from project values to a checked machine generation and safe rollback.
decisions.lesson:
A machine change should never mean “run this script and hope.” Jet can first build a complete candidate without touching the machine. It can show the difference, run checks, and switch only after those checks pass.

The old generation remains available. Rollback is simply choosing it again, not trying to reverse a long list of commands.

Files, users, services, boot settings, and images use the same named typed values as packages. A machine does not introduce a second module language.
decisions.story: Rin updates an API and its config on a home server. Rin wants to see the exact change, verify the health check, switch once, and recover instantly if the service fails later.

options.name: Build, show, check, switch, rollback
options.detail: A System is another typed project value. Jet builds a complete generation, shows its changes, proves it is ready, switches once, and keeps the previous generation.
options.technical: Files, users, boot, services, images, and checks enter the same receipt as packages. Service ordering is checked before activation. Switching is atomic.
options.code:
$ jet os build halcyon
$ jet os diff halcyon
$ jet os switch halcyon
$ jet os rollback halcyon

// every command uses the same System value and receipt

options.name: GNU Guix System directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Guix builds complete operating-system generations and switches as one safe step. People love one programmable package-and-system language plus reliable rollback.
options.technical: Jet would adopt Guix operating-system records, services, system builds, reconfigure, and generations.
options.code:
(operating-system
  (bootloader ...)
  (users ...)
  (services ...))

$ guix system reconfigure config.scm
$ guix system roll-back

options.name: NixOS modules directly
options.detail: Host language: Nix. NixOS combines a huge library of typed options into complete system generations. People love its service and hardware coverage plus rollback.
options.technical: JetOS would use recursive option modules, defaults, priorities, forced values, and Nix-style system generations.

options.name: Build images, deploy with a script
options.detail: Jet builds an image, then ordinary deployment code copies files, edits users, and restarts services. Experts can do anything, but preview and rollback depend on the script author.
options.technical: Machine changes are ordered commands rather than one desired System value.

options.name: Image-only machines
options.detail: JetOS only builds whole disk or container images. Replacing an image is simple, but laptops, servers, and small config changes still need another management layer.
options.technical: System state is one immutable image artifact. Live service, user, and file changes are outside JetOS.
options.code:
image :: Image.{ packages: [api], files: {...} }
$ jet image flash image --machine halcyon

comparisons.note: The best direct full-system lifecycle. Guix is liked because packages, services, builds, generations, and rollback stay in one model.
The broadest direct declarative operating-system ecosystem. NixOS is liked for reusable modules and huge service coverage.

recommendation.why: A keeps Guix and NixOS’s best promise—complete, reversible machines—while using the same clear Jet values as the rest of the project.

whyNot.reason: Guix proves the lifecycle, but Jet should not require Scheme to manage a Jet machine.
NixOS has unmatched coverage, but recursive modules, priorities, and Nix syntax are exactly the complexity JetOS should remove.
Scripts are flexible but cannot promise one safe preview, switch, proof, and rollback experience.
Image-only management leaves common live-machine needs to another tool.

recommendation.tradeoff: JetOS must grow a broad library of typed services and machine settings. That library is what makes the simple source and safe commands work.

decisions.title: How should one file grow into many?
decisions.gist: Choose how a complete one-file project splits while keeping one obvious control point.
decisions.lesson:
A tiny project should fit in one `project.jet`. Larger projects need several files so people can work independently.

Splitting should not introduce member manifests, role filenames, import lists, or file-order behavior. The root should still show where project pieces come from.

A project part is just a typed piece of the same Project value. Its declared names carry meaning. Project paths stay relative to the root, so moving a part does not silently retarget `apps/api`.
decisions.story: Rin starts with one package. Later, backend, development, release, and machines move into separate files. Rin wants the root to remain three lines and every part to keep the same syntax.

options.name: One root plus typed parts
options.detail: Start in `project.jet`. When it grows, add `parts: find("project")`. Each discovered file exports a normal `ProjectPart`; the root stays in charge.
options.technical: This replaces `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, and `workspace.jet` with one `project.jet`. For project pieces, `parts: find(...)` replaces role-module discovery. Normal Jet modules and `use` remain unchanged. A lone `.jet` program still needs no project file.

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Start with one Scheme program, then move values into Scheme modules. People love that splitting never leaves the language.
options.technical: The root imports ordinary Scheme modules and returns the final project or operating-system value.
options.code:
;; project.scm
(use-modules (project backend) (project machines))
(project (parts (list backend machines)))

options.name: Cargo directly
options.detail: Surface language: TOML. Engine language: Rust. Cargo uses one workspace root and a manifest in every member. People love the clear root and dependable tools.
options.technical: Jet would adopt workspace member patterns plus one manifest per member.
options.code:
# Cargo.toml
[workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]

# packages/api/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "api"

options.name: CUE directly
options.detail: Host language: CUE. Every peer file contributes automatically, with no special root. People love easy splitting and order-independent files.
options.technical: Project membership follows CUE package rules rather than one Jet-owned root.

options.name: One required file per role
options.detail: Packages, development setups, images, and machines each get a reserved filename. Purpose is obvious, but even a small complete project is spread across several roots.
options.technical: Keep today’s `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, and `workspace.jet`, plus role modules for images and systems.
options.code:
pkg.jet
env.jet
workspace.jet
images/server.jet
systems/halcyon.jet

comparisons.note: Best direct one-file-to-modules growth. Guile is liked because moving code into a module does not create a new language.
Best direct visible workspace root. TOML is easy to review; Rust makes the tools dependable.

recommendation.why: A gives the smallest beginning and the cleanest growth. The root stays obvious, while every split file remains a typed piece of the same project.

whyNot.reason: Guix grows beautifully, but Scheme modules and errors would make Jet projects feel foreign.
Cargo is clear, but a manifest in every member restores the repetition Jet should remove.
CUE splits effortlessly, but no root owns the whole project and another language becomes required.
Reserved role files force users to learn the build system before their project needs those roles.

recommendation.tradeoff: `project.jet` becomes a new canonical file and replaces current role filenames. The migration is worthwhile because it removes permanent ceremony.

decisions.comment: Ok with this conceptually but need a different word. Parts should be a convenience extensibility and modularity feature but a requirement

decisions.title: Callable contracts for runnable Outputs
decisions.gist: Choose how commands, services, and checks use ordinary functions.
decisions.lesson: Executable Outputs are user-invoked commands, so typed parameters can become checked flags through the ratified entry-parameter model. Services and checks run unattended; their settings belong in checked Package values. Every callable returns `Void` or `Void ?`. A service lives while its call lives. A check passes on normal return and fails on error.
decisions.story: Maya packages an export command, API service, and release check. CI and deployment must run the same service and check configuration as her laptop.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses `fn export(path: Path)`, parameterless `fn serve()`, and parameterless `fn verify_release()`. Output values carry service and check settings rather than invocation flags.

options.name: Role-specific ordinary functions
options.detail: Commands may take typed parameters. Services and checks take none. Each returns `Void` or `Void ?`.
options.code:
fn export(path: Path) -> Void ?
$ jet run export --path out.json
fn serve() -> Void ?
fn verify() -> Void ?
$ jet test verify
PASS verify

options.name: One permissive shape
options.detail: Every runnable Output may take typed parameters, including services and checks.
options.code:
fn verify(channel: String = "stable") -> Void ?
$ jet test verify
PASS verify
$ jet test verify --channel nightly
PASS verify

options.name: Lifecycle result types
options.detail: Each role returns a tool-facing result type instead of ordinary completion or failure.

recommendation.why: Typed command flags remain ergonomic while unattended service and check configuration has one checked source in the Package graph.

whyNot.reason: Service and check flags create alternate configurations that local runs and automation may select differently.
Business code must construct tool protocol values instead of using normal return and error flow.

recommendation.tradeoff: Services and checks cannot accept ad hoc invocation flags; their settings must be represented in checked graph values.

decisions.title: Default Output selection
decisions.gist: Choose the deterministic selection rule for singular Output intents while plural test runs every Check.
decisions.lesson: `jet test` is plural and runs every Check Output. `run`, `enter`, `publish`, and activation need one Output. The ordered selection rule can use an explicit address, the unchanged function-only `fn run` path, a sole capable Output, or a checked `defaults:` entry. Adding a second candidate must never silently retarget automation.
decisions.story: Maya's Package begins with one command, so `jet run` needs no extra configuration. After she adds an administrator command, Jet must stop and ask for an explicit default rather than choosing a different command by accident.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's hobby Package declares `defaults: .{ run: app, check: unit, enter: dev }`. Explicit addresses always win, and plural `jet test` still runs every Check.

options.name: Plural all; ordered singular rule
options.detail: Use explicit address, unchanged `fn run`, sole capable Output, checked default, then sorted candidate error.
options.code:
$ jet test
PASS unit
PASS release

$ jet run
Selected sole Executable `cli`.

# after adding admin
$ jet run
Choose one Output: admin, cli
Fix: add defaults: .{ run: cli } or run an explicit address.

options.name: Conventional keys
options.detail: Reserve Output keys such as `run` and `check` as implicit defaults.

options.name: Always explicit after Outputs
options.detail: Require an Output address whenever any Outputs are declared, even when only one can satisfy the command.
options.code:
$ jet run
name an Output; use jet run cli

recommendation.why: Small Packages stay automatic, larger Packages record checked intent, and a new Output cannot silently retarget an existing command.

whyNot.reason: Conventional keys turn ordinary Output names into reserved policy vocabulary.
Naming a sole capable Output adds typing without adding information.

recommendation.tradeoff: A Package with several Outputs for one singular capability carries a small `defaults:` record.

decisions.title: Facts stored in each Output value
decisions.gist: Decide whether Output values are thin typed projections or repeat graph slices.
decisions.lesson: An Output is a named result selected from one Package graph. Thin projection means the Output stores only its name and kind-specific facts. Sources, dependencies, actions, effects, policy, target facts, and provenance stay single-copy on the graph. `jet inspect output` reconstructs the complete path for audit.
decisions.story: Maya publishes a command and an image built from that command. She changes the command's source set once and expects both outputs and their audit views to use the same fact.
decisions.inWild: The proposal shows `todo.cli` as a small Executable value. `jet inspect output todo.cli` expands its source set, dependencies, action digest, target, effects, policy, and provenance from the Package graph.

options.name: Thin projections
options.detail: Outputs hold only name and kind-specific facts. Inspection reconstructs the complete path from the Package graph.

options.name: Explicit slice per Output
options.detail: Every Output repeats its source, dependency, action, and policy references.
options.code: cli: Output :: .Executable.{ name: "todo", entry: run, sources: [app], deps: [textkit], actions: [compile], policy: release }

options.name: Verb sections
options.detail: Each Output divides repeated facts into build, run, and publish sections.
options.code: cli: Output :: .Executable.{ name: "todo", build: .{ actions: [compile] }, run: .{ entry: run }, publish: .{ policy: release } }

recommendation.why: Facts remain single-copy and Output declarations stay readable while one inspect view supplies the full audit path.

whyNot.reason: Every Output repeats references that can disagree with the Package graph or another Output.
Stable facts become scattered by command verb and still repeat across Outputs.

recommendation.tradeoff: An isolated Output literal does not display its whole build path; users read that path through `jet inspect output`.

decisions.title: What should Jet call the complete project graph?
decisions.gist: Choose the ordinary type name for the value that connects everything one Jet project builds, runs, and deploys.
decisions.lesson:
Graph: a set of named values connected by checked references.
Root: the single top value from which Jet reaches that graph.
Binding: the lowercase variable name used for a value.
Checked: Jet verified every name, type, and connection.

The root can connect packages, environments, services, images, systems, and fleets. It describes their shared meaning without requiring one folder, repository, or file layout.

A beginner can still run a file containing only `fn run()`. Teams meet this type when one program grows into a package or deployed system. Experts use the same value for inspection and audit.

This ballot chooses only the type noun and conventional lowercase binding. Other decisions own graph scope, fields, files, composition, storage, and commands.
decisions.story: Rin's Greeter starts as one command. It gains an API package, development environment, release image, and home server. Documentation and diagnostics now need one stable noun for their connected definition.
decisions.inWild: Cargo calls a package group a workspace, but that word usually follows a checkout boundary. Terraform calls its entry configuration a root module. Nix flakes can expose packages, development shells, applications, and operating systems from one value. Jet needs an ordinary noun for a typed value that may cover all those roles.

options.name: Project
options.detail: Use `Project` and `project`. Beginners already know the word, and it can naturally own code, environments, services, images, machines, and fleets.
options.technical: Project names the complete checked value, not a directory or build invocation. Package, Environment, Service, Image, Fleet, and System keep narrower meanings.

options.name: Workspace
options.detail: Use `Workspace` and `workspace`. The name suggests related work managed together, especially in editors and monorepos.
options.technical: Workspace means a durable checked graph, not a checkout or editor session. That differs from common tool usage.

options.name: Stack
options.detail: Use `Stack` and `stack`. The word fits software, services, infrastructure, and operating-system pieces deployed together.
options.technical: Stack names the complete graph, not an ordered collection. It also appears in call-stack and data-structure diagnostics.

options.name: Graph
options.detail: Use `Graph` and `graph`. The name directly describes connected typed values and avoids implying a repository boundary.
options.technical: Jet also has narrower dependency, build, and execution graphs. Public copy must distinguish the complete Graph from those views.

options.name: Root
options.detail: Use `Root` and `root`. The word is short and describes the value from which all connected parts are reachable.
options.technical: Root describes graph position. It also means a filesystem boundary, package directory, tree node, or privileged operating-system account.

options.name: Configuration
options.detail: Use `Configuration` and `configuration`. The word makes desired state sound declarative and reviewable.
options.technical: The graph also contains executable packages, actions, realized outputs, and provenance. Configuration understates those values.

options.name: Model
options.detail: Use `Model` and `model`. The word suggests one checked description from which tools derive builds and deployments.
options.technical: Model is broad but generic. It collides with application data models, compiler models, and machine-learning models.

options.name: Platform
options.detail: Use `Platform` and `platform`. The word spans applications, shared services, tooling, infrastructure, and machines.
options.technical: Platform often means a reusable foundation rather than one complete product graph. Small projects may sound larger than they are.

options.name: Package
options.detail: Use `Package` for the complete repository-neutral semantic whole. A monorepo root lists independent member Packages by reference; a member cannot list members.
options.technical: The nearest `package.jet` defines one Package. Membership depth is capped at one. A single Package needs no `members:` field, and no second Workspace noun is introduced.
options.code: members: find("./packages")

comparisons.note: A flake exposes packages, apps, development shells, and machine configurations from one source value. Its noun requires Nix-specific teaching.
Terraform calls the top configuration a root module. Root explains graph position, while module explains composition.

recommendation.why: Package gives one noun from a small program through a fleet and fits Jetpack. Flat references keep monorepos explicit without recursive Package containment.

whyNot.reason: Project duplicates Package as a second noun for the same semantic whole.
Workspace introduces a checkout-oriented second noun and boundary.
Stack is overloaded and does not name a distribution unit.
Graph names representation instead of the user-owned unit.
Root names position and conflicts with filesystem and privilege terms.
Configuration understates executable outputs, actions, and provenance.
Model is generic and collides with application and compiler models.
Platform sounds like a reusable foundation rather than one package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Package must cover both an ordinary package and a monorepo root. The depth-one members law keeps that meaning finite.

decisions.checkInstructions: This naming remains conditional on the unified graph scope owned by D-ECO1. After ratification, replace the `<Root>` placeholder without adding aliases.

decisions.title: JetOS plan and historical proof
decisions.gist: Decide whether proof preserves the exact built delta from a captured parent generation.
decisions.lesson: `jet os plan` predicts changes from checked Package source and the active baseline before a machine changes. Build captures the parent generation. `jet os proof` records what was built and observed. Historical proof can store that exact baseline-relative delta, or omit it and leave only the current prediction path.
decisions.story: Rin changes Halcyon's API port during an incident. Before activation Rin needs a preview; later an auditor needs the exact change from gen-41 to gen-42 after newer generations are active.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's Package graph produces System Output `halcyon`. Plan predicts `gen-41 -> candidate`; proof for `gen-42` preserves baseline, built changes, output digests, readiness, activation, provenance, and rollback.
