options.detail: A template system makes text generation convenient and reviewable. It adds another interpolation language, escaping law, secret path, and ownership model beside Jet values.
options.code: generated_files: { ".env": template("env.tpl", values) }

comparisons.note: Typed declarations manage files and links with source ownership. Jet also needs project sync, seed behavior, and unified trust facts.
chezmoi handles templates, secrets, diffs, and apply workflows through a separate configuration product.

recommendation.why: A makes the common link short and gives experts exact write, generation, secret, conflict, drift, and audit control through one file graph.

whyNot.reason: Imperative tasks hide ownership and overwrite policy until execution.
A template manifest adds a second interpolation and secret-rendering system.

recommendation.tradeoff: An unmanaged ownership conflict stops synchronization and requires a user choice. Jet never guesses which file may be replaced.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove safe shorthand, conflict refusal, and Symlink, Seed, and Copy semantics. Also prove atomic recovery, path containment, permissions, redaction, source hashes, generated values, drift, plan confirmation, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: OCI images as one projection of the environment and image graphs
decisions.gist: Choose one existing image record with a simple environment source and full expert entrypoint, platform, layer, security, and provenance control.
decisions.lesson:
An environment graph already knows packages, variables, files, tasks, services, and locked sources. An Open Container Initiative, or OCI, image packages a filesystem and runtime settings.

A layer is one immutable filesystem change. An entrypoint is the first program the image starts. Provenance records the inputs, builder, and policy that made the image.

Not every environment fact belongs in an image. Host hooks, local secrets, mutable sockets, and unsupported services must fail or require an explicit replacement.

Beginners need `from: env.dev` and a useful shell image. Experts need service selection, platforms, users, layers, ports, health, entrypoints, secret rules, cache, and provenance. Jet can extend its existing image record.
decisions.story: Uma creates a development shell image with one source line. Her CI image later selects the API service, non-root user, two platforms, health probe, and exact layer policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: environment projection can copy secrets, activation hooks, host paths, impure outputs, or mutable state into layers. A second container record would split locks and publishing. The winner must classify every fact and refuse non-projectable state. It must use a non-root default, exclude secrets, show the projection plan, and preserve D-JPK-REMOTE1 for remote builds.

options.name: Progressive environment projection in the existing image record
options.detail: `from: env.dev` creates a locked shell image with safe non-root defaults. Experts select services, platforms, users, entrypoints, layers, ports, health, cache, and signatures on the same record. Host-only facts fail with a specific projection error.
options.technical: Projection records included, transformed, omitted, and rejected facts. Secrets use runtime mounts or references and never layers. Hangar owns content, cache, signing, archive, and publish. `.jet/lock` owns exact inputs and platforms. Remote builders use only prior D-JPK-REMOTE1 host bindings and grants.

options.name: Separate container environment records
options.detail: Container users get a focused namespace with its own layers, commands, ports, build, and publish fields. It duplicates image identity, locks, Hangar, provenance, and lifecycle.
options.code: container.api { environment: env.dev, command: api.run }

options.name: CLI-only environment projection
options.detail: One command creates ad hoc images without source changes. The image contract, service selection, platform policy, and security choices disappear from reviewable source.
options.code: jet os image build --env dev --services api

comparisons.note: OCI standardizes image content and runtime configuration. It does not define how a development environment becomes that image.
Nix can build layered images from a package closure. Jet also projects typed services, files, policy, and provenance.

recommendation.why: A makes a shell image one line and gives experts full OCI, security, platform, and provenance control without splitting Jet's image machinery.

whyNot.reason: A container namespace duplicates image identity, locking, storage, signing, and publishing.
CLI-only flags hide the image contract from source review and reproducible builds.

recommendation.tradeoff: A host-only or secret-bearing environment fact stops projection until the user replaces or omits it explicitly.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove shell defaults, service entrypoints, non-root policy, fact classes, secret exclusion, and host-only rejection. Also prove platform locks, deterministic layers, D-JPK-REMOTE1 bindings, Hangar reuse, signatures, publishing, plans, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Optional environment integrations through Jet-native typed modules
decisions.gist: Choose how simple presets and exact expert controls for platforms, certificates, hosts, and agents fit the existing module and grant systems.
decisions.lesson:
Optional integrations combine packages, variables, files, licenses, secrets, permissions, and host capabilities. Android and Apple toolchains are examples.

A beginner wants one named preset with safe locked defaults. An expert needs exact SDK versions, targets, paths, license decisions, certificates, host mappings, agent tools, and failure policy.

Adding top-level fields for every product would make the environment record grow forever. Raw recipes avoid that growth but lose validation and shared planning.

Jet already has typed modules, imports, packages, files, tasks, providers, and grants. First-party integration modules can compose those facts without creating another mechanism.
decisions.story: Devon imports an Android preset and gets a locked supported SDK. A mobile release environment expands versions, Apple targets, certificates, host aliases, and Codex MCP servers with exact grants.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: closed top-level domains can become a second package system, and direct devenv mirroring freezes foreign names. Generic recipes hide licenses, secrets, host support, and grants. The winner must use typed modules, lower to existing facts, support two depths, and import foreign configs with exact loss reports.

options.name: First-party typed integration modules over existing facts
options.detail: Beginners import a named module with locked safe defaults. Experts pass typed versions, targets, paths, licenses, certificates, hosts, agent tools, and policy. Each module lowers to existing package, file, task, provider, host-check, secret, and grant facts.
options.technical: Integration modules have no private resolver, lock, effect, or activation engine. Their public outputs are typed graph facts. Foreign devenv modules import into canonical editable Jet modules with TODO diagnostics for every unsupported fact.

options.name: Mirror devenv module roots
options.detail: Migration is direct and existing users recognize names. Jet inherits another product's taxonomy, enable flags, nesting, defaults, and compatibility burden as public law.

options.name: Packages and lifecycle tasks only
options.detail: Projects assemble each integration from packages and lifecycle tasks without a curated preset. Beginners repeat fragile recipes, while planning cannot validate licenses, host support, certificates, or agent authority.
options.code:
packages: [pkg.android_sdk]
on_enter: [configure_android]

comparisons.note: devenv offers many named modules with enable flags and nested options. Jet can import them without adopting their taxonomy.
Typed modules compose options and defaults. Jet's modules also lower to one package, task, file, and grant graph.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners curated presets and experts exact integration control while preserving one module, package, file, task, host, lock, and grant mechanism.

whyNot.reason: A direct mirror turns foreign organization and enable flags into permanent Jet law.
Recipes alone cannot provide shared validation, planning, diagnostics, or safe defaults.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only first-party integration schemas receive preset guarantees and tailored diagnostics. Unusual tools use ordinary module composition with less specific guidance.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove beginner presets, expert parameters, module composition, one lock, license checks, and host failures. Also prove certificate and secret handling, agent grants, devenv loss reports, TODO diagnostics, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Views with more than one possible owner
decisions.gist: Choose how one safe view can refer to several possible owners.
decisions.lesson:
A view reads or edits storage that another value owns. Provenance is the compiler record that links the view to that owner. Jet uses this record to stop the owner from moving while the view is live.

Current Jet requires one fixed owner path for each returned view. This works for `first(values)`, because the result always points into `values`. It rejects `longer(left, right)`, because the result can point into either input.

Rust describes this relation with lifetime parameters. Jet can keep those details hidden, but sema still needs an exact relation. The same issue appears when a list, enum, callback, or trait value carries views from several owners.
decisions.story: Mira writes a zero-copy protocol parser. Each packet contains many text fields that point into one of two receive buffers. Copying every field defeats the parser design.

options.name: One hidden set of possible owners
options.detail: Keep `View<T>` unchanged. Sema records a bounded set of possible owner paths and keeps every possible owner live. Containers and callbacks carry the same hidden relation.
options.technical: Public API metadata records source unions and their projections. All return paths must fit the declared union. Dynamic dispatch must publish one compatible union contract.

options.name: Explicit owner relation syntax
options.detail: Make expert APIs state owner relations in source. This gives full control, but it adds lifetime-like notation that every caller and library author must learn.
options.technical: The exact proposed form is `View<T from left | right>`. Generic relations use named owner parameters. Sema checks the written relation and publishes it.

options.name: Borrow only through callbacks
options.detail: Do not return a multi-owner view. A function receives a callback and calls it while the selected owner is known. This stays safe but makes composition and storage harder.
options.technical: The callback cannot return or store the view. It gives dynamic selection without extending public provenance metadata.

options.name: Keep one stable owner
options.detail: Keep the current rule. Programs copy data, use one fixed owner, or use Shared and Pool handles. This preserves a small model but leaves safe Rust programs inexpressible.
options.technical: E2305 and E2307 continue to reject source unions, view containers, view-returning function values, and open trait dispatch.

comparisons.note: A shared lifetime can link one result to either input. Containers and traits can also carry lifetime parameters.
comparisons.code: fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str

comparisons.note: Borrowing features use compiler-managed lifetime dependencies and aim to hide most explicit lifetime notation.
comparisons.code: // compiler tracks that a borrowed result depends on its input

recommendation.why: It closes the Rust capability gap while keeping Jet source free of lifetime notation. It also extends the existing provenance graph instead of adding another memory model.

whyNot.reason: It exposes compiler bookkeeping in routine APIs and makes the beginner surface harder to read.
It cannot support ordinary collections, returned parsers, or trait-backed lending APIs.
It keeps confirmed safe Rust patterns impossible without copying or changing the data model.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sema and API metadata become more complex because each live view can keep several possible owners stable.

decisions.title: Runtime proof for disjoint mutable views
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet safely edits several runtime-selected parts at once.
decisions.lesson:
Two write views are safe when they cannot reach the same storage. Jet proves different fields and constant ranges at compile time. It treats runtime indices and ranges as overlapping because their values are unknown during compilation.

A checked split can prove separation at runtime before any write starts. For example, splitting at index `mid` makes a left range below `mid` and a right range at or above `mid`. A multi-index check can reject duplicate indices before it returns write views.

Rust puts these proofs in trusted collection methods. Jet must choose whether the proof belongs in named methods, ordinary range syntax, or only unsafe code.
decisions.story: Andre updates two bodies in a physics world. Their indices come from collision detection. He needs direct mutable access to both bodies without cloning or serializing every update.
decisions.detail: `edit_disjoint`, `get_disjoint_write`, and `split_write` are three entry points into one proof mechanism. The closure form is the beginner default. Explicit views and the special split give experts direct control. All checks finish before any mutation. Failures use one typed bounds-or-overlap error. Ordinary range expressions never hide a runtime loan check.

options.name: Scoped edits and explicit views over one checked proof
options.detail: Beginners call `edit_disjoint` with targets and a closure. Jet checks all bounds and overlap before the closure starts. It lends each view, then releases every loan automatically. Experts use `get_disjoint_write` or `split_write` when views must cross helper calls. Ordinary ranges remain compile-time checked and never gain hidden runtime failure.
options.technical: All forms lower to one sema-visible disjointness proof for one owner. The runtime normalizes requested regions and completes every check before it creates any view. Slice splits need one bounds check. Index and key sets reject duplicates. The explicit form returns tracked `ViewMut` values under existing loan rules. Lending mutable iterators reuse the same proof and expose one element loan at a time.

options.name: Runtime checks on ordinary ranges
options.detail: Let ordinary dynamic write ranges coexist. Jet inserts one overlap check when sema cannot prove separation. This is concise, but a static-looking loan can now fail at runtime.
options.technical: Sema groups dynamic write windows by owner. It emits bounds and pairwise overlap checks before it creates any mutable reference.

options.name: Compile-time proof only
options.detail: Keep current behavior. Users rewrite algorithms around one write view, copy values, or use fixed ranges. The model stays simple but dynamic safe algorithms remain blocked.
options.technical: Dynamic projections always overlap. No standard API can mint several runtime-proven write views.

options.name: Unsafe split primitives
options.detail: Expose raw split operations only inside `#Unsafe`. Experts can proceed, but every caller must audit bounds and overlap manually.
options.technical: No safe API certifies disjointness. A raw pointer or unchecked view constructor carries the proof obligation.

comparisons.note: Slices use `split_at_mut`. Maps use `get_disjoint_mut`. Trusted methods check the relation and return safe mutable references.
Slices are simple pointer-length values. The programmer carries more alias responsibility, especially across mutable slices.
comparisons.code:
const left = values[0..mid];
const right = values[mid..];

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one short scoped call and gives experts retained views and a specialized split. Every form uses one visible proof rule. Ordinary place syntax stays predictable.

whyNot.reason: B hides runtime failure and overlap cost inside ordinary-looking loans.
C blocks safe dynamic updates and lending mutable iterators.
D repeats a standard collection proof in every unsafe caller.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds three method shapes. Clear staging must teach the closure first, then explicit views and the specialized split.

hybrid.synthesis: A combines automatic scoped loans with explicit expert views over one checked proof. It keeps ordinary ranges compile-time-only.

harvest.aspect: Named methods make checks and cost visible.
harvest.use: Keep all runtime proof behind the checked-disjoint method family.

harvest.aspect: Short multi-target code improves everyday ergonomics.
harvest.use: Put the short form in `edit_disjoint`, not ordinary range syntax.

harvest.aspect: Ordinary place syntax stays statically predictable.
harvest.use: Keep compile-time rejection when no checked method is present.

harvest.aspect: Experts need direct control over view lifetime and proof cost.
harvest.use: Give safe explicit views and specialized splits before unsafe primitives.

decisions.title: Borrowed captures in a taskgroup
decisions.gist: Choose which stack borrows taskgroup children may use.
decisions.lesson:
A detached task can outlive the function that created it. It must own its captured data. A scoped taskgroup is different because the group joins every child before the scope ends.

That join can make stack borrowing safe. Read-only data can be shared by many children. Mutable data needs exclusive or proven disjoint access for each child. The owner cannot move until all children finish.

Jet currently applies detached-task capture rules to taskgroups. The choice is whether taskgroups remain ownership-only or use their scope to admit safe borrows.
decisions.story: Leah loads a large image and runs four filters over separate bands. The group joins before the function returns. Copying the image or wrapping it in Shared adds needless cost.

options.name: Reads and proven disjoint writes
options.detail: Keep the current `g.task` spelling. Let children borrow reads freely and borrow writes only when sema proves disjoint places. The group owns every loan.
options.technical: Loans start before child launch and end after join or group cleanup. Cancellation, panic, return, and error paths join before owner invalidation.

options.name: Read borrows only
options.detail: Let children read borrowed data, but require ownership or Shared for every write. This closes common analysis cases with a smaller race proof.
options.technical: All borrowed captures are shared views. Mutable captures remain E1101, even when ranges are statically disjoint.

options.name: Separate borrowed-task spelling
options.detail: Keep `g.task` ownership-only. Add `g.borrow` for scoped reads and proven disjoint writes. The boundary is explicit, but users must choose between two task forms.
options.technical: `g.borrow` handles cannot detach or enter channels. Its result cannot contain a view that escapes the group.

options.name: Keep ownership-only groups
options.detail: Keep current rules. Every child owns, copies, channels, or uses Shared. The task model stays uniform but ignores the group's lifetime guarantee.
options.technical: Taskgroups continue to change cancellation and join behavior only. E1101 and E1102 remain identical to `tasks.spawn`.

comparisons.note: `std::thread::scope` lets scoped threads borrow non-static data because all threads join before the scope returns.
Task groups use structured lifetimes, but strict concurrency rules still restrict unsafe shared mutation.

recommendation.why: It uses the guarantee taskgroup already provides and reaches Rust scoped-thread capability without another task spelling.

whyNot.reason: It still forces copies or locks for parallel updates that sema can prove disjoint.
It creates two scoped child mechanisms with the same lifetime and cancellation behavior.
It keeps a confirmed expressiveness gap and wastes the group's join guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sema must track loans across scheduler edges and prove every exceptional group exit joins before storage changes.

decisions.title: Safe address-stable values
decisions.gist: Choose how safe code prevents an address-sensitive value from moving.
decisions.lesson:
Most values remain valid when moved to another address. A self-referential value is different because one field points into another field. An intrusive collection can also keep pointers between nodes.

A pin contract starts an address-sensitive state. Safe code can still read or edit the value, but it cannot move or replace the pinned storage. Unsafe construction may rely on this promise.

Rust exposes `Pin`. Jet has stable allocator storage and raw pointers, but it has no reusable source-level contract. The choice must cover stack values, caller storage, arenas, cleanup, and safe library boundaries.
decisions.story: Noah writes a zero-allocation event loop. Each operation stores links into a caller-owned queue. The library needs one audited constructor and safe use everywhere else.

options.name: Borrowed Pin<T> contract
options.detail: Add `mem.pin(&place) -> Pin<T>`. The pin is a tracked write view that blocks movement and replacement. Libraries accept or return `Pin<T>` where address stability matters.
options.technical: Pin provenance reuses the owner graph. Structural field projection is declared by the type implementation. Dropping the final pin ends the no-move loan.

options.name: Owned Stable<T> handle
options.detail: Move the value into stable storage and return a copyable handle. The handle can move, but the value cannot. Storage can use heap, arena, or Fixed backing.
options.technical: The owner is the stable allocation, not the local handle. Self-reference starts only after placement. Deallocation waits for all safe views and links.

options.name: Pinned type marker
options.detail: Mark a whole type as non-movable after construction. This is visible at the declaration, but it adds a new language marker and can burden values that are not yet address-sensitive.
options.technical: `#Pinned` suppresses ordinary movement after initialization. APIs use views to access the value. Construction and projection rules become type-level law.

options.name: Keep allocator and unsafe workarounds
options.detail: Use Pool IDs, arena views, Shared handles, or raw pointers. These solve many designs, but no common contract lets safe code rely on address stability.
options.technical: Each library owns its representation and unsafe proof. Sema does not prevent movement for an address-sensitive user type.

comparisons.note: `Pin<Ptr>` prevents safe code from moving an address-sensitive pointee and supports self-referential futures and intrusive collections.
comparisons.code: fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>)

comparisons.note: Libraries often rely on heap addresses and conventions. The type system does not provide one standard no-move contract.

recommendation.why: It gives zero-allocation parity and reuses Jet's existing place, loan, and provenance model. The pin lasts only as long as the address-sensitive use.

whyNot.reason: It changes representation and can require storage indirection where Rust can pin an existing place.
It adds syntax and makes the whole type non-movable before address sensitivity starts.
It cannot support reusable safe APIs whose implementation depends on a no-move promise.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pinned APIs add an expert type and stricter projection rules that library authors must state and audit.

decisions.title: Stack-local interior mutability
decisions.gist: Choose how read-only code updates private local state safely.
decisions.lesson:
Interior mutability means a type can change private state through a read-only reference. A cache is a common example: the object looks unchanged to callers, but it saves a computed result inside.

The type must still enforce the reader-writer rule. A simple cell moves or copies values without lending a reference. A borrow cell checks active read and write guards at runtime. These local types must not cross tasks without synchronization.

Jet can use `Shared<T>` today, but that adds a copyable synchronized handle and lock even when one thread owns the object.
decisions.story: Iris builds a syntax tree with a lazy line index. Read methods fill the cache on first use. The tree stays local and never needs an Arc or operating-system lock.

options.name: One local Cell<T> family
options.detail: Add one non-sendable `Cell<T>`. Value methods handle get, set, replace, and initialization. Read, edit, and guard methods provide runtime-checked borrowed access.
options.technical: The runtime borrow state permits many readers or one writer. Guards carry view provenance. Sema rejects every task, channel, Shared, and parallel crossing.
options.code:
cache :: Cell<[Int]?>.new(None)
cache.set(Val(offsets))
value :: cache.read(lines => lines.len())
guard :: cache.guard_edit()?

options.name: Separate Cell and BorrowCell types
options.detail: Use `Cell<T>` for replace-style access and `BorrowCell<T>` for runtime guards. Each type has a smaller rule, but users must choose and migrate between two containers.
options.technical: `Cell<T>` never returns a view. `BorrowCell<T>` returns tracked read and write guards and checks conflicts at runtime.
options.code:
hits :: Cell<Int>.new(0)
cache :: BorrowCell<Map<Key, Value>>.new(Map.new())
cache.edit(map => map.insert(key, value))

options.name: Shared<T> only
options.detail: Keep one shared-mutation type for local and cross-task use. This is simple to teach, but local caches pay synchronization and shared-ownership costs.
options.technical: No local dynamic-borrow primitive is added. `Shared<T>` remains Arc plus a read-write lock.
options.code:
cache :: Shared.new(Map<Key, Value>.new())
cache.edit(map => map.insert(key, value))

options.name: Implicit mutation in read methods
options.detail: Let private fields change in a read method when they do not affect public equality. This looks easy but hides mutation and needs a new compiler rule for logical state.
options.technical: The compiler would classify fields as observational or cached. This creates a second mutability rule outside explicit capability types.

comparisons.note: `Cell<T>` uses replace-style access. `RefCell<T>` checks borrowed reads and writes at runtime. Both are not Sync.
Reference types and property wrappers can hide mutation, but exclusivity and thread safety depend on the chosen wrapper.

recommendation.why: One explicit local type keeps the beginner model small and gives experts both cheap value operations and checked borrowed access.

whyNot.reason: It creates two closely related local mutation containers and forces an early choice that one type can avoid.
It keeps needless shared ownership and synchronization in single-threaded code.
It hides real mutation and adds a second field-level capability system.

recommendation.tradeoff: One type has a wider method set, so documentation must separate value access from guard access clearly.

decisions.title: Expert guards and waiting for Shared<T>
decisions.gist: Choose how experts hold and wait on Shared access.
decisions.lesson:
`Shared.read` and `Shared.edit` lock one value for one closure. This short scope prevents many deadlocks and makes release automatic.

Some protocols need a lock across several helper calls. Others wait until a protected condition changes. A correct wait must register interest and release the write lock as one atomic action. It reacquires the lock before it checks the condition again.

A guard is an owned lock token. Safe cleanup releases it on return, error, panic, or cancellation. Jet must keep short closures as the default while choosing an expert form.
decisions.story: Sam builds a bounded work queue. A producer must wait while the queue is full. The wait must not miss the consumer signal between checking the size and sleeping.
decisions.inWild:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: Explicit Shared guards and Condition
options.detail: Keep `read` and `edit` unchanged. Add expert `guard_read`, `guard_edit`, and `Condition`. Guards can map, split, and wait with automatic cleanup.
options.technical: A wait atomically registers, releases, parks, reacquires, and rechecks. Cancellation unregisters before guard release. Lock-order receipts cover nested guards.
options.code:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(space_ready, q => q.len() < limit)?
guard.value.push(job)
space_ready.notify_one()

options.name: Closure-only wait methods
options.detail: Do not expose guards. Add `edit_when` and notification methods that keep the whole protocol inside one closure. This is safer but cannot span helper APIs.
options.technical: The runtime owns registration, release, park, reacquire, predicate checks, and edit execution. User code never receives a lock token.

options.name: Raw lock type family
options.detail: Expose Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, and their guards. This matches common systems APIs but creates several overlapping shared-state mechanisms.
options.technical: Users select lock types and control ordering. `#Transact` remains separate. Sema tracks guard cleanup but cannot prevent every protocol deadlock.
options.code:
lock :: Mutex.new(queue)
ready :: Condvar.new()
guard :: lock.lock()
ready.wait(&guard, q => q.len() < limit)?

options.name: Keep short closures and channels
options.detail: Keep current Shared access. Rewrite wait protocols as channels, task loops, or transactions. This avoids guards but makes some state protocols indirect.
options.technical: No guard or condition surface is added. Shared locks remain scoped to one closure call.

comparisons.note: Mutex and RwLock return guards. Condvar waits release and reacquire a Mutex guard while callers loop on the predicate.
comparisons.code: let mut q = cv.wait_while(q, |q| q.len() == limit)?;

comparisons.note: Mutex and Cond expose manual lock protocols. Channels often give a clearer ownership design, but shared conditions still exist.

recommendation.why: It preserves Jet's short safe default and adds the control needed for established lock and condition protocols through one Shared family.

whyNot.reason: It cannot pass guarded access through helper layers or support protocols that need several guarded operations.
It duplicates Shared and #Transact with several lower-level public lock families.
It keeps direct condition and guard protocols needlessly awkward or unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Expert guards can create longer lock scopes, so diagnostics and lock-order audit output become required.

decisions.title: Which per-card statuses belong in catch-up?
decisions.gist: Choose what one catch-up row means and how Tower measures active progress.
decisions.lesson:
An activity feed lists every event. A status snapshot lists each subject once, using its current state. Catch-up is easier to scan as a snapshot because old development lines disappear when a card changes again.

A completed card needs no progress story. Its number and title identify the outcome. An active card needs a progress measure. Tower already has exit criteria, which are the card's checklist for completion.

A criterion can be open, met, or verified. Met means the builder finished it. Verified means a separate reviewer confirmed it. Counting met and verified criteria measures work completed. Counting only verified criteria measures independently confirmed work.

The inclusion rule controls the remaining noise. Tower can show only outcomes and active work, or it can also show ready, planning, blocked, and frozen cards. The broader list preserves more transitions but can still be long after bulk board updates.
decisions.story: Nate opens Tower after several agents worked. One card produced many events before it closed. He wants one useful line for that card, not its development diary.
decisions.inWild:
Recent work

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete

options.name: Outcomes and active work
options.detail: Show only cards now done, building, or in verification. Done rows contain only identity. Active progress counts criteria that are met or verified.
options.technical: Group unseen events by card. Resolve the current card projection. Keep phase done, building, or verify. Percent is round(100 × count(status in {met, verified}) / criterion count). A card without criteria reports 0%.
options.code:
12 cards changed

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete

options.name: Every changed card
options.detail: Show one row for every changed card. Done and active rows follow option A. Other rows show current states such as Ready, Planning, Blocked, or Frozen.
options.technical: Group unseen events by card without a phase filter. Active percent uses met or verified criteria. Non-active rows use the current projected phase or blocked lane.
options.code:

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete

options.name: Verified progress only
options.detail: Show the same focused card set as option A, but count only independently verified criteria. Progress stays conservative while review is pending.
options.technical: Keep phase done, building, or verify. Percent is round(100 × count(status == verified) / criterion count). A met criterion does not increase the displayed value.

recommendation.why: It matches the requested two useful cases and removes status churn. In the current event-heavy sample, only 5 of 110 card snapshots were done or active.

whyNot.reason: It reduces repeated events but keeps most bulk-update noise. The current sample would still contain 110 rows.
It labels finished builder work as incomplete until review, so the number describes proof rather than completion.

recommendation.tradeoff: Catch-up will not report that a card became ready, blocked, planning, or frozen. Those states remain visible on the board.

decisions.title: How yielding loops materialize values
decisions.gist: A finite loop with `->` eagerly returns `List<T>`. Maps, sets, and lazy iteration remain ordinary collection APIs.
decisions.lesson: Yield selection and storage timing are separate questions. A fixed eager List result gives one predictable rule. Making an expected type or source family change timing would make a harmless-looking refactor change when effects run.
decisions.story: Maya writes one compact loop and immediately gets the collection most programs expect. When she needs a Map, she uses ordinary Map operations. When she needs a Set, she uses Set.from. When she needs laziness, she starts with the existing iterator adapter so delayed work is also visible.
decisions.inWild:
names :: loop user; users if user.active -> user.name

by_id := [UserId: User].{}
loop user; users by_id.add(user.id, user)

unique_names :: Set.from(loop user; users -> user.name)
lazy_names :: users.map(user => user.name)
decisions.detail: Every finite yielding loop executes immediately and returns an eager List in iteration order. It never selects a collector or evaluation timing from an expected type or source family. Multiple source clauses still yield one flat List, while an explicitly nested yielding loop yields nested Lists. `next` omits an item and `break` returns the accumulated prefix. Maps use ordinary explicit Map construction. Sets use `Set.from(...)`. Lazy work uses the existing iterator adapters. No implicit flattening, failure swallowing, repeated-key policy, custom collector protocol, or second iterator mechanism is introduced.

options.name: Always eager List
options.detail: A yielding loop returns `List<T>` immediately. Other result shapes use ordinary APIs.
options.technical: The source and body execute at binding evaluation. Items append in loop order. The collector is fixed and does not inspect the expected type. Maps use ordinary explicit construction, Sets use `Set.from(...)`, and lazy iteration stays on the existing `Iter` path.

options.name: Lazy iterator by default
options.detail: Every yielding loop returns `Iter<T>` and needs a terminal for storage.
options.technical: This supports unbounded pipelines, but delays effects and adds terminal ceremony to ordinary list construction.
options.code: names :: (loop user; users -> user.name).to_list()

options.name: Expected-type collector
options.detail: The expected result type selects List, Map, Set, or Iter.
options.technical: This can remove conversions, but a type annotation can change allocation, repeated-key behavior, ownership, and evaluation timing.
options.code: names: Iter<String> :: loop user; users -> user.name

comparisons.note: Array comprehensions are visibly eager, while generator delimiters visibly select laziness.
comparisons.code:
[f(x) for x in xs]
(f(x) for x in xs)

comparisons.note: Collections are eager and Sequence makes delayed work explicit.

recommendation.why: A makes the common result concise and keeps every non-List allocation or timing choice visible through ordinary collection APIs.

whyNot.reason: It makes the everyday eager case noisy and moves effects away from the binding.
It lets type context silently change runtime timing and collector semantics.

recommendation.tradeoff: Map and Set construction stay visible, and lazy pipelines use adapters instead of the loop surface.
